codes.sample: 457 Chinese university students from six universities in northern, eastern and southwestern China, recruited by purposive sampling through an online cross-sectional survey; 49.7% female; mostly aged 18–25.
codes.ai_system: Generative AI tools in general (e.g., ChatGPT, Gemini, Copilot) used for academic work
codes.dependence_measures: AI Dependency Scale (ADS-R; Zhu et al., 2026), 15 items adapted from Young's Internet Addiction Test. It has two factors: Cognitive Integration and Habit (9 items) and Autonomy Erosion (6 items); α = 0.951. Only the total score is correlated (Table 5).
codes.possible_duplicate: The ADS-R comes from Zhu et al. (2026), and the Chinese learned helplessness scale is cited from Wu et al. (2026). Check whether either paper uses an overlapping sample of Chinese students.
codes.note: AI dependency is correlated (Pearson, Table 5) only with learned helplessness (r = 0.580), AI literacy (r = −0.216) and intrinsic motivation (r = −0.281). None of these are on the list of eligible correlates. A reviewer may want to consider whether learned helplessness could count under psychological distress; I did not count it. The supplementary material was not reviewed.

codes.sample: 33 students, Faculty of Education (Fakultas Ilmu Pendidikan), Universitas Negeri Medan, Indonesia; probability sampling; ex post facto correlational design.
codes.ai_system: Artificial Intelligence in general (AI tools for academic tasks); no specific system named.
codes.dependence_measures: Ad hoc 5-point Likert questionnaire 'Ketergantungan AI' (AI dependence) with three indicators: intensity of use, dependence in completing assignments, and instant use of AI (p. 3). The number of items and reliability are not reported.
codes.note: Only outcome: academic independence (kemandirian akademik: self-regulated learning, responsibility, time management, critical thinking), not an eligible correlate. Simple regression: R = 0,600, Beta = -0,600 (pp. 4, 6). Stats are internally inconsistent: F = 7,100 does not fit R² = 0,360 with n = 33, and t = -2,665 does not fit p = 0,004. Use with caution.

codes.sample: 635 students at Nueva Ecija University of Science and Technology – Gabaldon campus, Philippines; online survey via Google Forms (1235 invited), May–July 2023.
codes.ai_system: AI tools in higher education in general (e.g., ChatGPT, Google Bard, PhotoMath, Grammarly, Quillbot)
codes.dependence_measures: AI Dependency subscale of a newly developed 48-item 'Impact of AI in Higher Education' instrument. Initially 10 items (AID1–AID10), 8 retained after EFA/CFA/Rasch, alpha = .86. Items include 'I heavily rely on AI tools to support my study-related activities.' Most items are about perceived benefit (e.g., 'AI has increased my efficiency...').
codes.possible_duplicate: Scale-development paper (Capinding, 2024). Later substantive papers by the same author that use this instrument may draw on the same or an overlapping NEUST Gabaldon sample.
codes.note: Other constructs are perceived AI impact on learning experience, academic performance, career guidance, motivation, self-reliance and social interaction. None is an eligible correlate ('self-reliance' is AI's perceived effect on autonomy, not self-efficacy). No inter-construct correlations are reported. AID validity as a dependence measure is doubtful: most items describe positive impact.

codes.sample: 108 vocational high-school (SMK) Office Management students at SMK IPIEMS Surabaya, Indonesia, aged 15–18, who use AI for learning. Purposive sampling from a population of 150. Note: Table 2 demographic counts add up to 110 (28 male + 82 female).
codes.ai_system: AI in general for learning (ChatGPT, Gemini, Meta AI)
codes.dependence_measures: AI Dependence: a 5-item Likert 1–5 scale (AID1–AID5) "dari Hasin et al. (2014)", which refers to adapted DSM-5 substance use disorder criteria. Cronbach's alpha = 0.895. Analysed as a latent construct in PLS-SEM.
codes.possible_duplicate: None found. The design is similar to Zhang et al. (2024) and Acosta-Enriquez et al. (2025), but the sample is different.
codes.note: Correlates measured: academic self-efficacy, academic stress. Only reported: PLS paths (SE->AID -0.231; AS->AID 0.458), HTMT (AID–AS 0.080, AID–SE 0.102), item cross-loadings. No Fornell–Larcker or latent correlation table. Back-deriving r from paths gives about 0.58 for SE, but this conflicts with near-zero HTMT/cross-loadings, so results are inconsistent.

codes.sample: 5764 Chinese university students (undergraduate and graduate) from 37 universities; age 16–38 (M = 20.87, SD = 2.44); 70.80% female; convenience/snowball sampling, fall 2024, cross-sectional.
codes.ai_system: AI / "general AI" tools in general (e.g., conversational AI, generative AI) used by college students
codes.dependence_measures: Chinese AI Dependence Scale adapted by Huang et al. (2024) from the revised Smartphone Addiction Scale; 5 items (e.g., "I have tried to reduce the amount of time I spend on AI but failed"), 4-point Likert, total score; omega = 0.889.

correlations.correlate: Escape motivation for AI use (escapism motive)
correlations.correlate_instrument: AI Use Motivation Scale (Huang et al., 2024), escape subscale, 3 items

codes.possible_duplicate: Same group as Huang et al. (2024), who developed the dependence and motivation scales. This sample (n = 5764, fall 2024) looks separate; check for other papers using this Zhengzhou dataset (IRB 2023ZZUEDU0808).
codes.note: Only possible correlate: escape motivation for AI use ("avoid or retreat from real-life difficulties and stressors"), counted as an escapism motive. It is AI-specific, so the reviewer should confirm it fits; if not, the decision becomes no_eligible_correlate. The other motives, AI literacy and creativity are not eligible. None of the seven primary correlates was measured.

codes.sample: 650 undergraduate health professions students (medicine, nursing, dentistry, pharmacy, physiotherapy), aged 18–25 (M = 21.35), 65.8% female, one health sciences university in Türkiye, convenience sample, Jan–Mar 2026.
codes.ai_system: AI tools in general, used for academic purposes (generative AI)
codes.dependence_measures: None. The only AI measure is the AI Use Scale (AIUS; Yilmaz, 2026): 8 items, rated 1 = never to 5 = always, on how often students use AI for academic tasks. The authors say: "higher scores should not be interpreted as indicating AI dependency or psychological reliance."
codes.possible_duplicate: The AIUS was developed and validated in this same sample (Yilmaz, 2026). Yilmaz and Serin (2026) may be a related publication.
codes.note: The exposure measures only how often and how intensively students use AI, not dependence; the authors stress this repeatedly. For reference, Table 1 gives AIUS r = 0.39 with academic and clinical learning loneliness (a context-specific scale), r = 0.34 with learned helplessness, and r = −0.22 with academic wellbeing (n = 650).

codes.sample: 1,869 undergraduate and postgraduate students (860 male, 1,009 female; aged 18+) from three higher education institutions in Changde, Hunan, China, who had used generative AI for learning in the past month; cross-sectional online survey, March 2026.
codes.ai_system: Generative AI tools in general, with each student answering about the tool they used most for learning in the past month
codes.dependence_measures: Chinese version of the Generative AI Dependency Scale (Goh et al., 2025): 11 items on a 5-point scale, with three dimensions (cognitive distress, negative consequences, withdrawal reactions). Only the total mean score (GAID) was correlated with other variables.

correlations.correlate_instrument: Academic Procrastination Scale-Short Form (Yockey, 2016), Chinese version, 5 items
correlations.quote: GAID was negatively correlated with MSR (r = −0.273, p < 0.001) and positively correlated with AP (r = 0.338, p < 0.001)

codes.possible_duplicate: None identified.
codes.note: The only eligible correlate is academic procrastination (Table 2). Perceived usefulness (a TAM construct) and metacognitive self-regulation (MSLQ) are not eligible. Reviewer to decide whether MSR counts as self-control (GAID–MSR r = −0.273). No subscale correlations are given. The PROCESS betas include covariates, so they are not zero-order.

codes.sample: No empirical sample. This is an essay or opinion article by a student and a supervisor, published in an Uzbek journal. It includes one anecdote about a 17-year-old girl.
codes.ai_system: ChatGPT / AI in general (chatbots, Siri, Alexa, Google Assistant mentioned)
codes.dependence_measures: None. Dependence on AI is discussed in prose only. No quantitative measure is used.
codes.note: The full text was retrieved (4 pages). It is an opinion article with no methods, data or statistics. It has only anecdotes and references to other studies (e.g., 'According to a study conducted in Switzerland...'). The Annotation says it 'discusses the consequences of dependence on artificial intelligence.'

codes.sample: N = 131 adults with prior AI chatbot experience, recruited via social media (Instagram, Reddit), university boards and online research platforms; M age = 27.2 (SD = 7.4, range 18–55); 55.7% female, 42.0% male, 2.3% gender-diverse; 59% students; Germany-based author (IU Erfurt). Cross-sectional online survey.
codes.ai_system: AI-based interaction systems / AI chatbots and AI assistants in general (unspecified)
codes.dependence_measures: AI Emotional Dependence Scale (AEDS): 10-item self-report, 5-point Likert, measuring the need for and reliance on AI systems for emotional coping and support (e.g., "I feel I need my AI assistant to cope with difficult emotions"); α = .92, ω = .93; M = 3.36, SD = 0.80. Origin and validation not cited (appears ad hoc).

correlations.quote: Neuroticism showed the strongest positive correlation (r = .58, p < .001)
Openness showed the weakest bivariate corre-lation, which was nevertheless significant (r = -.18, p = .038)
agreeableness (r = -.28, p < .01) were all negatively correlated with AI emotional dependence

codes.possible_duplicate: None identified.
codes.note: Loneliness was measured, but there is no zero-order loneliness–AEDS r, only the b-path controlling for neuroticism (β=.55), so it is left out. Integrity flags: alphas .78–.86 for 2-item BFI scales are implausible; no loneliness M/SD; c'+indirect (.64) ≠ r(N,AEDS)=.58; AEDS has no source; "Dr. Dr." single author.

codes.sample: 1063 responses, 1045 valid, 986 AI chatbot users; medical students at public and private institutions across Pakistan, July–August 2025; mean age 21.7 ± 2.1; 53.5% male.
codes.ai_system: AI chatbots in general
codes.dependence_measures: Ad hoc questionnaire sections: 'emotional and psychological dependence' and 'relationship-style dependency', plus an overall dependence score. Scores were grouped as low, moderate or high using mean ± SD thresholds.
codes.possible_duplicate: This is a conference abstract (2025 IJMS World Conference of Medical Student Research, Suppl 1, S186). A full article on the same sample may be published later. Check for one.
codes.note: Correlates measured: satisfaction with the chatbot (not life satisfaction), emotional expression, psychological help-seeking, academic performance, region. None is eligible. 'Mental well-being' appears only in the conclusion, not as a measure. Spearman intercorrelations are mentioned but no r values are given. If a full paper appears, check it for stress or well-being.

codes.sample: Chinese adults aged 21-40 recruited via Credamo. Experiment 1 (autonomous driving scenario): n=125 valid; it did not measure AI dependence. Experiment 2 (laptop purchase scenario with an AI shopping assistant): n=269 (83 human-dominant, 93 collaborative, 93 AI-dominant).
codes.ai_system: Hypothetical AI decision systems in vignettes: autonomous driving AI (Exp 1) and an e-commerce recommendation/decision aid for buying a laptop (Exp 2)
codes.dependence_measures: State 'AI dependence' scale, adapted, Likert, alpha=0.874 (Exp 2). The items are only in the Supplementary Appendix. The authors define it explicitly as 'functional dependence on AI within task settings, as opposed to compulsive usage, technological addiction, or loss of behavioral control.'
codes.note: E3: 'dependence' here means functional task reliance after a vignette, not addiction or problematic use, and the AI is a driving or shopping system, not a conversational one. E4 also applies: eudaimonic well-being was measured, but its only link to AI dependence is a multivariable b=0.155 (with autonomy and condition dummies). No correlation matrix is given.

codes.sample: 412 undergraduate business students from 3 universities in Oman (1 public, 2 private); cross-sectional survey, Feb–Jun 2025; 54.4% female; mostly aged 18–25.
codes.ai_system: Generative AI tools in general (ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, Microsoft Copilot) used for academic tasks
codes.dependence_measures: GenAI dependence (AID): 5 reflective items on a 7-point Likert scale, adapted from validated instruments (cites Morales-García et al., 2024, the dependence on AI scale). Covers habitual reliance, difficulty doing tasks without AI, limited checking of AI outputs, discomfort without access, and a feeling of weaker independent thinking. α = 0.892, CR = 0.920, AVE = 0.698.
codes.possible_duplicate: None found.
codes.note: The only constructs measured besides AID are GenAI use, critical-thinking disposition and self-perceived employability; none is an eligible correlate. The Fornell–Larcker table (Table 4, p. 7) gives latent r AID–CT −0.311 and AID–ES −0.361, but these outcomes are not on the eligible list. No depression, anxiety, stress, self-efficacy or other eligible variable was measured.

codes.sample: No sample; no empirical data collected.
codes.ai_system: AI chatbots in general (mentions Gemini, Claude, Microsoft Copilot); discussion of model updates
codes.dependence_measures: None. The essay criticises the concept/label of "AI addiction" but uses no quantitative dependence measure.
codes.possible_duplicate: The text says it was also published on Medium (@crimsoncherry); no overlapping empirical sample.
codes.note: This is an opinion/theory essay ("This is— social theory.", p.1) that argues the "AI addiction" label is structural violence. It has no methods, no participants, no measures and no statistics, so it is excluded as E5_design (theoretical/commentary paper).

codes.sample: 1,622 Chinese junior high school students (grades 7–9) from 4 areas, aged 10–19 (M = 14.64, SD = 1.65); 49.14% boys; multistage stratified sampling; paper survey in November 2025.
codes.ai_system: Large language models (LLMs) in general, with no specific commercial platform
codes.dependence_measures: An adapted 5-item LLM emotional dependence measure (items from Sirvent-Ruiz et al.'s Affective Dependence Scale and Nomura & Kanda's Rapport–Expectation with a Robot Scale, rewritten for LLMs). Rated 1–5, total 5–25, α = .948. EFA and CFA support one factor (CR = 0.949, AVE = 0.788).

correlations.exposure: LLM emotional dependence (5-item adapted measure, total)
correlations.quote: Anxiety symptoms were positively correlated with emotional dependence on LLMs (r=0.146, P<0.001)

codes.possible_duplicate: None identified.
codes.note: Only anxiety is an eligible correlate. Narcissism (FFNI-SF total) and physical activity (PARS-3) are not on the list: r = 0.301 and −0.075 with dependence. The measure is an ad hoc emotional-dependence scale adapted partly from a human–robot rapport scale, but its target is LLMs. Table 2 also gives M/SD (dependence 12.27/6.24; anxiety 1.96/1.74).

codes.sample: Secondary analysis of four public datasets: global ChatGPT student survey (Ravšelj et al., 2025; N=23,218, 110 countries) and three regional student datasets: Bangladesh (Islam et al., 2026; N=1,104), Colombia (Correa, 2026; N=357) and Ecuador (Acosta-Vargas, 2026; N=540).
codes.ai_system: ChatGPT / generative AI tools
codes.dependence_measures: Regional datasets only, reported as % endorsing single items: Bangladesh nine-item AI dependency battery (two items reported: critical thinking weakened by AI reliance; submitted work without understanding); Colombia 'perceives self as AI dependent' (37.3%); Ecuador UTAUT-adapted items incl. 'addicted to ChatGPT' (5.6%). No dependence measure in the global dataset.
codes.possible_duplicate: Reanalyses publicly archived datasets: Ravšelj et al. (2025, PLOS ONE), Islam et al. (2026), Correa (2026) and Acosta-Vargas (2026), all on Mendeley Data. The original datasets could have eligible variables, but this report does not analyse them.
codes.note: Dependence indicators are given only as descriptive percentages (Table 5, p. 8). No eligible psychological correlate (depression, anxiety, stress, etc.) is measured alongside them, and no correlations are computed; the only tests are chi-square/Cramér's V for region. Global-dataset 'ethical concern' items are opinions about AI risk, not AI anxiety, and are not linked to dependence.

codes.sample: 353 Chinese employees recruited via Credamo, three-wave survey (T1: 500 invited, 400 valid; T2: 372; T3: 353). 48.73% male; 58.36% aged 31–40; 85.84% held a bachelor's degree or higher.
codes.ai_system: AI in general at work ("AI tools", AI-assisted decision support); no specific chatbot or LLM is named
codes.dependence_measures: Dependence on AI Usage (DAU): a 3-item scale from Tang et al. (2023), 5-point Likert, α = 0.828. Example item: "I rely on AI to handle or assist with work-related activities". It measures reliance and dependence, though the items look close to usage reliance.
codes.note: Only candidate correlate: AI Awareness (Brougham & Haar; job-replacement worry). It may count as AI-related anxiety; reviewer to judge. The AIA–DAU r would be in Table 3, missing from the text; the text reports no AIA–DAU r. POQ, RAU, EAC, IP and EP are not eligible. If AIA is not accepted, decision = not_eligible / no_eligible_correlate.

codes.sample: 917 Prolific crowdworkers from the US and UK (1,026 recruited), randomised in a 2×3 between-subjects experiment (video length × no AI / helpful AI / deceiving AI); 8,253 information-seeking tasks.
codes.ai_system: Gemini-3-flash LLM chat assistant with access to YouTube video content (helpful and deceiving versions)
codes.dependence_measures: None. "Over-reliance" is measured only as behaviour in the experiment: answer accuracy when the deceiving AI gave false answers, and action sequences (asking the AI vs watching the video). The surveys contain single items on AI usage frequency, trust in AI, and AI-vs-search and AI-task preference, but no items on dependence or addiction.
codes.note: Over-reliance is measured only as behaviour in an experimental task, which is explicitly excluded under E1. None of the eligible psychological correlates were measured either: the surveys cover only demographics, social media time, AI use, trust and topic knowledge.

codes.sample: 345 Chinese university design majors (undergraduate 280, graduate 65; 60.87% female; aged 18–25). Recruited by snowball sampling through an online survey on SoJump.
codes.ai_system: AI-assisted design tools / generative AI (AIGC) used in design education
codes.dependence_measures: AI Dependence (DEP): 4 items adapted from Morales-García et al. (2024) Dependence on AI scale, rated on a 5-point Likert scale (CA = 0.864, CR = 0.921, AVE = 0.700).

correlations.correlate_instrument: Big Five items adapted from Laouiti et al. (2022), 4 items
Big Five items adapted from Laouiti et al. (2022), 4 items
Big Five items adapted from Laouiti et al. (2022), 4 items
Big Five items adapted from Laouiti et al. (2022), 4 items
Big Five items adapted from Laouiti et al. (2022), 4 items

codes.possible_duplicate: None identified.
codes.note: These are PLS-SEM construct correlations taken from the Fornell–Larcker table; they are not item-level Pearson r. None of the seven primary correlates was measured; the only eligible correlates are the Big Five. Some figures look off: AGR CR = 1.062 is impossible, and the DEP diagonal of 0.812 does not equal √0.700 = 0.837. All item labels are printed as 'EXT1', 'AGR1', etc.

codes.sample: Chinese college students; the corrected Table 1 (EFA) note gives N = 547. No other sample details are in this correction notice.
codes.ai_system: Conversational AI (general)
codes.dependence_measures: Conversational AI Dependence Scale (CAIDS): 20 items in 4 dimensions (Negative impacts, Mood modification, Withdrawal symptoms, Uncontrollability). Only the corrected EFA loadings table is given.
codes.possible_duplicate: This is a correction notice for the original article 'Development and validation of the conversational AI dependence scale for Chinese college students' (Frontiers in Psychology, 2025). Any correlates belong to that original article, which should be screened on its own.
codes.note: An erratum/correction notice: it only fixes the order of the Table 1 column headers (factor loadings). No correlates and no association data are reported, so the record is excluded as a correction notice (similar to E5_design). Screen the original CAIDS validation article separately for possible correlates (e.g., validity correlations).

codes.sample: 70 college students in India, surveyed with a Google Form (p. 3: "information was gathered from 70 college students using a structured survey instrument administered via Google Forms").
codes.ai_system: AI tools / AI chatbots in general, used for academic tasks and for personal or emotional problems
codes.dependence_measures: No AI dependence scale. Closed-ended single items reported only as percentages: turning to AI instead of peers or teachers (70%); AI summarising PDFs (61.4%); skills declined "due to over-reliance on these tools" (77.1%); prefer AI for private problems (31.4%). The items in the 1–5 rating section are not in the text.
codes.note: Descriptive conference paper (ICOGE 2026) reporting only percentages. AI items cover use frequency or perceived harm to skills, not dependence, addiction or inability to stop. No eligible correlate was measured and no correlations are reported. If the over-reliance item is counted as a dependence measure, the reason should be no_eligible_correlate.

codes.sample: Adults recruited via Prolific, mostly from Western countries. N = 491 in the main (CFA/path) phase: 52% men, Mage = 43.92, SD 11.46, ages 28–83. A separate EFA phase had N = 360.
codes.ai_system: Generative AI in general (e.g., ChatGPT, Gemini)
codes.dependence_measures: Problematic Generative AI Use Scale (PGAIUS): adapted from Hu et al. (2023)'s problematic conversational AI use scale, with "CAI" replaced by "GAI". It has 6 items on a 5-point scale, averaged into one score (α = 0.84). Example item: "I felt an urge to use GAI more and more."
codes.note: Valid dependence measure (PGAIUS) and a Pearson table (Table 2), but PGAIUS is only correlated with ineligible variables: unethical GAI use, moral disengagement, Dark Triad (narcissism .33, Machiavellianism .14, psychopathy .06), gender, age, daily time. No Big Five, impulsivity, anxiety or depression measured.

codes.sample: 426 valid online questionnaire responses from generative AI users in China (Wenjuanxing, recruited via social media); 65.3% female, 81.7% aged 25 or under, 72.1% undergraduates.
codes.ai_system: Generative AI / AI tools in general (e.g., ChatGPT)
codes.dependence_measures: AI dependence: 4 items adapted from Huang et al. (2024), 7-point Likert scale (e.g., "I spend way too much time using AI"; "When I cannot use AI, I feel anxious and uneasy"; "I tried to reduce my AI usage time, but it didn't work out"). CR 0.865, α 0.843, AVE 0.566.

correlations.correlate_instrument: AI anxiety items adapted from Wang and Wang (2022), 8 items
correlations.location: Table 3 (Reliability and validity of the measurement)
correlations.quote: AID | 0.293 | 0.318 | 0.355 | 0.364 | 0.348 | 0.341 — text: 'Discriminant validity was tested using the heterotrait-monotrait ratio (HTMT)... all HTMT values... well below this threshold'

codes.note: Only eligible correlate: AI anxiety. Table 3 is a lower-triangle matrix with no √AVE diagonal, and the text says HTMT was used, so the values look like HTMT ratios. The rest is SmartPLS paths and a moderation. No zero-order r. Reviewer should check Table 3: if these are latent correlations, AID–AIA = 0.348 would make the report eligible.

codes.sample: 80 Computer Studies students and 10 faculty members at Saint Francis College Guihulngan, Negros Oriental, Philippines, selected by purposive sampling (p. 2–3).
codes.ai_system: AI tools in general (ChatGPT, grammar applications, content generators) used for academic tasks
codes.dependence_measures: No AI dependence scale is reported. The authors wrote their own needs-assessment questionnaire about portal features, student difficulties and feelings about AI. They analysed it by "tallying and averaging" and by reading the open-ended answers for common themes (p. 3). Results are given only as narrative themes, e.g. "frequent reliance reduced their initiative" (p. 4).
codes.note: This is a system-development paper (a web portal built with the Prototype Model) with a descriptive needs assessment. The results are qualitative themes only. There is no quantitative dependence measure, no eligible correlate (e.g., depression, anxiety, stress, loneliness, self-esteem, procrastination) and no correlational statistics. E1_no_dependence_measure would also apply.

codes.sample: 50 undergraduate practical (popular) music majors at Korean universities, convenience sample, online survey. Gender is given as 24 M / 26 F in Table 9 but as 25/25 in section 4.1, and generative AI experience as 37 vs 34, so the reported counts are inconsistent.
codes.ai_system: Generative AI music-production tools (Suno AI, Soundraw, AIVA, BandLab SongStarter; ChatGPT-based music systems mentioned)
codes.dependence_measures: AI Dependency Perception (AI 의존 인식): ad hoc 5-item, 5-point Likert scale, α=.801, adapted from Atkinson & Barker (2023) and Peng et al. (2026). Example items: "음악 제작 시 생성형 AI에 의존하는 편이다." and "AI의 도움 없이 음악을 만드는 것이 어렵다고 느낀다." It also covers perceived change in creative ability and perceived AI replaceability.

correlations.correlate_instrument: Ad hoc 5-item creative self-efficacy scale based on Bandura (1997) and Peng et al. (2026), α=.884
correlations.quote: AI 의존 인식 ... 창작 자기효능감과의 상관관계(r=-.204)는 통계적으로 유의하지 않은 것으로 확인되었다(p>.05)

codes.possible_duplicate: None identified.
codes.note: Valid dependence measure and zero-order matrix (Table 16). Only candidate correlate is music-creation self-efficacy (domain-specific); reviewer must decide if it counts as general/academic self-efficacy. If not: not_eligible, no_eligible_correlate. Data concerns: inconsistent sample counts; r=.611 given p<.05; abstract in future tense.

codes.sample: 850 undergraduate and postgraduate students with GenAI experience from 14 Chinese universities (Guangdong, Shandong, Sichuan, Guizhou, Heilongjiang); online survey (Wenjuanxing), Nov–Dec 2025; 47.4% male.
codes.ai_system: Generative AI (GenAI) tools used for learning in general
codes.dependence_measures: AI dependency (AD): latent construct, 5-point Likert, CR = 0.809, AVE = 0.520. Defined as "an over-reliant, maladaptive state in academic tasks" and adapted from Bozoglan et al. 2014 and Zhang et al. 2024 (AI dependency). The item wording is only in Supplementary Table S1, which is not in the retrieved text.

correlations.correlate: AI anxiety (AI usage anxiety: apprehension about AI complexity, reliability, privacy risks)
correlations.correlate_instrument: AI anxiety scale (AA), adapted items, 5-point Likert; CR = 0.880
correlations.location: Page 24, Table 4 Latent Construct Correlation Matrix
correlations.quote: AA row: .007 (AL), .654 (AS), .062 (AD); Note. Values represent standardized latent correlations estimated from the measurement model (N = 850).

Check: the authors say the instrument "primarily captures the frequency and intensity of AI reliance" (possible E1 concern). AI anxiety is counted as an AI-related anxiety correlate. Sense of gain and AI usage shame are not eligible correlates.

codes.note: Anxiety scale is about AI but also covers general symptoms; code as anxiety or AI-related anxiety. Check: QoL (higher = better) correlates positively with anxiety (.343) and with Ai-Dep, suggesting a scoring or sign problem. Mapping digital stress to stress and SAA to social anxiety is a judgement call. Network edges are partial correlations, so they were not used.

codes.sample: 25 university-level ESL learners purposively selected from higher-education institutions in Pakistan; semi-structured interviews (p. 8).
codes.ai_system: Generative AI (e.g., ChatGPT) for English language learning
codes.dependence_measures: None quantitative. Dependence was explored only qualitatively through semi-structured interviews and reflexive thematic analysis, using codes such as 'Answer substitution', 'Habitual use' and 'Automatic acceptance' (Table 1, pp. 9-11).
codes.note: Qualitative multiple-case study: 'This study employs a qualitative multiple-case study design... rather than with measuring the effectiveness of AI through numerical outcomes' (p. 7). There is no quantitative dependence scale and no psychological correlates. The keywords (Stress, Work-Life Balance, Paramedics) do not match the content and look like a template error.

codes.sample: 395 healthcare professional students (medical, paramedical, allied health) in India, aged 18–35 (M = 25.25, SD = 5.361); 236 male, 159 female; online Google Form survey; cross-sectional.
codes.ai_system: AI tools in general (e.g., ChatGPT), used for academic and clinical purposes
codes.dependence_measures: AI-Health Professionals & Students Dependency Index (7 items, score range 0–21; categories Mild 15–21, Moderate 8–14, Complete 0–7; ref 16, Yogeshwar et al. 2025). Note: the items ask mostly about AI use and preference for clinical/study tasks rather than addiction-type symptoms.
codes.possible_duplicate: The dependence index comes from the authors' own scale-development paper: Yogeshwar D et al., 2025, Bulletin of Faculty of Physical Therapy 30(1):64. That paper may report data from an overlapping sample, but this is not confirmed.
codes.note: The only correlates were academic performance (Academic Performance Scale) and critical thinking (Critical Thinking Evaluation Scale), and neither is on the eligible list. Table 4 gives only p-values (no r values), and the cross-tabulations are inconsistent. Discussion: "stress and anxiety... were not specifically assessed in the current study."

codes.sample: 65 secondary and university teachers in Ecuador (convenience sample), reporting their perceptions of students' AI use; no students were surveyed directly.
codes.ai_system: AI tools in general / generative AI used by students for academic tasks
codes.dependence_measures: No individual-level dependence scale. Teachers answered ad hoc closed questions about how dependent their students are on AI in general (e.g., Table 4: "Totalmente dependiente de IA" 56.9%, "No dependiente de IA" 7.7%) and rated perceived negative effects (Table 5 means/SDs).
codes.note: The dependence items are teachers' aggregate views of students, not a per-student score. No eligible correlate was measured: outcomes are critical skills, problem solving, autonomous learning, research skills and academic performance. Only frequencies, means/SDs and an ANOVA by discipline (F=5.12). If the teacher items counted as a measure, exclude as no_eligible_correlate.

codes.sample: 1,553 ChatGPT users in China (49.5% male), recruited online through SoJump/wjx.cn in August 2023 using convenience and snowball sampling. Ages ranged from under 18 to 66+; 17.4% were full-time students. Cross-sectional SEM study.
codes.ai_system: ChatGPT (chatbot)
codes.dependence_measures: A 5-item Media dependency scale adapted from Chan-Olmsted & Xiao (alpha = 0.914). Items include 'I usually interact with ChatGPT', 'I would seek help from ChatGPT' and 'I'll spend time on ChatGPT'. The scale is labelled as reliance on ChatGPT, but the items mostly capture how much people use it and intend to use it.
codes.note: Measured: social/task attraction, competence, warmth, para-social interaction, emotional support from ChatGPT (not general social support), usage intention, media dependency. None is an eligible correlate. Only SEM paths, mediation estimates and example Fornell–Larcker correlations are reported. E1 is a possible alternative, since the dependency items mostly measure use.

codes.sample: 284 Indonesian EFL graduate students (48.6% doctoral, 51.4% master's; 69% female) from five universities in Indonesia, recruited by purposive sampling; they had used ChatGPT for at least 1 month.
codes.ai_system: ChatGPT
codes.dependence_measures: None. The AI measure is the 'ChatGPT Usage' scale (UGPT), adapted from Nemt-allah et al. (2024). Its items cover using ChatGPT as a writing aid, for academic tasks, and reliance/trust (e.g., 'I use ChatGPT to generate ideas for my academic writing'). The authors call it an 'AI-mediated support practice'. It measures usage, not dependence or addiction.
codes.note: The title says 'dependence', but the scale measures usage/support. Outcomes are self-rated academic reading, writing and research skill. Research skill uses research self-efficacy items (Hemmings & Kay), which might count as academic self-efficacy. Only HTMT and PLS paths are reported: UGPT->RS β = -0.156 (single predictor; HTMT 0.161). No correlation matrix.

codes.sample: 226 undergraduate students (out of 300 approached) from rural (n=88) and urban (n=138) areas, India; 150 female, 75 male, 1 other; ages 8–27 as printed (mostly 18–20); Google Forms survey.
codes.ai_system: AI tools in general (ChatGPT 88.5%, Google Gemini, Microsoft Copilot, Grammarly, QuillBot, Canva, other)
codes.dependence_measures: Ad hoc 5-point Likert AI dependency items (Table 9, e.g., "I rely on AI tools to complete my academic tasks", "I cant imagine my Academic Work without AI") and behavioural dependency items (Table 14, e.g., "I feel anxious when I cannot access AI tools"). Only item-level descriptives; no total score.
codes.note: The study has a dependence exposure but none of the eligible correlates. Other variables: gender, locality, awareness, AI use frequency, perceived loss of critical thinking/creativity, usefulness. The only correlations are gender/locality with use frequency (Tables 8, 20). "I feel anxious when I cannot access AI tools" is a dependence item, not an anxiety measure.

codes.sample: Young adults aged 18–27 in Chandigarh, India. They were recruited through a Google Form, which the paper calls simple random sampling. The Methods section says n = 55, but Tables 1 and 2 give N = 56.
codes.ai_system: AI in general (ChatGPT and DeepSeek are named in the keywords)
codes.dependence_measures: Dependence on Artificial Intelligence scale (DAI; Morales-García et al., 2024), 5 items on a Likert scale. Only the total score was used.

correlations.correlate_instrument: Impulsive Behavior Short Scale (IBS-8; Groskurth et al., 2022), Urgency subscale

codes.possible_duplicate: None found.
codes.note: Methods gives N = 55, tables give N = 56. The Discussion misprints the urgency r as "0.0302"; Table 2 gives 0.302*. Only the 4 IBS-8 subscales are reported, no impulsivity total. The first value in the AI Dependence row (-0.044) is with Reflective Thinking and was not extracted. Critical thinking is not an eligible correlate.

codes.sample: 97 university students at the University of Malta
codes.ai_system: Generative AI tools in general, used for AI-assisted learning tasks
codes.dependence_measures: "AI dependence (DEP)" was a construct in a PLS-SEM model. The retrieved text does not describe the items or the source of the scale.
codes.possible_duplicate: None identified
codes.note: Only a short abstract was retrieved. It reports PLS-SEM paths only (e.g., DEP → CIT β = 0.085), which are not zero-order. The full paper may have a Fornell–Larcker table. The only possible correlate is creative IT self-efficacy, which is domain-specific and may not count as general/academic self-efficacy. Reviewer should check the full text.

codes.sample: 84 technical university students (approx. 90% undergraduates, 60% male), National University of Science and Technology Politehnica of Bucharest, Romania; convenience sample, March 2024.
codes.ai_system: ChatGPT
codes.dependence_measures: None explicit. Ad hoc 38-item Likert questionnaire factor-analysed into 6 usage factors. F6 is called 'Learning Gains and Dependence' once in the H3 results, but its items (I12 'Ask to explain in detail if unsure', I2 'Helpful for understanding concepts') are verification items, not dependence items.
codes.note: No dependence/addiction/over-reliance scale; F6 is labelled 'Verification behavior' in Tables 3-5 and 'Learning Gains and Dependence (F6)' only once in the H3 results. In any case, none of the eligible psychological correlates was measured; the factors are only correlated with each other (Table 5). Supplementary material/OSF data were not checked.

codes.sample: N = 242 Ukrainian university students who were active AI users (71.5% female; age 18–30, M = 19.5, SD = 1.4). Online anonymous survey. Some analyses use N = 234 after missing values were excluded.
codes.ai_system: Generative AI tools in general (ChatGPT 85.5%, Gemini 69.4%, Copilot 15.3%, Claude 9.1%)
codes.dependence_measures: Authors' AI-Addiction Scale, initial AIAS-11 v3.0: 11 items, 5-point Likert. Total = General Dependence Index (ЗІЗ). Subscales: Factor A (artificial intimacy), B (cognitive atrophy), V (loss of control). Revised into AIAS-10+1 v4.0 (F1 socio-emotional, F2 behavioural-cognitive). Also one single item: 'Do you have an AI dependence?'

The logistic OR (1.521) and the regression/mediation coefficients are adjusted or unstandardised and were excluded. The Discussion is inconsistent on which factor 0.237 belongs to.

codes.sample: 100 college students aged 17–25 (38 male, 62 female; mean age 20.6), purposive sample of regular users of AI tools (ChatGPT, Perplexity, Gemini, Meta AI); cross-sectional; India (Rathinam College, Coimbatore).
codes.ai_system: AI tools in general (ChatGPT, Gemini, Perplexity, Meta AI)
codes.dependence_measures: Dependence on Artificial Intelligence Scale (DAIS; Morales-García et al., 2024), α = 0.87; total score only (M male 16.24, female 14.52).

correlations.correlate_instrument: Digital Well-Being Scale (Gomes et al., 2023), α = 0.921
correlations.quote: Table 3 Correlation Between AI Dependence and Digital Well-Being (N = 100) ... Digital Well-Being –0.725

codes.possible_duplicate: None identified.
codes.note: Check 1: the correlate is "digital well-being" (healthy tech use), not general well-being, so it may not qualify. Check 2: r is inconsistent. Table 3 and the abstract give -0.725/-0.72, but the results text says "r = –0.32 ... moderate". I used the table value. Low-quality paper; no other eligible correlates.

codes.sample: N = 565 pre-service teachers (education majors in teacher-preparation programmes) in China, mostly in Shandong; 76.8% female; 60.5% first-year. All were GenAI users. Convenience/snowball sampling via WeChat. There was also a separate validation sample (N = 144), but no correlations are reported for it. Five people were interviewed.
codes.ai_system: Generative AI tools in general (ChatGPT, DeepSeek, Doubao, etc.)
codes.dependence_measures: Behavioural GenAI dependency (DEP): 4 items written for this study, on a 7-point Likert scale. The items cover over-reliance, e.g. 'AI has become an indispensable part of my learning' and 'After a while without AI, I feel unaccustomed'. α = 0.91, CR = 0.91, AVE = 0.71; M = 3.89, SD = 1.46.

correlations.quote: Table 4: DEP row, IMP column = 0.58; 'r = 0.58 for dependency with impulsivity'

correlations.correlate: AI anxiety / fear of missing out
correlations.quote: Table 4: DEP row, ANX column = 0.49; Table 1: AI anxiety/FOMO | 0.15 | 0.005 ** | 0.49

codes.possible_duplicate: None identified.
codes.note: Not stated whether Table 4 r's are observed or latent; coded as Pearson. ANX is one combined AI anxiety/FOMO construct; its items are in Appendix A, which was not in the text. Impulsivity is a 2-item ad hoc scale. Trust, attachment, AI literacy and norms are not eligible correlates. Do not use the SEM betas.

codes.sample: 617 business and management university students (323 male, 294 female; undergraduate and graduate) at public and private universities in southern Punjab, Pakistan. 1,100 questionnaires were distributed and 678 returned.
codes.ai_system: ChatGPT (academic use)
codes.dependence_measures: Excessive Use of ChatGPT (EUGPT), a Likert scale (alpha 0.828, CR 0.917, AVE 0.639) described as adapted from established scales. Items are not reported. Excessive use is defined as "extended and obsessive usage of technology that disturbs the routine activities, personal relations, and overall welfare" (Turel & Ferguson, 2020).
codes.note: Social isolation/"social loneliness" (loneliness-type) was measured. Results are only PLS-SEM path and indirect effects (Tables 7–8). There is no correlation matrix, Fornell–Larcker table or single-predictor beta, and SI has no direct path to EUGPT. Possible alternative reason: E1, because the EUGPT items are not shown, so it is unclear whether they measure dependence.

codes.sample: 328 college students in China, recruited online through convenience and snowball sampling; cross-sectional questionnaire.
codes.ai_system: Conversational / anthropomorphic AI used for social compensation (general AI chatbots and companions)
codes.dependence_measures: 'AI social compensation', measured with the AI Attachment Scale (Kasturiratna & Hartanto, 2026; 15 items, 5-point Likert), scored as a Likert mean. The authors describe it as 'overreliance on AI for social compensation', but the scale measures attachment to AI, not dependence or addiction as such.

correlations.quote: AI social compensation was significantly positively correlated with loneliness (r = 0.353, p <.001)

codes.note: The open question is I1. The exposure is the AI Attachment Scale, relabelled 'AI social compensation' and framed as over-reliance on AI. It measures attachment, not dependence or addiction. If the reviewer counts AI attachment as emotional dependence, the study is eligible: Table 1 gives zero-order r values for loneliness and depression. Social presence is not an eligible correlate.

codes.sample: No participants. Narrative documentary review of 28 documents plus 12 classic texts (p. 10: "una selección final de n= 28 documentos que conforman el corpus de análisis principal, más 12 textos clásicos fundacionales").
codes.ai_system: Generative AI in general (ChatGPT, Gemini, Claude), discussed only in theory
codes.dependence_measures: None. The paper defines AI dependence conceptually and proposes three dimensions (p. 5), but administers no instrument.
codes.note: Methods, p. 8: "enfoque cualitativo, de tipo revisión documental y narrativa"; p. 9: "no se trabaja con población humana directa". It reports no original quantitative data. Some cited studies may be worth screening on their own (e.g., Lee et al., 2025, CAEAI 8:100352; Gerlich, 2025, Societies), but they are not on this review's eligible-correlate list.

codes.sample: 402 young Pakistanis aged 18–30 (58.2% female, mean age 22.7, SD 3.1). They were recruited from universities, community youth groups and online, and all knew of or had used AI mental health tools. Cross-sectional survey.
codes.ai_system: AI-based mental health tools: chatbots such as Woebot and Wysa, plus local mental health apps
codes.dependence_measures: Dependence on AI Mental Health Support Scale (DAI-MH): 10 items adapted from the Smartphone Addiction Scale (Kwon et al., 2013) for AI mental health tools (e.g., "I feel anxious if I can't use my mental health AI app"). Rated 1–5; α = .89. The paper calls it "unhealthy dependence".

correlations.quote: Unhealthy dependence was positively related with trait anxiety (r = .55, p < .001)

codes.possible_duplicate: None identified.
codes.note: Table 2 gives r = –.29 for dependence and digital self-efficacy. Left out: the scale measures confidence with digital health tools, not general or academic self-efficacy; reviewer may decide. Integrity concerns: data dated Jan–Apr 2026 but paper received 11 Feb 2026; df differ between text and Table 3; some references look implausible (e.g., a 10.1234 DOI).

codes.sample: 666 adults in China (aged 18+, mostly 18–35; 210 male, 283 female, 123 other, 50 undisclosed) who had used an AI companion app in the past month. Recruited through AI companion user communities on Weibo and Xiaohongshu; online survey via Wenjuanxing, Feb–Apr 2026.
codes.ai_system: AI companion / companion-oriented conversational AI (Maoxiang, Zhumengdao, Xingye, Replika, Character.AI, other)
codes.dependence_measures: Problematic Emotional Dependence (PED): 6-item ad hoc scale, 7-point Likert, adapted from addiction / problematic-use scales (Andreassen 2012; Yu 2024; Maral 2025). Covers failed cutting down, irritability or anxiety when unable to use, loss of control, emotional reliance, and putting the AI ahead of people. α = 0.913; single factor.

correlations.correlate_instrument: 6 adapted UCLA Loneliness Scale v3 / Three-Item Loneliness Scale items (LO4–LO6 reverse-scored)
correlations.quote: TABLE 8 Pearson correlations among core variables ... LO 0.188*** 0.338*** 0.194*** 1 (row LO, column PED)

codes.possible_duplicate: The first author (T. Liu) also published Liu et al. (2026), Front. Psychol. 16:1687686, on long-term use of AI virtual companion apps among Chinese users. That may be a related sample, but this study's data (Feb–Apr 2026, N = 666) look separate. Worth checking.
codes.note: Attachment anxiety (adapted ECR items) was measured, but its only link to PED is an HTMT value (0.205), so it is not usable. Loneliness's HTMT with PED was 0.209; use the Pearson r of 0.194. The text conflicts on scale length: the introduction says 'five-item outcome', but the Methods and Table 2 list 6 items. The Table 8 footnote calls it 'PD'. p < 0.001.

codes.sample: 405 full-time employees in China, recruited by convenience sampling on Credamo across three waves (Dec 2024–Feb 2025); 67.4% female; most aged 21–40.
codes.ai_system: AI tools in general used at work (generative AI / intelligent tools)
codes.dependence_measures: Dependence on AI (DAI): 3-item scale from Tang et al. (2023), 5-point Likert, α = 0.781. Example item: "I depend on artificial intelligence to process or assist in work-related activities."
codes.note: Besides DAI, the only measured variables are job complexity (Shaw & Gupta), cognitive flexibility (CFI), innovative behaviour (Scott & Bruce), and demographic controls. None of these is an eligible correlate. Table 2 (correlations) was not included in the retrieved text, but that does not matter because there is no eligible correlate in it.

codes.sample: 200 undergraduate students in Santa Rosa del Aguaray, Paraguay, who had used an AI chatbot in the previous 4 weeks. Mean age 23.7 ± 6.1 (range 18–55), 60.5% women, 50% medical/health sciences. Cross-sectional online survey, Oct–Dec 2025.

codes.dependence_measures: Spanish version of the Artificial Intelligence Chatbot Dependence Scale (AICDS): 8 items, unidimensional, 7-point Likert scale, total score (α = 0.833, ω = 0.903; M = 21.84 ± 10.6).

codes.note: Main effect sizes are the zero-order Pearson r values for continuous GAD-7 and PHQ-2. Regression betas (Table 4, Models 1/2) are covariate-adjusted, so not eligible. Group sizes are calculated from percentages (37.5% anxiety-positive, 42% depression-positive), not printed. The d signs reflect group coding. No page markers in the text, so section labels are used.

codes.sample: 458 ND/HND students at the School of Health Technology, Akure, Nigeria (46.7% male, mean age about 21), recruited by convenience/self-selection; cross-sectional survey.
codes.ai_system: AI self-diagnostic tools: ChatGPT (20.1%), Gemini, Google AI, Ada Health, WebMD, plus wearables/health apps (Fitbit, Apple Watch etc.)
codes.dependence_measures: No dependence or addiction scale. 'Utilization' (Q5–14) is 10 items adapted from UTAUT/mHealth utilisation instruments; 'Fascination/Trust' (Q15–30) is 16 items from TAM and the Trust in Automation Scale. The 'AI Dependence' outcome in Table 7 is never defined as its own instrument and seems to be the utilisation composite.
codes.note: The AI measures are acceptance/use (UTAUT), TAM and trust scales, not a dependence measure. 'AI dependence' in Table 7 has no separate instrument. Even if it were counted, no eligible correlate was measured: the only correlates are fascination, trust and gender. So this would also be excluded as no_eligible_correlate. Also, the tools are mixed and include non-conversational wearables.

codes.sample: No primary sample. This is a systematic review (PRISMA 2020) of 17 documents: 7 primary studies and 10 secondary/synthesis documents. Primary samples summarised include Bastani et al. (~1,000), Darvishi et al. (1,625), Gerlich (666), Kosmyna et al. (54), Hashmi et al. (861), Tian & Zhang (698) and Chen et al. (30).
codes.ai_system: Generative AI in education in general (ChatGPT, GPT-4, other LLMs, intelligent tutoring systems)
codes.dependence_measures: None collected by the authors. The review only describes "AI dependency" and over-reliance as findings of the included studies.
codes.possible_duplicate: None. Two of the included primary studies could be screened on their own for the meta-analysis: Tian & Zhang (2026), Humanit Soc Sci Commun 13:1015, which measures AI dependency in 698 Chinese university students, and Gerlich (2025), Societies 15(1):6.
codes.note: Abstract (p. 2): "This systematic review analyzed the relationship between metacognition, self-regulation, retrieval practice, and patterns of cognitive dependence..." The paper is a thematic synthesis with no meta-analysis and no new data, so it is excluded under E5 (review).

codes.sample: 442 full-time undergraduates from several universities in China (267 male, 175 female); classes randomly selected, online survey run February–April 2025; cross-sectional.
codes.ai_system: AI tools in general, used for academic work (generic "AI tools" for completing academic tasks)
codes.dependence_measures: AI Dependence Scale (Huang et al. [23]): 5 items adapted from smartphone addiction/problematic use measures, rated on a 5-point Likert scale and scored as a mean; α = 0.896. Measures "students' tendency to rely excessively on AI tools to complete academic work".

correlations.exposure: AI dependency (AI Dependence Scale, Huang et al.; mean score)
correlations.correlate: Future anxiety (anxiety about one's academic/career future)

correlations.exposure: AI dependency (AI Dependence Scale, Huang et al.)
correlations.correlate: Future anxiety (anxiety about one's academic/career future)

codes.possible_duplicate: None found. The AI Dependence Scale comes from Huang et al. [23], which used a different sample. Check other reports by Li, Liu and Yang (Fuzhou University of International Studies and Trade) for overlapping data.
codes.note: Borderline: the only candidate correlate is future anxiety (Dark Future Scale, worry about the future). If the reviewer does not accept it as "anxiety", the reason becomes no_eligible_correlate: cognitive load, task complexity and task motivation are not eligible correlates. Table 11 gives only SEM paths, so it was not used.

codes.sample: N=1,200 university students aged 18-30 (M=21.4, SD=2.7), 58% female, convenience sample from Palembang, Indonesia. Only 48% reported using an AI companion platform. Cross-sectional survey, data collected in 2025.
codes.ai_system: AI companions / conversational agents (Replika, Character.AI, Snapchat My AI)
codes.dependence_measures: Emotional Attachment to AI, measured with the AI Attachment Scale (AIAS; Xie & Pentina 2022; Effendy et al. 2026), 7-point Likert, α=.90. It "evaluates feelings of closeness, dependence, and emotional investment in the AI companion", and the paper calls it "emotional dependence". AI Parasocial Interaction Scale (AIPIS) was also measured but is not a dependence measure.
codes.possible_duplicate: Possible overlap with Effendy et al. (2026). This paper says its sampling follows Effendy et al. (Palembang, Indonesia) and uses the same measures. Its key betas (.254 for loneliness, .238 for burnout) are the same values the literature review attributes to Effendy et al. (2026).
codes.note: Borderline exposure: the scale measures attachment, but it includes dependence and the paper calls it emotional dependence. Integrity red flags: betas match those cited from Effendy et al., two predictors share t=7.67, and the sample is called Indonesian yet "ethnically diverse". Social-interaction burnout is not an eligible correlate. Table 2 betas are multivariable, so they don't count.

codes.sample: 433 UK adults (207 Prolific participants, 226 students), age 18–94, M=28.41 (SD 13.32); online cross-sectional survey.
codes.ai_system: AI and digital technologies in general (AI, algorithmic surveillance, voice assistants, data collection), measured as cyber paranoia/fear
codes.dependence_measures: No measure of dependence on AI. The CPFS-U (19 items) measures cyber paranoia and fear. Its Factor 1, "AI and Digital Dependence Concerns", is described as "apprehension about AI expansion, automation and potential loss of human control". That is fear of AI, not the respondent's own dependence on or problematic use of AI.
codes.note: Excluded under E1: the only AI measure is fear/paranoia about AI. GAD-7 anxiety correlated with the CPFS-U (total r=0.37; Data Vulnerability r=0.41; Surveillance r=-0.28). The full correlation matrix is in supplemental table 3, which was not retrieved. The reviewer may want to check the Factor 1 items (supplemental tables 2 and 4).

codes.sample: None. This is a theoretical philosophy paper with no participants or empirical data.
codes.ai_system: Deep neural networks in science, mainly AlphaFold2 (used as a philosophical case study); LLMs mentioned briefly
codes.dependence_measures: None. 'Epistemic dependence' is used in its social-epistemology sense (justified reliance on opaque instruments or peers). It is not a psychometric measure of dependence or addiction.
codes.note: Theoretical paper in philosophy of science and social epistemology (Synthese), responding to Koskinen (2023). It argues that 'for epistemic reliance on an opaque system, trust is not necessary, but reliability is.' No quantitative data, no psychological correlates. 'Dependence' is meant epistemically, so E3 would also apply, but E5 comes first in the order.

codes.sample: 930 valid questionnaires from Chinese medical students (undergraduate to postgraduate) at two medical universities (A: n=515; B: n=415); 1295 surveyed, 76.24% female. There were also 16 medical educators in the qualitative phase.
codes.ai_system: Generative AI in general (Doubao, DeepSeek, ChatGPT, Kimi, etc.)
codes.dependence_measures: 8-item GenAI dependence scale adapted from the Chinese Artificial Intelligence Chatbot Dependence Scale (ref 59), 5-point Likert, total up to 40; M = 21.91 ± 6.75. Also a single self-report yes/no item on dependence (60.32% said yes).
codes.note: Eligible correlates: academic pressure and self-efficacy (possibly task-specific). Only multivariable betas reported (Table 1: academic pressure β=0.746; self-efficacy β=0.126; 7 predictors + controls). No correlation matrix; supplementary tables described as reliability/KMO/ANOVA. Raw data public on GitHub (LiangruZhou), so r could be computed; reviewer may reconsider.

codes.sample: 3843 Chinese adolescents (1848 male, Mage = 13.21 ± 2.55) who completed both waves of a cohort study (T1 spring 2022, n = 5057; T2 autumn 2022); northern, central and southwestern China; paper-and-pencil questionnaires in schools.

codes.sample: 190 undergraduate and postgraduate students at Babylon University and Al-Qasim Green University in Babylon, Iraq. Convenience sample recruited through an online Google Forms questionnaire.
codes.ai_system: AI tools in general, with ChatGPT given as the example

codes.note: The dependency index is correlated only with perceived understanding (r = 0.156) and perceived critical thinking (r = 0.013) (p. 10). Neither is an eligible correlate. codes.sample: 300 participants from urban families (150 users of AI companions, 150 non-users as controls), recruited by stratified random sampling; metro cities, apparently India.
codes.ai_system: AI companions in general: virtual assistants (Alexa, Google Assistant), mental health chatbots, AI-based social robots
codes.dependence_measures: None. The only AI measures are whether someone uses AI (users vs non-users) and how often they engage with it each week (Mean 5.4 ± SD 2.1). Emotional dependency comes up only in the abstract and literature review, and 'AI reliance' only as an ethical concern in the findings. No scale or item measures it.
codes.note: Loneliness and emotional well-being were measured, but only against AI user status and engagement frequency (r = 0.72 with well-being, multiple-regression B values). Neither of these is a dependence measure. The reporting also has inconsistencies: the ANOVA, described as among 'AI users', has df = 299 total, which implies N = 300 rather than 150. The scales used are not described.

codes.sample: 690 Chinese undergraduate students who had used AI tools before, from one university in Suzhou, China (69.1% female, ages 17–25, M age 19.55). Convenience sample from an online survey run January–February 2025.
codes.ai_system: AI tools in general (e.g., ChatGPT, DeepSeek, Kimi, Doubao, Wenxin Yiyan)
codes.dependence_measures: AI dependency scale by Zhang et al. (ref 9). It is symptom-based, drawn from behavioural addiction research (salience, tolerance, mood modification, withdrawal, conflict, failed attempts to cut down), rated 1–5 (α = 0.94). Example item: "I tried to cut down on my use of AI without success". Only a total score is reported.

Academic procrastination scale, 3 items (Wohl et al.)

Academic workload (feeling overburdened by studies) is included only as a possible academic-stress correlate, for the reviewer to decide. Satisfaction with AI (r = 0.51) is not an eligible correlate.

codes.sample: 563 Chinese online adult users (18+) who had used at least one AI chatbot; 54.35% male; 47.6% aged 20–29; 31.4% students, 40.1% enterprise employees. Recruited by virtual snowball sampling via wjx.cn (643 collected, 80 excluded).
codes.ai_system: AI chatbots in general (e.g., ChatGPT, Replika mentioned)
codes.dependence_measures: Problematic AI Chatbot Use (PACU): 5 items adapted from the Bergen Social Media Addiction Scale (BSMAS; Andreassen et al., 2012) and the Chinese BSMAS (Leung et al., 2020), with the escape item B3 removed; 5-point Likert; α = 0.877, CR = 0.878.

Problematic AI chatbot use (PACU, adapted BSMAS)

codes.note: Values are latent correlations from the CFA/Fornell–Larcker table (Table 4), not the HTMT values (Table 5) or path coefficients (Table 6). The escapism items are specific to AI chatbots (one item is about avoiding loneliness). AI chatbot flow (0.455) is not an eligible correlate. There are no page markers, so locations are given by table.

codes.sample: No human participants. The data are scientometric papers published in Scientometrics and Journal of Informetrics.
codes.ai_system: Machine learning and deep learning methods used as research tools in scientometrics, not an interactive AI system used by individuals
codes.dependence_measures: None at the individual level. The study defines "dependency" as a bibliometric count: "we calculated the number of scientometric papers that use AI technologies". It also reports the lag time between when an AI term was first proposed and when it was first used in scientometrics.
codes.note: Conference poster (#239). Here "dependency" means the share of papers in the field that use AI methods, not a person's psychological dependence on AI. AI is the researchers' analysis method. There are no psychological measures or correlates. E1 or E5 could also be argued, but E3 fits best.

codes.sample: 380 adults in Guangzhou, China (190 per condition; 57.1% women; M age 25.20). All had used conversational GenAI before. Two-condition randomized online experiment.
codes.ai_system: A custom GenAI companion running on OpenAI GPT-5.5 (gpt-5.5-2026-04-23), Chinese-language chat interface, three turns
codes.dependence_measures: Two study-specific state measures taken after one 3-turn session: 'Short-term AI-reliance intentions' (6 items, α=.88) and 'Perceived AI emotional necessity' (5 items, α=.90). The authors say plainly: "We do not label the score 'emotional dependence'" and that the outcomes "should not be interpreted as emotional dependence."
codes.note: E1: reliance measures are short-term intentions after one session; authors say they are not dependence. If accepted anyway: correlates are only state emotion-regulation self-efficacy (not general/academic) and state PANAS negative affect. Only HTMT (.36, self-efficacy vs reliance) and adjusted betas are given, no zero-order r, so E4 or no_eligible_correlate would also apply.

codes.sample: 120 Grade 10–12 Electrical Technology learners from four public technical high schools in Gauteng Province, South Africa (simple random sampling). Table 1 compares High AI Users (n=60) and Low AI Users (n=40).
codes.ai_system: AI tools in general (ChatGPT, Google Bard, Quillbot)
codes.dependence_measures: There is no dependence scale. The 33-item questionnaire was "designed to assess the frequency, purpose, and observed effects of using AI" (p. 4). Learners were grouped as High vs Low AI users by how often they used AI (p. 4–5, Table 1). "AI dependence" is used as a label for frequency of use, not measured as a construct.
codes.note: The AI measure only covers frequency and purpose of use (E1). No eligible correlate either: outcomes were problem-solving, practical competence and task-specific confidence on practical tasks, not general or academic self-efficacy. Pearson correlation and regression are mentioned (p. 4), but no coefficients are reported. Table 1 gives only competence percentages.

codes.sample: No real participants. This is a proposed survey study (target 200–250 Indian university students; the questionnaire was not administered). The analyses use a synthetic Kaggle dataset ("ai_student_impact_dataset, n = 50,000 simulated student records"; pp. 6–7).
codes.ai_system: Generative AI tools in general (ChatGPT, Gemini, Copilot, Claude)
codes.dependence_measures: The synthetic dataset includes a variable "Perceived AI Dependency" (scored 1–10; M = 3.51, SD = 1.82; descriptives table on p. 8). The proposed questionnaire measures 'dependency' as weekly GenAI hours, tool diversity and paid subscription. It also has reliance-type agreement items, e.g. 'My reliance on GenAI has reduced the time I spend on traditional study methods.'
codes.note: Questionnaire only proposed; no data collected. Results come from simulated Kaggle records, so they are a proof-of-concept, not empirical data. Even otherwise E4 applies: 'Anxiety Level (Exams)' and 'Perceived AI Dependency' appear only in the descriptives, with no correlation between them. The only r reported is GenAI hours with study hours (-0.157), not an eligible pair.

codes.sample: 381 Chinese competitive athletes aged 16–25 (M = 19.6, SD = 2.2; 54.6% male), from university and provincial/municipal teams and training centres; 196 in physically dominant sports, 185 in skill-dominant sports. Cross-sectional.
codes.ai_system: AI training recommendation systems (algorithmic, wearable- or ML-based training advice); not conversational or generative AI
codes.dependence_measures: AI Training Recommendation Dependence (ATRD), 6 items written for this study, 5-point Likert (α = 0.89, CR = 0.89, AVE = 0.58). Example item: "Without AI training recommendations, I would find it difficult to accurately assess my training status."

correlations.correlate: Reduced training self-efficacy (sport-specific, AI-contingent; probably not eligible)
correlations.correlate_instrument: Ad hoc 6-item Diminished Training Self-Efficacy scale (α = 0.89)
correlations.quote: dependence on AI training recommendations was significantly and positively correlated with ... diminished training self-efficacy (r = 0.22, p < 0.001)

codes.possible_duplicate: None identified.
codes.note: I2 is doubtful: the AI is a sport training-recommendation system, not interactive AI. The only near-eligible correlate is an ad hoc training self-efficacy scale whose items mention AI, so it is not general or academic self-efficacy. The other correlates (body-signal outsourcing, reduced self-regulation, decision hesitation) are not eligible. Reviewer should check both points.

codes.sample: 180 postgraduate students (107 female, 73 male; 167 Master's, 13 PhD) at KPPIM, Universiti Teknologi MARA, Malaysia; cross-sectional online survey (p. 5)
codes.ai_system: Generative AI tools in general (e.g., ChatGPT, Grammarly)
codes.dependence_measures: 20-item AI Dependency scale adapted from Morales-García et al. (2024) DAI. The original five dimensions were vulnerability, performance, image, validation and obsolescence. EFA reduced it to two factors: Factor 1 (validation/academic support dependency) and Factor 2 (emotional dependency/helplessness) (pp. 6–8).
codes.possible_duplicate: May overlap with a UiTM thesis or dissertation on the same sample, since the text refers to "Chapter 2" (p. 9).
codes.note: The only correlate is academic integrity, from Ramdani's (2018) scale: Honesty, Fairness, Respect, Trust and Responsibility (Table 4, p. 8). None of these is an eligible correlate. Items about anxiety or obsolescence belong to the dependence scale, not to a separate correlate measure. The abstract mentions TAM constructs (PU/PEOU), but these were not analysed.

codes.sample: 30 accounting students in a Research Methodology course at State University of Makassar, Indonesia, chosen by purposive sampling (p. 1, p. 5–6).
codes.ai_system: Generative AI tools, mainly ChatGPT, used for academic tasks such as writing research proposals.
codes.dependence_measures: None. The study is qualitative and uses semi-structured interviews analysed with the Miles, Huberman & Saldaña model (p. 6). It uses no quantitative dependence scale. AI-detector scores of student submissions (45–82%) are mentioned, but these are not self-report measures of dependence.
codes.note: This is a qualitative descriptive study: "A qualitative research method was employed in this study" (p. 5), and "Data were collected through semi-structured interviews" (p. 6). It has no quantitative dependence measure, and no eligible correlates were measured quantitatively. Stress and self-efficacy appear only as interview themes or in citations.

codes.sample: None. This is a narrative/multidisciplinary review with no primary data collection.
codes.ai_system: Generative AI / LLMs in general (ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini), discussed conceptually
codes.dependence_measures: None. 'AI dependency' is discussed conceptually; the paper uses no quantitative dependence scale.
codes.note: The paper calls itself a review: 'This paper undertakes a multidisciplinary review' (p. 1). It brings together cognitive science and Islamic epistemology and proposes the BHAIF framework. It reports no original data, no dependence measure and no correlations. Its reference list may be worth checking for primary studies.

codes.sample: None. This is a narrative or argumentative essay with no participants and no data collection.
codes.ai_system: AI tools in general (AI-powered tools used by students for essays, summaries and assignments)
codes.dependence_measures: None. Dependence on AI is discussed only conceptually; no quantitative measure is given.

The sections are Introduction, Main Body and Conclusion, arguing for and against AI dependence. It has no method, sample, measures or statistics, so it is a theoretical/commentary piece. codes.sample: 180 undergraduate ESL students from three universities and four autonomous colleges in six districts of Gujarat, India (49% female, CEFR A2–B2). 30 of them were interviewed.
codes.ai_system: ChatGPT used for academic writing
codes.dependence_measures: There is no dependence, addiction or over-reliance scale. The 28-item survey measured how often students use ChatGPT, which writing tasks they hand over to it (percentages), a writing agency subscale (α=0.83) and a metacognitive awareness subscale (α=0.79). 'Overreliance' and 'prompt dependency' appear only as interpretations and as qualitative interview themes.
codes.note: The only AI measures are use frequency and task delegation. No eligible correlate was measured quantitatively: exam anxiety appears only as an interview theme, and writing confidence is a single item. The analysis was descriptive and cross-tabulation only, and no r values or group statistics are reported. So even if delegation counted as dependence, the report would still fail I3 and I4.

codes.sample: 651 college students enrolled in CHED-accredited public (n=348) and private (n=303) HEIs in Pampanga, Philippines (M age = 20.22, SD = 1.91); snowball sampling via Google Forms, October 2024 to January 2025.
codes.ai_system: Generative AI tools used for academic tasks (e.g., ChatGPT), referred to generally as AI tools
codes.dependence_measures: Ad hoc 24-item instrument developed by the authors. It measures AI dependency and academic skill substitution across five domains: critical thinking (α=.93), writing skills (α=.93), learning independence (α=.97), research skills (α=.92) and academic engagement (α=.93). Latent class analysis produced 4 profiles.
codes.possible_duplicate: None identified.
codes.note: There is a dependence measure (an ad hoc AI-dependency instrument). The only variables analysed against it are gender, academic year and self-reported academic performance (chi-square tests on the LCA classes). None of these is an eligible psychological correlate. No correlation matrix is reported.

codes.sample: 200 active undergraduate (S1) students at Universitas Sebelas Maret, Indonesia, from 14 faculties (71% from the 2022 cohort), recruited by purposive sampling; all had used AI for academic work.
codes.ai_system: Generative AI in general (ChatGPT 59%, Claude 43.5%, Perplexity 36%, Gemini 34%)
codes.dependence_measures: GenAI Dependency: a 5-point Likert questionnaire built from the cognitive, behavioral and affective dependency indicators of Jia et al. (2025). Items X6 and X7 were dropped for low loadings; AVE = 0,619; Cronbach's alpha and CR > 0,90.
codes.possible_duplicate: None apparent. The study adapts the model and instruments of Jia et al. (2025), but it uses a different (Indonesian) sample.
codes.note: Eligible correlate: academic self-efficacy (AVE 0,626). Only PLS-SEM results are given: R²/f² (Tab 1), paths and interactions (Tab 2), indirect effects (Tab 3, −0,203). Self-efficacy is predicted by X, Z and X×Z, so there is no single-predictor beta. The text says Fornell-Larcker was met, but no table is printed. The authors could be asked for it.

codes.sample: 492 English Language undergraduates at Nnamdi Azikiwe University, Awka, and University of Benin, Nigeria; online survey via Google Form.
codes.ai_system: AI tools in general (ChatGPT, Gemini, Claude, Grammarly, QuillBot)
codes.dependence_measures: AI Dependence Scale (AI-DS), adapted from Wang et al. (2024): 15 items on a 5-point Likert scale, with 3 dimensions: Cognitive Offloading (5), Emotional Reliance (5) and Behavioural Dependence (5). Only the total score was correlated (M = 3.85, SD = 0.72).
codes.note: The only correlates were critical thinking disposition (r = -.38) and self-reported writing competence (r = -.42). Neither is on the list of eligible correlates. No other psychological variables were measured.

codes.sample: 469 preservice mathematics teachers (68.02% female; 84.43% aged 18–22; undergraduate and master's students) at Qinghai Normal University, China. Purposive sample of seminar attendees, online survey.
codes.ai_system: Generative AI in general (Gen-AI tools such as ChatGPT and DeepSeek)
codes.dependence_measures: Self-designed 3-item "AI dependency" scale (5-point Likert), described as "measured the extent to which participants relied on AI for teaching and problem-solving"; alpha 0.811, CR 0.706, AVE 0.651. Item wording is not reported.

correlations.correlate_instrument: Self-designed 3-item self-confidence scale (21st-century skills development via AI use)

codes.possible_duplicate: None identified.
codes.note: The correlates are 21st-century skills, none on the eligible list. Borderline: "self-confidence". Is it general self-efficacy? Its items are not reported and were framed as skill enhancement through AI use. If the reviewer accepts it, the latent r = −0.728 (Table 2) makes the report eligible.

codes.sample: 2,614 university students from public and private universities in Bangladesh (59.3% male; 60.7% undergraduate); cross-sectional online survey.
codes.ai_system: Generative AI tools in general (ChatGPT, Gemini, DeepSeek)
codes.dependence_measures: Cognitive Dependence: an ad hoc 5-item Likert scale (α = 0.706) defined as "the extent to which students relied on AI tools for learning and problem-solving activities". The items are not reported.
codes.possible_duplicate: The dataset is published separately: Arifen, Rahman & Khandakar (2026), "Dataset on Cognitive Dependence on Generative AI Tools among Bangladeshi University Students", Mendeley Data, doi:10.17632/7m94b7yr8w.2. Check for other reports from the same sample.
codes.note: The only correlates measured were Generative AI Usage, Trust in AI, Critical Thinking and Academic Decision-Making. None of these is on the eligible list. Table 6 (p.4) gives zero-order r with CD: TAI 0.707, ADM 0.534, GAIU 0.450, CT 0.321. The dependence scale may also count only as borderline because it measures cognitive reliance, not addiction.

codes.sample: Students at the Faculty of Social Sciences, University of Ljubljana, Slovenia (web survey + CAPI, May 2023). 340 completed; 318 report using ChatGPT; n = 231 for the factor analyses and correlations; n = 191 for the regressions.
codes.ai_system: ChatGPT, including ChatGPT-based plugins and apps
codes.dependence_measures: No dependence or addiction measure. The 'Problematic use' factor (alpha .78; items rated 1 never to 3 frequently) measures how often students use ChatGPT for academic dishonesty, e.g. 'Producing entire homework assignments...', 'Achieving better grades with less effort'. 'Dependent users' (6.2%) is only a label for one cluster of use patterns, not a measured construct.
codes.note: 'Problematic use' means cheating and plagiarism with ChatGPT, measured as frequency of use, not compulsive use or dependence. E3 could also apply, but E1 comes first. Table 4 correlates problematic use with 'Escapism' (r = .27), but that is a type of ChatGPT use, not a trait or coping motive. No other eligible correlate (depression, anxiety, stress, etc.) was measured.

codes.sample: 413 university students (64% Thai, 25% Myanmar, 11% other; 77.7% undergraduate) at Thai universities, mostly in and around Bangkok, recruited by convenience sampling through an online Google Forms survey.
codes.ai_system: AI tools in general for academic use (e.g., ChatGPT, Grammarly, Duolingo)
codes.dependence_measures: One 5-point Likert item labelled "Over-reliance on AI" (M = 3.03, SD = 1.20, Table 2), from the 'Barriers and ethical concerns' section. Its exact wording is not reported. It may be a perception of risk rather than self-reported dependence. No multi-item dependence scale was used.
codes.note: Over-reliance was related only to critical thinking (β = −0.29, Table 4), which is not an eligible correlate. Engagement, self-regulated learning and the confidence items are not eligible either. Table 3 correlations involve only AI usage frequency. There is no zero-order r for over-reliance. E1 may also apply, because the item's wording is unclear.

codes.sample: 1,623 undergraduate students at universities in China, recruited by convenience online sampling; 46.27% male; mean age 19.47 (SD 1.08).
codes.ai_system: Generative AI tools in general (ChatGPT, Gemini and DeepSeek are named) used for academic work
codes.dependence_measures: DAI scale (Dependence on AI, developed by ref [24]). It has 5 items rated on a 5-point Likert scale, is based on DSM-5 dependence criteria, and had α = 0.76 in this study. Only the total score is reported.
