The PROCESS path betas (e.g., stress→AI dependence β = 0.264, controlling for gender, grade and major) are not zero-order, so the Table 1 Pearson r values are used instead.

codes.sample: First-year LLB undergraduates at a Sri Lankan state university (General Sir John Kotelawala Defence University). Cross-sections n = 126 (M1), 107 (M2), 122 (M3); 79 women and 47 men, aged 20–21. Matched panel n = 51 (n = 49 for the dependency–anxiety correlation).
codes.ai_system: Generative AI tools (free web versions of ChatGPT and Gemini) used for course assignments
codes.dependence_measures: Self-authored 3-item "AI dependency" scale on a 5-point Likert format (reliance on AI, anticipated difficulty without AI, discomfort working without AI). Score is the mean of the items. α = .67 (M1), .66 (M2), .77 (M3).

correlations.exposure: AI dependency at baseline (M1), 3-item self-authored scale
correlations.correlate: Academic anxiety at M3 (task anxiety, worry about mistakes, course-related stress)
correlations.quote: Students who entered the course more dependent on AI became significantly more anxious once support was faded (Fig. 3, ρ = .38, p = .007, n = 49).

codes.possible_duplicate: None identified.
codes.note: Only one zero-order result, and it is cross-lagged: M1 dependency with M3 anxiety (Spearman, n = 49). No same-wave correlations are printed. Self-efficacy was measured, but its correlation with dependency is not reported. Panel data are on Mendeley (doi 10.17632/gggvjcpnrz.1). All scales were written for this study.

codes.sample: 52 undergraduates from a local university in Singapore (86 recruited). Within-subjects experiment: 5 days of friendlike ChatGPT interaction vs 5 days of journaling control, counterbalanced, March–June 2025.
codes.ai_system: ChatGPT (free version, GPT-4o), used as a friendlike AI companion; dependency measured on generative AI in general
codes.dependence_measures: 11-item Generative AI Dependency scale (Goh et al., 2025), with cognitive preoccupation, negative consequences and withdrawal subscales; total score is the mean of the subscale means (α = 0.92 AI condition; α = 0.93 journaling condition).
codes.possible_duplicate: None apparent. Goh et al. (2025) is cited as the source of the GAID scale, but it is not described as the same sample.
codes.note: Eligible correlates were measured: STAI-6, perceived stress, UCLA loneliness, RSE, life satisfaction, sleep quality and social support. Only paired t-tests between conditions are reported (Tables 2–3). There is no correlation between GAID and any correlate, and no supplementary correlation matrix is mentioned.

codes.sample: English Language Education university students at Universitas Muhammadiyah Gresik, Indonesia (sequential explanatory mixed-methods). Sample size not reported in the retrieved text; the pilot interviews in the background section involved 5 students.
codes.ai_system: AI tools in general (ChatGPT, Grammarly, QuillBot and similar) used for English language learning
codes.dependence_measures: A survey instrument measuring AI dependency, based on Zhai (2024): cognitive, decision-making, ethical and technical dependency, with motivational dependency also listed in the definitions (p. 4, 6–7). The instrument's items, scoring and reliability are not in the retrieved text.
codes.possible_duplicate: The retrieved text is Chapter I of a thesis ("throughout the thesis", p. 6), but the record is the 2026 TEACHING Jurnal Inovasi Keguruan dan Ilmu Pendidikan article. The thesis and the article probably report the same sample.
codes.note: Only Chapter I (Introduction, pp. 1–8) was retrieved; the methods and results are missing. The only stated correlate is independent learning / learner autonomy (p. 4–5), which is not an eligible correlate. This makes no_eligible_correlate the likely outcome, but we need the full article to check for other measures (e.g., self-efficacy) and for any correlation results.

codes.sample: 64 high school students at SMA St. Petrus Medan, Indonesia. The abstract says total sampling and the Methods say purposive sampling. Survey plus FGDs.
codes.ai_system: AI in general, mainly AI chatbots (81%) and social media with AI integration (73%)
codes.dependence_measures: There is no dependence or addiction scale. The researchers wrote their own questionnaire covering 'the patterns of use of AI, including the frequency, intensity, and purpose of its use' (p.3), plus items on stress, anxiety and depression. Results are only descriptive percentages.
codes.note: The title mentions 'AI addiction', but the only AI measures are use frequency, intensity and purpose. Analysis is descriptive plus thematic, so no correlation with stress, anxiety or depression is reported. The text says 'a significant link with depression has not been found' but gives no statistics. If a dependence measure were accepted, E4_no_zero_order would apply.

codes.sample: No sample. The document is only the questionnaire form, aimed at secondary-school students ("estudiantes de educación secundaria").
codes.ai_system: AI in general for academic tasks: "IA = Inteligencia Artificial (chatbots, ChatGPT, Cici, Canva, etc)"
codes.dependence_measures: SAID questionnaire (Garcia Castro et al.), meant to "Evaluar el nivel de dependencia de la inteligencia artificial en tareas académicas". It uses a 5-point Likert scale. The listed items are numbered 1-3, 6-11 and 15-18, so items 4-5 and 12-14 are missing. The items cover trust, frequency or preference of use, and AI literacy/discernment.
codes.possible_duplicate: This is probably the instrument file supporting an empirical study by Garcia Castro, Llapa Medina, Mayta Cachicatari & Bartesaghi Aste (2024) on AI dependence in Peruvian secondary students. That study should be found and screened separately.
codes.note: The figshare file is the questionnaire alone. It has no data, no participants, no psychological correlates and no statistics, so I chose 'other' (instrument document only, no empirical results); E5_design could also apply. The scale's content is mostly trust, use frequency and AI literacy rather than dependence itself.

codes.sample: 217 university students in Morocco (Sidi Mohammed Ben Abdellah University, Fez); 52.5% female; 144 ChatGPT users. Recruited through convenience, snowball and purposive sampling.
codes.ai_system: ChatGPT
codes.dependence_measures: There is no dependence measure. The only related item is one perceived-risk item asking about fear of over-reliance: "I fear over-reliance on ChatGPT could weaken my skills" (Chatgpt_overReliance). It measures worry about a risk, not actual dependence. The other AI measures are TAM ease of use and usefulness, a yes/no use question, usage time and frequency of use.
codes.note: The AI measures are acceptance (TAM), perceived risk/concerns, and use time or frequency. The technology anxiety scale (ATAS) measures general technology anxiety, not dependence. The only analyses are gender t-tests; no correlations are reported. Even if the over-reliance item counted, no eligible correlate is linked to it.

codes.sample: No sample. This is a narrative/theoretical essay with no participants or data collection.
codes.ai_system: AI translation and writing assistants (Google Translate, DeepL, ChatGPT) used by EFL learners
codes.dependence_measures: None. The paper discusses 'over-reliance' and 'AI dependency' conceptually only and uses no quantitative measure.
codes.note: Short theoretical/argumentative paper by an undergraduate student. It has no methods, sample, measures or results, and only cites textbooks (Krashen 1982, Nation 2001, etc.). It mentions error anxiety and low self-belief only as speculative drivers, without measuring them.

codes.sample: No human participants. The units of analysis are four LLM releases (Olmo 3, Nemotron 3 Super, DR Tulu, SmolLM3) and their dependency graphs: 2,526 artifact nodes and 9,112 edges.
codes.ai_system: ModSleuth, an agentic system built on Claude Code that traces model-to-model and model-to-dataset dependencies across LLM releases.
codes.dependence_measures: None in the psychological sense. Here 'dependency' means one model or dataset artifact being built from another (e.g., training data, data generation, filtering, evaluation). It is counted as verified graph edges, not as a self-report measure of human dependence on AI.
codes.note: This is a computer-science paper on auditing hidden technical dependencies between LLMs ('Auditing Invisible Dependencies in Modern LLMs'). 'Dependence' is used in another sense, so it is out of scope. It has no human sample, no psychological correlates and no correlations. E1 (no dependence measure) would also apply, but E3 describes the problem more exactly.

codes.sample: No sample. This is a non-empirical Arabic-language essay with no participants or data.
codes.ai_system: AI chatbots/conversational AI and AI companions in general (described narratively)
codes.dependence_measures: None. AI addiction/dependence is only discussed conceptually (causes, symptoms, diagnosis, treatment, prevention). No scale or quantitative measure is given.
codes.note: This is a 5-page narrative/educational commentary on Zenodo. It names loneliness as a main cause of AI addiction and cites unnamed studies, but it collects no data, has no methods or results, and its reference list has no data of its own. Excluded as a commentary/theoretical piece.

codes.sample: 1,157 Chinese graduate students (master's and doctoral) recruited by online convenience sampling via Wenjuanxing/WeChat; 553 male, 604 female (Table 1, p.5).
codes.ai_system: Generative AI (GenAI) in general, e.g., large language models such as ChatGPT, used for academic research
codes.dependence_measures: AI Dependence Questionnaire adapted from Li et al. (2025), the Large Language Model Dependence Scale: 18 items, 5-point Likert, with two dimensions, functional dependence and existential dependence; α = 0.913 (Section 3.2, p.5).
codes.possible_duplicate: None identified. Li et al. (2025, Int J Inform Manag) is the source scale-development paper and appears to use a different sample.
codes.note: A valid dependence measure is present, with zero-order correlations in Table 2 (p.7). But the only correlates are critical thinking, human–AI collaboration quality and research creativity, and none of these is on the eligible list. No depression, anxiety, stress, loneliness, self-esteem, procrastination, self-efficacy or similar measures were collected.

codes.sample: 128 students at Banaras Hindu University, India (67 female, 61 male), recruited by convenience sampling through an online Google Form survey.
codes.ai_system: AI tools in general (artificial intelligence used in education; not further specified)
codes.dependence_measures: None. The AI measure is "seven items assessing artificial intelligence ... adopting measures used by Suh & Ahn (2022)" (α=0.854). This is a general AI use/attitude scale, not a measure of dependence, addiction, problematic use or over-reliance. The other measures are privacy and safety (Youn, 2009) and human laziness (Dautov, 2020).
codes.note: The title mentions "digital dependency", but no dependence scale was given. The AI construct (Suh & Ahn, 2022) measures AI use/attitudes. The correlates are also out of scope: Table 7 correlates AI with privacy/safety (r=.588) and laziness (r=.634), and neither is an eligible correlate. The design closely follows Ahmad et al. (2023).

codes.sample: 546 participants, mostly Chinese students (386, 70.7%), recruited via Credamo in October 2025. Between-subjects experiment: 273 saw an identical GAI (e.g., DeepSeek) answer labelled as hallucinated and 273 saw it labelled as accurate.
codes.ai_system: Generative AI in general (stimulus framed as e.g. DeepSeek output)
codes.dependence_measures: GAI dependence: 4 items (DEPE1–DEPE4) adapted from Andreassen et al. (2012, Bergen Facebook Addiction Scale) and Hu et al. (2023). They cover escape-oriented use, difficulty reducing use, discomfort when access is restricted, and adverse academic/occupational consequences. 7-point scale, α = 0.954, measured after exposure.

correlations.correlate: GAI self-efficacy (borderline: technology-specific, not general/academic self-efficacy)
correlations.correlate_instrument: 10 items adapted from Rodríguez-Ruiz et al. (2025) and Shao et al. (2025)

codes.possible_duplicate: None identified.
codes.note: Table 7 gives r with dependence only for trust, dissonance, controllability, frustration, GAI literacy and GAI self-efficacy; none clearly eligible. The self-efficacy scale is GAI-specific ('complete any desired task using the GAI technology'), not general/academic. It is listed for the reviewer; if accepted, the decision becomes eligible (r = 0.385).

codes.sample: 310 first-year students at high school I in Japan, in an Information class; single-group pre-post-follow-up teaching practice with three survey waves (pre, immediately post, about 6 months later). The text says 2024 in the body but April–July 2025 in the abstract.
codes.ai_system: Generative AI in general (生成AI)
codes.dependence_measures: Generative AI Dependence Tendency Scale for high-school and university students (生成AI依存傾向測定尺度; Tsuruta, Ishikawa & Tanaka, 2024). It has 22 items, a 4-point scale and 5 factors: mental dependence, anxiety about AI responses, long-time use, multitasking use and face-to-face communication anxiety.
codes.possible_duplicate: Same author group as the scale-development paper (Tsuruta, Ishikawa & Tanaka 2024, AI時代の教育論文誌 6, pp.40-45). That paper probably used a different sample.
codes.note: Internet addiction tendency (39-item scale with 5 factors, an eligible problematic internet use correlate) was measured together with GenAI dependence at all three waves. However, only factor means/SDs per wave and repeated-measures ANOVA F values are reported (Tables 3 and 5). No correlation between the two scales is reported, and none can be derived. Gaming time is not an eligible correlate.

codes.sample: 412 Chinese college students from higher education institutions in Fujian Province (78.2% female; 93.7% undergraduates; film/TV, digital media, journalism majors); cross-sectional online/offline survey, June–September 2025.
codes.ai_system: AI tools in general used for learning (AI-assisted learning)
codes.dependence_measures: AI Dependence scale (Morales-García et al., 2024), 4 items in the model, Chinese translation, α = 0.815; AI Addiction scale (Pantic, 2025, AIAS), 4 items in the model, α = 0.854.
codes.note: Other variables: perceived usefulness, inert thinking, perceived enjoyment, learning burnout (Schaufeli 2002). None is an eligible correlate. Table 4 (Fornell–Larcker) has latent r: AID–LB 0.71, AIA–LB 0.731. These count only if burnout is treated as academic stress or distress. Supplementary files (SmartPLS output, dataset) were not received.

codes.sample: 120 first- and second-year BSEd Mathematics students (74 first-year, 46 second-year) at Davao del Norte State College, Philippines, chosen by simple random sampling.
codes.ai_system: AI tools in general, used to solve mathematics problems
codes.dependence_measures: A 13-item "AI Reliance Scale" (dependency on AI) adapted from Al-Tkhayneh et al. (2023), plus one item from Morales-García et al. (2024). It has three subscales: usage (4 items, e.g. "I depend on artificial intelligence to solve my math problems"), benefits (5 items) and risks (4 items). It uses a 5-point scale; pilot alpha = 0.78.
codes.possible_duplicate: The acknowledgements mention a Thesis Review Panel, so this article is probably based on an undergraduate thesis from Davao del Norte State College that used the same sample.
codes.note: AI dependency is correlated only with geometry achievement (r = -0.120, Table 17). Neither study habits nor geometry achievement is an eligible correlate, and AI dependency was not correlated with study habits. E1 is also arguable: the benefits and risks subscales measure perceptions of AI rather than dependence.

codes.sample: 700 undergraduates (386 female; M_age = 19.81, SD = 1.27) in applied statistics, statistics and data science programmes at three universities in Shijiazhuang, Hebei, China. Cross-sectional online survey, March–May 2026.
codes.ai_system: AI tools in general used for statistics coursework (chat assistants, code generators, automated explainers)
codes.dependence_measures: AI dependence: 7 items written for this study (α = 0.90). Two domains: difficulty completing academic tasks without AI (4 items) and uncritical acceptance of AI output (3 items), which correlate at 0.75 as factors. Only the total score is correlated with other variables.

correlations.correlate_instrument: 8 items adapted from MSLQ self-efficacy subscale (Pintrich & De Groot, 1990); α = 0.88
correlations.quote: 5. AI dependence 2.82 0.78 0.90 0.20*** 0.19*** −0.12** −0.08* —; text: "weakly and negatively with AI dependence (r = −0.12)"

codes.possible_duplicate: None found. The AI dependence scale draws on Liu & Liu (2026), but that study used a different sample (Changde).
codes.note: Self-efficacy is the only clearly eligible correlate. A negative achievement emotions composite (AI-context anxiety + boredom, AEQ-adapted) correlated r = 0.19*** with AI dependence (Table 1). It is combined, not a pure anxiety score, and no anxiety-facet r is reported, so the reviewer should decide whether it counts as anxiety.

codes.sample: Turkish adult ChatGPT users, convenience online samples. Study I: N=391 (61.4% female, mean age 30.89, range 18-59). Study II: N=473 (74.4% male, mean age 28.25, range 18-75). The Study II mediation reports t(334), which may mean an analytic n of about 337.
codes.ai_system: ChatGPT (plus AI technologies in general for the DAIS in Study I)
codes.dependence_measures: Turkish 9-item Problematic ChatGPT Use Scale (PCGUS; Yu et al., 2024; items 1 and 4 removed; α=.903 in Study I, .877 in Study II). Dependence to Artificial Intelligence Scale (DAIS; Morales-García et al., 2024; 5 items; Turkish version by Savaş, 2024; α=.80; Study I only). The DAIS was only correlated with the PCGUS (r=.425), not with any correlate.

correlations.correlate_instrument: General Well-Being Scale – Short Form (GWB-SF; Longo et al.)
Brief Multidimensional Self-Control Scale (BMSCS; Nilsen et al., 2020)
Young Internet Addiction Test – Short Form (YIBT-SF, 12 items)
correlations.location: Table 3, Study I, p. 7 (2375); text p. 10
Table 3, Study I, p. 7; text p. 11

correlations.quote: correlation was observed with conscientiousness (r = − 0.163, p < 0.001)

correlations.location: Table 3, Study I, p. 7; text p. 11

codes.possible_duplicate: No overlapping sample was found. The PCGUS was originally developed by Yu et al. (2024, Current Psychology), but on a different, non-Turkish sample. Other papers by the same authors (Maral, Satici) using these Turkish samples could exist.
codes.note: Only the DASS-21 total is correlated with the PCGUS. The depression, anxiety and stress subscale r values are not reported. Gaming disorder (r=.225) and DAIS (r=.425) were left out as non-eligible correlates. Study II n is 473, but the mediation reports t(334), so the n behind the correlations is uncertain. Mediation paths are unstandardized and were not used.

codes.sample: 239 pre-service teachers (education majors) in Eastern China, 92.9% female, convenience sample taken from a larger web-based survey of university students' GenAI use; analysed from 264 teacher-track respondents after excluding never-users and invariant responders.
codes.ai_system: Generative AI (GenAI) tools in general, e.g., ChatGPT
codes.dependence_measures: Behavioral GenAI dependency (DEP; 4 items, 7-point Likert, adopted from Jiang & Wang, 2026; CR = 0.80, AVE = 0.58). Defined as habitual default reliance, difficulty working without AI, and uncritical adoption of outputs.
codes.possible_duplicate: The ANX, IMP and DEP scales were adopted from Jiang and Wang (2026), and the sample was drawn from 'a larger, voluntary web-based survey of university students' GenAI use'. Jiang & Wang (2026) may report the same or an overlapping larger sample; check it.
codes.note: AI anxiety/FOMO (one combined factor) and impulsivity were measured, but no correlation matrix is given. With DEP, only joint SEM betas (ANX→DEP 0.28, IMP→DEP 0.31, R²=0.26) and HTMT ≤0.50 are reported. The only φ given is ANX–TSC (0.42). Latent r could be backed out from the rounded betas and R² (about .43/.45). Could ask the authors.

codes.sample: Reported: Study 1 N = 465 Indian adults (M age 28.1); Study 2 N = 652 Indian adults (M age 28.8). The authors say these results come from synthetic data generated to demonstrate the analysis pipeline, not from real participants (p. 22).
codes.ai_system: AI chatbots in general (ChatGPT, Gemini, Character.AI mentioned), used both as assistants and as companions
codes.dependence_measures: Emotional Delegation to AI Scale (EDIAS/EDAIS), 13 items, 6-point Likert; defined as how much a person routinely relies on an AI chatbot for emotional validation, perspective-taking, reflective processing and reassurance. A borderline emotional-reliance measure. A 4-item 'General Technology Dependence' measure (non-AI) was also used.
codes.possible_duplicate: Research Square preprint (DOI 10.21203/rs.3.rs-9765754/v1). The authors plan a later version using primary data after OSF pre-registration; check for that version.
codes.note: Synthetic data: p. 22 says 'the present results are based on synthetic data generated to demonstrate the analytical pipeline'. Methods are in future tense, like a protocol. Also no eligible correlate (digital empathy, social presence, AI empathy, emotional literacy, AI use, parasocial attachment). Borderline: EDIAS vs general technology dependence r = .21 (p. 14).

codes.sample: 420 undergraduate students at the University of Calabar and the University of Cross River State, Nigeria (population 32,000), recruited by multistage sampling. Paper questionnaires.
codes.ai_system: AI tools in general / generative AI tools used for academic work (e.g., ChatGPT)
codes.dependence_measures: Researcher-developed 15-item Over-Reliance on Artificial Intelligence Scale (Section B of the ORAISLCQ), 4-point Likert. Items include "dependence on AI for answering academic questions" and "difficulty completing academic tasks without AI". Higher score means more over-reliance (M = 42.18, SD = 8.21).
codes.note: Only correlates are 5-item subscales: critical thinking, creativity, independent learning, human interaction (r = -.480, -.410, -.440, -.360; N = 420; Tables 1, 3, 5, 7). None eligible (independent learning is not self-efficacy or self-control). Flags: text says "Plateau State" in places; Table 9 gives R² = .280 for critical thinking where Table 2 gives .230.

codes.sample: 1,460 Peruvian systems/informatics engineering students over a 16-week longitudinal study (Aug–Dec 2024), grouped by Copilot use: Intensive (n=487, >80% use), Moderate (n=521, 30–80%), Minimal (n=452, <30%).
codes.ai_system: GitHub Copilot (AI programming assistant)
codes.dependence_measures: No dependence, addiction or problematic-use scale. The title and abstract say "cognitive dependency", but the exposure was measured only as Copilot use intensity: "1. Uso Copilot (%)" M=61.3 (SD 28.7), which was used to form the groups (">80% uso" etc.). The instruments were a syntactic retention test (SRT, 45 items), speed metrics and a 9-item cognitive load scale.
codes.note: The exposure is use intensity (% Copilot use), not dependence. The variables correlated with it in Table V (p.6) were retention, unassisted time, syntax errors, germane cognitive load and programming confidence. None is an eligible correlate. Several statistics look implausible, but that does not change the decision.

codes.sample: Exp 1: 338 junior-level business students at a US university (University of Arizona). Exp 2: 563 US Amazon MTurk workers (mean age 31.7, 78% male).
codes.ai_system: Generative AI (GenAI) tools in general; stimuli were summaries generated by GPT-4o
codes.dependence_measures: Learned dependency on GenAI. Exp 1 used a 6-item GenAI dependency scale adapted from Ye et al. (2025) ChatGPT dependence (α=.782). Exp 2 used a 17-item scale made of those 6 items plus 11 items adapted from the Goh et al. (2025) Generative AI Dependency Scale (α=.932). Both used 5-point Likert responses.
codes.note: The only outcome correlated with dependency is trust in AI-generated health information. The Fornell-Larcker inter-construct r is .697 in Exp 1 and .643 in Exp 2 (p.17), but trust is not an eligible correlate. Apart from demographics, no eligible psychological correlate was measured, so this is a randomized 2x2 experiment on trust calibration.

codes.sample: 100 undergraduate education students at Polytechnic University of the Philippines – Lopez, Quezon campus; survey run March 15 to September 27, 2025.
codes.ai_system: AI tools in general (intelligent search engines, writing assistants, generative AI platforms)
codes.dependence_measures: Ad hoc 'AI dependency' questionnaire with 15 items on a 4-point Likert scale and three subscales: academic assistance, information retrieval and assignment completion. Many items are about how often AI is used (e.g., 'Use AI to search for information'). Others are about reliance (e.g., 'Rely on AI-generated explanations when studying', 'Depend on AI tools to clarify topics').
codes.possible_duplicate: The same article seems to appear in Oriental Studies (ISSN 2619-0990), Vol. 26, Issue 6, pp. 257–270. Check this Zenodo record against that journal record.
codes.note: The only correlate measured is critical thinking (analysis, evaluation, problem solving), which is not on the eligible list. Table 11 (p. 268) reports Pearson's r = 0.81 between AI dependency and critical thinking. It is not reported here because the correlate is ineligible. A reviewer might also judge this an E1 case, since most items measure how often AI is used, not dependence.

codes.sample: 812 undergraduate students at the University of Lagos, Nigeria (345 male, 467 female; aged 16–30); convenience sample in the validation phase. Phase one was a town-hall meeting with 21 students and phase two a pilot with 15 students.
codes.ai_system: AI tools in general (ChatGPT, Gemini, Meta AI, Copilot, etc.) used for schoolwork and social media
codes.dependence_measures: Artificial Intelligence Dependence Questionnaire (AIDQ/ADIQ), newly developed, 13 items, Likert-type, alpha = .85 (one item later dropped after factor analysis)
codes.possible_duplicate: None identified.
codes.note: This scale-development study measured only demographics (age, gender) and the AIDQ. It reports split-half reliability, alpha, item-total correlations and EFA results. Anxiety comes up only as a qualitative finding from the phase-one meeting. The data-analysis section lists Pearson r, t-tests and regression, but none involving psychological correlates are reported.

codes.sample: 387 Turkish adults who use LLMs regularly (68.5% female; mean age 25.22 ± 7.13; 96.9% university-educated; 65.1% students). Data collected Sept–Oct 2025. A test–retest subsample of n = 55 was re-surveyed after one week.
codes.ai_system: LLMs in general (ChatGPT, Gemini, Claude, Copilot, DeepSeek, etc.); 83.5% used ChatGPT as their main LLM
codes.dependence_measures: Turkish LLM-D12 (11 items after RSAT was removed; 6-point scale). It has two subscales: Instrumental Dependency (6 items, α = 0.831) and Relational Dependency (5 items, α = 0.876). Total α = 0.868.
codes.possible_duplicate: No overlapping sample found. Related validations of the same scale used different samples: the original LLM-D12 (Yankouskaya et al., 2025, UK) and the Arabic version (AlShakhsi et al., 2025, arXiv:2508.17063).
codes.note: Eligible correlates measured: Internet Addiction (IAT-7, α = 0.836) and ATAI Fear (fear of AI, α = 0.624). Both were tested against the two subscales only in a multivariate multiple regression (e.g., IA: Wilks' Λ = 0.907, F(2,380) = 19.39, p. 18). No zero-order r is reported. Raw data are on OSF (osf.io/cs5rw), so r could be computed from them.

codes.sample: 1750 in-service teachers (84.57% female; kindergarten to high school) in Huanghua, Hebei Province, China, who use or have used generative AI. Online survey run 15 Jan–10 Feb 2025.
codes.ai_system: Generative AI tools / LLM chatbots in general (DeepSeek 64%, ERNIE Bot 48.9%, 360 Zhinao, ChatGPT, Tencent Hunyuan, etc.) used for teaching tasks
codes.dependence_measures: Generative AI addiction (GA): 4 items adapted from Hu et al. (2023), 5-point Likert, e.g. 'I have tried to limit my use of generative AI tools, but I find it difficult to do so', 'I feel uneasy or frustrated when I am unable to use generative AI tools'. α = 0.93, CR = 0.93, AVE = 0.77.

correlations.correlate: Mood regulation via AI (using GenAI to reduce stress and workload; coping motive)
correlations.correlate_instrument: 3 items adapted from Hutchison & Gunthert (2013), e.g. 'I use generative AI tools to reduce the stress...'
correlations.quote: TABLE 4 | Correlation matrix. ... GA −0.65 −0.86 −0.84 −0.88 −0.06 −0.92 0.87 (columns SE NC MR PU CA PA GA)

correlations.correlate: Self-efficacy (AI-specific: confidence in using generative AI for teaching)
correlations.correlate_instrument: 3 items adapted from Wang & Chuang (2024) AI self-efficacy scale

codes.possible_duplicate: None identified. The same authors (Du, Tang, Wang, Zou) have other GenAI papers, e.g. Du et al. 2025 on ChatGPT acceptance, but those use different samples.
codes.note: Borderline correlates: self-efficacy is AI-specific, not general or academic; mood regulation is AI use to cope with stress (possible coping motive). Table 4 looks doubtful: GA is strongly negative with every construct, yet the CA→GA path is β=0.75 while latent r(CA,GA)=−0.06. PU–PA r=0.94 also breaks Fornell–Larcker. Signs may be wrong.

codes.sample: 504 Chinese adults who used conversational AI, recruited via Wenjuanxing, March–April 2024 (572 recruited). 248 male and 261 female as reported, which sums to 509. Ages 17–54 (M = 22.540, SD = 5.146). The abstract says "Fifty-four", which conflicts with the Methods (n = 504).
codes.ai_system: Conversational AI (CAI) in general: chatbots and virtual assistants
codes.dependence_measures: Problematic Use of Conversational AI (PUCAI) scale by Hu et al.: 6 items on a 5-point scale (e.g., "I tried to reduce my use of CAI but was unsuccessful"), α = 0.934. The emotional attachment to CAI scale (Jimenez & Voss, 4 items) is a mediator, not a dependence measure.

correlations.correlate_instrument: Short Experiences in Close Relationships (ECR) attachment anxiety subscale adapted by Chen (6 items), α = 0.726
correlations.location: Table 1; Results, Descriptive Statistics and Correlation Analysis
correlations.quote: attachment anxiety is positively correlated with emotional attachment (r = 0.502, p < 0.001), anthropomorphic tendency (r = 0.480, p < 0.001), and the PUCAI (r = 0.475, p < 0.001)

codes.possible_duplicate: The PUCAI scale comes from Hu et al. (ref 12), but no sample overlap is stated. The raw data are on Mendeley Data (DOI 10.17632/jgpmrmmz8t.1).
codes.note: The only eligible correlate is attachment anxiety (r = .475). Emotional attachment to CAI and anthropomorphic tendency are not eligible correlates. Check the n: the abstract says 54, the Methods say 504, and the sex counts add up to 509. Use 504 from the Methods. The Table 2 betas come from a multivariable model and are not usable.

codes.sample: 500 health professionals (doctors, nurses, medical technologists, administrators) and educators (school teachers, lecturers, professors) in Punjab, Pakistan; described as simple random sampling; cross-sectional survey, analysed in SPSS.
codes.ai_system: AI tools at work in general (diagnostic/decision support, AI grading, LMS, chatbots/virtual assistants); not limited to conversational AI
codes.dependence_measures: "Emotional Dependency on AI" (ad hoc Likert items; Table 1 M=3.66, SD=1.14, N=500). The items are described only as "regarding job satisfaction and stress levels due to the real dependence on AI". No item content, item count or reliability is reported. Other AI measures are usage frequency, duration and context, which are not dependence measures.
codes.note: Emotional stress (ad hoc, AI-attributed) was measured. Table 2 (p.300) correlates only AI usage frequency, duration and context with overload, attention, stress and dependency. Dependency is never correlated with stress. Table 3 gives only multivariable betas. Reporting is poor (inconsistent significance notation) and the AI scope includes non-interactive systems.

codes.sample: 395 Indonesian higher-education students (vocational and academic programmes, ages 18–25, 56.46% female), recruited by convenience sampling through an online survey; cross-sectional design
codes.ai_system: Generative AI in general (ChatGPT or similar LLM-based tools) used for academic purposes
codes.dependence_measures: Generative AI Dependency (GAD) scale adapted from Goh et al. (2025). It has 11 items on a 5-point Likert scale and three dimensions: cognitive preoccupation, negative consequences and withdrawal. It was modelled as a higher-order construct in PLS-SEM.
codes.note: The only correlates measured were critical thinking dispositions and Need for Cognition, and neither is an eligible correlate. Fornell–Larcker latent correlations are reported (CT–GAD = –.218; GAD–NFC = .060; p. 121), but they involve only these ineligible constructs. No depression, anxiety, stress, loneliness or other eligible correlate was measured.

codes.sample: 10 fourth-semester English Education (EFL) students at STKIP Taman Siswa Bima, Indonesia, recruited by purposive sampling in the 2025/2026 academic year.
codes.ai_system: ChatGPT used for EFL academic writing
codes.dependence_measures: An ad hoc 16-item questionnaire on a 5-point Likert scale with two subscales: Functional Dependency on ChatGPT (FD1–FD8, α = .830, M = 3.66) and Cognitive Dependency on ChatGPT (CD1–CD8, α = .632, M = 3.29). Content validity was based on expert judgment.
codes.note: The study measures dependency on ChatGPT, but it measures no eligible correlate. The analysis is descriptive only: item frequencies, subscale means, a comparison by gender, and a thematic analysis of self-reflections. Item FD5 on writing confidence is a single dependency item, not a measure of self-efficacy. No correlations are reported, and with n = 10 the sample is very small.

codes.sample: 400 Pakistani youth aged 15–25 (200 male, 200 female), recruited by convenience sampling from high schools, colleges, universities and online communities; cross-sectional survey.
codes.ai_system: "AI technologies" in general: chatbots and learning tools, but also algorithmic social media feeds and AR filters
codes.dependence_measures: The exposure is called "AI overuse" but was measured only with the Artificial Intelligence Attitude Scale (AIAS; Grassini, 2023). The paper says it measures "attitudes, perceptions, and intentions... toward AI" and that "higher scores indicate more positive attitudes to AI." This is an attitude measure, not a dependence measure.

correlations.quote: Depression (r = .42, p < .01), anxiety (r =.38, p <.01), and stress (r =.35, p <.01) were positively and significantly correlated with AI overuse
stress (r =.35, p <.01) were positively and significantly correlated with AI overuse

codes.possible_duplicate: None identified.
codes.note: Excluded under E1: the exposure was measured with an attitude scale (AIAS), and the AI covered includes social media. The rs are listed only for reviewer checking. Data-quality concerns: demographic splits are suspiciously round, t values do not match the βs, and loneliness is mentioned in the text but was never measured.

codes.sample: 958 Chinese university students (undergraduate and postgraduate) who use ChatGPT for academic work, recruited via Sojump; age 18–28, M = 21.67, SD = 2.46; 51.6% male.
codes.ai_system: ChatGPT (generative AI used for academic work)
codes.dependence_measures: ChatGPT dependency: 6 ad hoc items adapted from prior studies [12, 44] (e.g., "I tried to reduce my use of ChatGPT to help with my assignment, but I failed"), 5-point Likert, McDonald's ω = 0.863.
codes.note: Neuroticism (NEO-FFI), impulsivity (BIS-15) and negative academic emotion (AEQ-S, incl. anxiety) were measured. The Pearson matrix is only in S1 Table, which was not in the text I received. The main text gives only HTMT (Table 4) and SEM paths, which don't count. Get S1 Table or the OSF data (osf.io/rys9q).

codes.sample: 63 undergraduate students in India, aged 18–25, who had used AI chatbots; recruited by convenience sampling through Instagram and Discord (St. Claret College, Bangalore authors). Cross-sectional online survey via Google Forms.
codes.ai_system: AI chatbots in general (conversational AI)
codes.dependence_measures: Ad hoc 15-item "Emotional Attachment to AI Scale" (5-point Likert), described as measuring "emotional reliance, comfort, and perceived connection". The items reflect emotional closeness, social substitution and normative regard (e.g., "I try to treat AI respectfully"). Total score M = 38.90, SD = 11.46. No reliability is reported.

correlations.exposure: Emotional Attachment to AI Scale (total, 15 items)
correlations.correlate_instrument: 8 extraversion items from the Big Five Inventory (BFI)
correlations.location: Page 12 (p. 233), Results; Table 1 referenced but not reproduced
correlations.quote: a weak positive correlation between participants' extraversion scores and their emotional attachment scores toward AI chatbots, r (61) = .22, p > .05.

codes.possible_duplicate: None found.
codes.note: Unclear: the exposure is "emotional attachment" to AI. It includes reliance items but also non-dependence items on respectful treatment of AI. If the reviewer accepts it as emotional dependence, the report is eligible (extraversion r = .22, n = 63). The keywords don't match the study. Table 1 is missing from the text.

codes.sample: 40 participants recruited by convenience sampling (appear to be students/young adults in Bengaluru, India); "A sample of 40 participants was recruited using convenience sampling" (p. 5).
codes.ai_system: AI conversational agents/chatbots in general (ChatGPT, Character.AI, Replika mentioned)
codes.dependence_measures: No quantitative dependence measure. Loneliness: Loneliness Inventory (Meenakshi & Krishnan, 2010). AI use: open-ended survey, with researchers coding socioemotional engagement as none/low/moderate/high by thematic analysis. A 50-item emotional dependency statement list appears in the notes (pp. 48-49), but nothing shows it was administered or scored.
codes.possible_duplicate: The PDF contains several drafts of the same study: "revised paper", "Copy of revised paper" titled "The Impact of AI Dependency on Loneliness", a "ST claret abstract" version, and raw notes. All use the same N=40 sample.
codes.note: Mixed-methods pilot. AI dependence was only coded qualitatively by the researchers; there was no self-report dependence scale. No r, means/SDs or odds ratio links loneliness to dependence; the claim is narrative only ("These results suggest a positive correlation", p. 34). E5_design is a reasonable alternative reason.

codes.sample: Two Prolific samples of English-speaking higher education students who had used GenAI for learning. Sample 1 (EFA): n = 756. Sample 2 (CFA/validation): n = 789. Total N = 1,545.
codes.ai_system: Generative AI / LLM tools used for learning in general (no single platform)
codes.dependence_measures: ED-AIL Scale (Epistemic Dependence in AI-Mediated Learning). It has 23 items rated 1–5 and five subscales: knowledge acquisition, conceptual interpretation, epistemic evaluation, knowledge production and epistemic regulation dependence. It measures uncritical epistemic dependence (over-reliance) on GenAI. Alpha for the total score = .90.
codes.note: Table 15 (p.15) correlates ED-AIL only with AI reliance, AI trust, cognitive offloading, use frequency, AI literacy, source verification, self-regulated learning, unverified output acceptance and two tasks. None is an eligible correlate; self-regulated learning is not self-control. The authors say academic self-efficacy was not measured (pp.5, 8).

codes.sample: No sample. This is a proposed study with no data collected. It plans to survey college students about AI adoption.
codes.ai_system: Generative AI chatbots in general (ChatGPT, Co-Pilot, Claude)
codes.dependence_measures: None administered. The paper defines AI addiction conceptually, following Zhou & Zhang (2024): "a psychological state [in which] people develop excessive [psychological] dependence and find it difficult to discontinue using generative AI systems". It names no measurement instrument and reports no data.
codes.possible_duplicate: The AISeL cover title mentions "Addiction and Psychopathy", but the paper's own title says only "The Role of Addiction". A later full paper by Ndagi, Muriungi, Rabaa'i & Serva with real data may exist and should be checked separately.
codes.note: AMCIS 2025 Emergent Research Forum paper: literature review, UTAUT model and hypotheses H1–H4 only ("This proposed research..."). No methods, sample, measures or results, so it is a protocol without results (E5). The planned variables (PE, EE, SI, intention to use) are not eligible correlates anyway.

codes.sample: N = 402 German-speaking active LLM users aged 18-40 (mean age 30.93, SD 6.08; 205 male, 194 female), recruited via Prolific, Aug-Sep 2025; cross-sectional online survey.
codes.ai_system: Primary LLM (e.g., ChatGPT, DeepSeek, Gemini, Copilot)
codes.dependence_measures: LLM-D12-DE (German Large Language Model Dependency Scale): Instrumental Dependency (6 items) and Relationship Dependency (6 items), 6-point Likert; optional total score.
codes.possible_duplicate: Preprint of the version published in Discover Artificial Intelligence (2026), doi 10.1007/s44163-026-01781-4; same sample. Related LLM-D12 validations (UK: Yankouskaya et al. 2025 arXiv 2506.06874; Arabic: AlShakhsi et al.) use different samples.
codes.note: Eligible correlates measured: internet addiction (IAT-7; problematic internet use) and ATAI Fear (AI-related anxiety). They are analysed only in multivariable robust MM regressions (Table 3, with PT-LLM, ATAI acceptance, NFC as co-predictors); no correlation table or zero-order r. Raw data on OSF (osf.io/j58mq) could allow derivation; check the published version for a correlation matrix.

codes.sample: 390 valid US adult Prolific participants (400 recruited), online 2x2 split-plot experiment (AI false-positive rate within subjects, risk manipulation between subjects).
codes.ai_system: A made-up ('notional') deepfake image detection AI that gives real/synthetic labels; no real AI system was used
codes.dependence_measures: Behaviour only. Compliance = 'the proportion of synthetic images identified as synthetic, out of the total number of predicted synthetic images'; reliance = the same for images labelled real (p.9). No self-report dependence scale. Other measures: trust in AI (alpha 0.89) and perceived deepfake risk (alpha 0.84).
codes.possible_duplicate: arXiv preprint 2508.01906v1 of the same PACM HCI paper.
codes.note: 'Dependence' here is behavioural compliance/reliance in an experimental task (E1). The AI is a simulated image-labelling detector, not an interactive assistant, so I2 is doubtful. No eligible correlate was measured (only trust, perceived deepfake risk, general trust in AI). Results are ANOVA and PROCESS path coefficients only; there is no correlation table.

codes.sample: 576 Chinese university students (469 undergraduate, 107 postgraduate; 70% female; aged 18–25), cross-sectional survey; 751 questionnaires distributed, 576 valid. Ethics approval from Tsinghua University.
codes.ai_system: Generative AI tools in general (AI tools used for work/study)
codes.dependence_measures: AI Dependency Scale (ADS-R): 15 items adapted from Young's Internet Addiction Test, 5-point Likert; two factors: Y_FunctionalDep (Cognitive Integration and Habit, 9 items, α=0.91) and Y_AutonomyLoss (Autonomy Erosion and Life Proxy, 6 items, α=0.89); overall α=0.92. Only the overall score appears in the correlation matrix.

correlations.correlate: Task-domain self-efficacy (confidence in completing tasks independently in one's main AI-use domain)
correlations.correlate_instrument: 3 items adapted from Venkatesh et al. (2003) self-efficacy scale (Mo_TaskSE), α=0.82

correlations.correlate: Preference for instant gratification (reward sensitivity; possible impulsivity proxy)
correlations.correlate_instrument: 4 items developed from SPSRQ reward sensitivity concepts (Torrubia et al., 2001), α=0.72

correlations.correlate: Erosion of self-efficacy (perceived decline in own ability attributed to AI use)
correlations.correlate_instrument: 4 ad hoc items based on Bandura's SCT (M_Erosion), α=0.83

codes.possible_duplicate: None identified.
codes.note: Borderline. Hinges on task-domain self-efficacy (r=.235) counting as academic self-efficacy; its items ask about the main AI-use domain. Instant gratification is reward sensitivity, not an impulsivity scale. Erosion of self-efficacy is AI-specific. No subscale r values given. * means p<.10. If neither proxy is accepted, use no_eligible_correlate.

codes.sample: No participants or empirical data. This is a theoretical/conceptual position paper by a single author.
codes.ai_system: AI-based test agents / LLM-assisted software testing tools
codes.dependence_measures: None. Overreliance is described only conceptually, as a taxonomy of modes (Table 1). The proposed future reliance measures are behavioural (e.g., "acceptance of incorrect claims, the frequency of challenged outputs, evidence inspection behavior, human overrides"), not self-report scales.
codes.note: Conceptual framework paper (arXiv preprint / LNCS). The author says: "Without case study evidence, claims about the overreliance remain interpretive" (p.7). There is no quantitative dependence measure and no psychological correlate. If the design reason did not apply, E1 (no dependence measure) would also apply.

codes.sample: N = 402 German-speaking active LLM users recruited via Prolific (Germany, Austria, Switzerland), aged 18–40 (M = 30.93, SD = 6.08); 205 male, 194 female, 3 no response; data collected Aug–Sep 2025.
codes.ai_system: Primary LLM (e.g., ChatGPT, DeepSeek, Gemini, Copilot)
codes.dependence_measures: German Large Language Model Dependency Scale (LLM-D12-DE), 12 items on a 6-point scale, with two subscales: Instrumental Dependency (6 items) and Relationship Dependency (6 items). A total score can optionally be computed.
codes.possible_duplicate: No sample overlap is apparent. The same team published a UK validation (Yankouskaya et al., 2025, ACM Trans Web) and an Arabic validation (AlShakhsi et al., 2026, Arab J Sci Eng), but those used different samples.
codes.note: Two eligible correlates were measured: internet addiction (IAT-7) and ATAI Fear (AI-related anxiety). But their links to LLM-D12 subscales are reported only as robust multiple regression coefficients (Table 3, p.15) with PT-LLM, ATAI acceptance, ATAI fear, NFC and IA entered together. No correlation matrix is given. The raw data on OSF (osf.io/j58mq) could let a reviewer compute zero-order r.

codes.sample: No primary sample. "Primary data collection from field surveys is not performed." (p. 1). Secondary data-driven conceptual paper.
codes.ai_system: Virtual assistants, chatbots, AI companions (general)
codes.dependence_measures: None. Emotional dependency on AI is discussed conceptually only; no quantitative scale or item administered.
codes.note: This is a theoretical/narrative paper relying on secondary sources (p. 1: "A secondary data-driven approach is adopted... Primary data collection from field surveys is not performed."). It mentions "basic statistical methods" but reports no data, measures or statistics. Discussion of loneliness/stress/well-being is narrative only.

codes.sample: 373 undergraduate nursing students (254 female, 119 male; mean age 20.84±3.54) at Muğla Sıtkı Koçman University, Türkiye; convenience sample; face-to-face survey, February 2025; cross-sectional.
codes.ai_system: Artificial intelligence in general (AI tools), measured with the Scale for Dependence on Artificial Intelligence
codes.dependence_measures: Scale for Dependence on Artificial Intelligence (DAI; Morales-García et al., 2024; Turkish adaptation by Savaş, 2024): 5 items, one dimension, 5-point Likert, total score 5–25; α = .82 in this study; M = 12.39, SD = 4.28.

correlations.correlate_instrument: Artificial Intelligence Anxiety Scale (AIAS; Wang & Wang 2022, Turkish adaptation by Terzi), 21 items, total score
correlations.quote: a moderate positive correlation was identified between AIAS and DAI scores (r = .415, p <0.001)

codes.possible_duplicate: Presented as an oral presentation at the 8th International and 12th National Congress of Psychiatric Nursing (Diyarbakır, April 2025), so a conference abstract may cover the same sample. A related MSc thesis (Sarıtaş) is possible.
codes.note: The only eligible correlate is AI-related anxiety (the AIAS, a fear-of-AI scale). The other variables are attitudes toward AI (GAAIS-PA and GAAIS-NA), which are not eligible correlates. The regression betas in Table 4 combine two predictors, so they do not count as zero-order associations.

codes.sample: 152 Gen Z respondents in India (aged 18–30; 55.26% female), recruited by convenience sampling through an online Google Forms survey
codes.ai_system: AI chatbots in general (ChatGPT 72.37%, Gemini, Claude, Perplexity, Copilot/Grok)
codes.dependence_measures: Single ad hoc Likert/multiple-choice items reported only as frequencies. Examples: "felt emotionally dependent on AI for comfort and reassurance" (Fig. 32), "Anxiety When Unable to Access AI" (Fig. 29), "Attachment Making It Hard to Reduce AI Use" (Fig. 31), "AI as First Option for Emotional Stress" (Fig. 30). Fig. 32 explicitly asks about dependence.
codes.note: Descriptive percentages only; no correlations or group comparisons. No eligible correlate measured: "feeling less lonely after AI interaction" (Fig. 15) is a perceived AI effect, not loneliness, and "anxiety when unable to access AI" is a dependence indicator. Even if either counted, no zero-order association is reported, so it would fail on E4.

codes.sample: Convenience sample of 718 nursing researchers (master's/PhD) from Egypt and Saudi Arabia, split at random into two halves of 359 for EFA and CFA; 82.6% female, mean age 33.39 (SD 5.469). Online survey, March–June 2024. A separate pilot of 40 researchers was used for face validity.
codes.ai_system: AI tools for research in general (ChatGPT, Gemini, GitHub Copilot, Poe)
codes.dependence_measures: Researcher Artificial Intelligence Addiction Scale (RAIAS), developed in this study: 22 items rated 1–5, with five dimensions (compulsive behavior, overdependency, functional impairment, withdrawal, tolerance). Alpha = 0.924, omega = 0.870.
codes.possible_duplicate: Unknown from this text. The same RAIAS sample (Egypt/Saudi nursing researchers, 2024) could be reused in later substantive papers by El-Sayed, Asal, Alasqah et al.
codes.note: This is a psychometric study of the scale only. The survey had three parts (screening, demographics, RAIAS items) and contained no external psychological measures. The only correlations reported are between the RAIAS subscales (latent r = 0.408–0.621, Table 4). The supplement is described as holding only the scale items and the EFA variance table, so nothing relevant appears to be missing.

codes.sample: No human participants. Corpus data come from Universal Dependencies treebanks in eight low-resource languages (e.g., Bambara, Bhojpuri, Cantonese, Erzya, Kiche, Komi Zyrian, Nigerian Pidgin and Yoruba).
codes.ai_system: GPT-4o, Gemini 2.0 Flash, Command R+ and Llama 3.1, used as syntactic dependency parsers
codes.dependence_measures: None. Here "dependency" means syntactic dependency parsing, an NLP task scored with UAS/LAS. There is no psychological measure of dependence on AI.
codes.note: This is a computational linguistics paper about LLM-based syntactic dependency parsing ("We study whether incorporating symbolic rules can aid large language models in dependency parsing"). "Dependence" is used in another sense, so it is out of scope (E3). E1 could also be argued, since there is no dependence measure. No psychological correlates were measured and there are no human participants.

codes.sample: Students at Eastlake High School who took an anonymous survey. N = 557 completed entries (the abstract says "over 600"). The AI-hours vs GPA analysis used n = 27 and the sleep vs GPA analysis used n = 21.
codes.ai_system: Generative AI tools for homework (ChatGPT, Claude, Microsoft Copilot mentioned)
codes.dependence_measures: There is no dependence measure. The paper calls it "AI Homework Dependency", but the only AI variable is "AI Homework Duration (Hours/Wk)" (Table 1, p.14), described as "weekly homework time spent using AI tools" (p.8). That is a measure of how long students used AI, not a dependence, addiction or over-reliance scale.
codes.note: Excluded under E1 because the AI measure is only hours of use, despite the "dependency" label. Even with a lenient reading, it would not qualify: the only correlate reported with the AI variable is GPA (r = −0.573, n = 27), which is not an eligible correlate. Sleep duration (not sleep quality) was correlated only with GPA, not with AI use. No correlation matrix is given.

codes.sample: 50 EFL teachers selected by purposive sampling from urban and rural institutions (country not stated; authors based in Multan/Bahawalpur, Pakistan). They took part in semi-structured interviews.
codes.ai_system: ChatGPT and Meta AI (BlenderBot, LLaMA) used by L2/EFL learners for academic purposes
codes.dependence_measures: None. The study does not use a quantitative measure of dependence. 'Over-dependence' on AI appears only as a theme from thematic analysis of teacher interviews.
codes.note: Qualitative design (p. 918): "This study employed a qualitative research design, focusing on semi-structured interviews with 50 EFL teachers... Thematic analysis was used." No scales, no psychological correlates and no statistics. The references use placeholder DOIs (10.xxxx/yyyy).

codes.sample: 200 B.Sc. Nursing students (Generation Z, ages 17–28, 74% female) at the College of Nursing, L.L.R.M Medical College, Meerut, India. Convenience sample, data collected April 2026.
codes.ai_system: AI dialogue tools in general (ChatGPT 54.5%, Google, Meta AI; Gemini and Copilot named in the intro)
codes.dependence_measures: Self-structured "level of AI usage" tool (score range 18–90; low/moderate/high), reported throughout as "AI reliance" / over-reliance on AI dialogue. The items and their content are not described.

correlations.exposure: AI reliance (self-structured level of AI usage tool, total)

codes.possible_duplicate: none
codes.note: The exposure is weakly specified. The tool is named "level of AI usage", so it might measure use rather than reliance; check against E1. The paper is internally inconsistent: the abstract conclusion gives r=0.38 for academic stress, but Table 6 and the Discussion give 0.36. Signs and table numbers are also mixed up. Cognitive ability is not an eligible correlate.

codes.sample: 872 tertiary students (301 STEM, 571 non-STEM) from public and private HEIs in Luzon, Philippines; mean age 19.32 (SD 6.34); 54.7% female; online survey, November 2024.
codes.ai_system: Meta AI chatbot in Facebook Messenger (Llama-based LLM chatbot)
codes.dependence_measures: Ad hoc 27-item, 4-point Likert instrument with nine domains of 'AI chatbot dependency' (Table 2). These include an 'AI chatbot reliance' domain (e.g., unease when unable to access, dependency to manage academic challenges; M = 2.29, SD = 0.58) and a 'Dependency risks' domain. Cronbach's alpha is reported only as >0.70.
codes.note: Descriptive only: domain means/SDs and Mann-Whitney U tests of STEM vs non-STEM. No eligible correlate was measured. The 'Psychological' domain asks whether the chatbot reduces anxiety/stress or boosts confidence; that is a perceived benefit, not a measure of anxiety, stress or self-esteem. No correlations are reported.

codes.sample: 300 university students (150 male, 150 female), aged 18–40, undergraduate and postgraduate, from universities in Islamabad, Pakistan; convenience sample, surveyed online and face to face.
codes.ai_system: Generative AI tools in general for academic use (ChatGPT 51%, Google Gemini, Quillbot, Microsoft Copilot, Grammarly AI, Claude)
codes.dependence_measures: Generative AI Dependency Scale (GAIDS; Goh et al., cited in the text as 2015 but listed as 2025 in the references): 11 items, 5-point Likert scale; dimensions are cognitive preoccupation, negative consequences and withdrawal; alpha = .978. Only the total score is used in the analyses.

correlations.quote: there was weak and non-significant correlation between AI dependency and academic procrastination r = .034, p > .05

codes.possible_duplicate: None identified.
codes.note: Table 4 prints .03 and the text gives .034. Table 7 is a single-predictor regression with the same value (β = .034). The only other variable, AI literacy, is not an eligible correlate. No subscale correlations are reported. The text has inconsistencies: it calls the indirect effect significant although its CI upper bound is printed as -0.00.

codes.sample: 110 adolescents in Uzbekistan (60 boys, 54.5%; 50 girls, 45.5%) (p. 198, Table 1).
codes.ai_system: Artificial intelligence technologies in general (chatbots, educational platforms, virtual assistants), discussed in theory only and not measured.
codes.dependence_measures: None. The only instruments listed are Rogers & Diamond's 'Social-psychological adaptation' questionnaire and Rezapkina's 'Social intelligence' questionnaire (p. 198). The study has no measure of excessive or problematic AI use, AI dependence or AI use frequency.
codes.note: The title refers to 'excessive use of AI', but the only results are Mann-Whitney comparisons between girls and boys on the Rogers-Diamond adaptation subscales, including Escapism (U=5332.500, p=0.154). The study never links AI use or dependence to any variable, and it reports no correlations. The Social Intelligence results are mentioned but not reported.

codes.sample: Turkish university students who had used ChatGPT, recruited by convenience sampling. Phase 1 (scale adaptation): N = 413 (67.8% female, mean age 21.55). Phase 2 (mediation model): a separate sample of N = 449 (58.8% female, mean age 21.83).
codes.ai_system: ChatGPT (generative AI chatbot)
codes.dependence_measures: None. The only AI measure is the ChatGPT Usage Scale (Abbas et al., 2024), Turkish adaptation: 8 items such as "I use ChatGPT for my course assignments", rated 1 (never) to 6 (always), α = 0.94. It measures how often or how much ChatGPT is used, not dependence, addiction, problematic use or over-reliance.
codes.note: The AI measure only covers how often ChatGPT is used. The Discussion mentions "reliance", but no dependence scale was given. Self-control (Brief Self-Control Scale) and academic wellbeing were measured, but the text has only PROCESS/SEM paths controlling for age (usage→self-control β = −0.13) and no correlation table. So E4 would also apply.

codes.sample: 44 undergraduate psychology students at Kwantlen Polytechnic University, Canada, who use ChatGPT; online Qualtrics survey with bonus points/course credit as incentive.
codes.ai_system: ChatGPT
codes.dependence_measures: "GPT Dependence": an author-designed 5-point Likert measure, apparently one item among the ten core survey questions. The wording of the item is not reported. The authors describe it as "dependence on the tool" or "over-reliance". Mean 2.861, SD 1.167, N = 44.

correlations.correlate_instrument: Ad hoc 5-point Likert item, author-designed (wording not reported)
correlations.quote: 2. Procrastination .546** ... significant moderate positive correlation between GPT Dependence and Procrastination (r = .546, p < .001)

codes.possible_duplicate: None found. The authors plan a separate qualitative paper on the open-ended responses from the same survey; it would not be a quantitative duplicate.
codes.note: Borderline. The exposure looks like one ad hoc item with unreported wording; it counts only if it explicitly asks about dependence (the label suggests so). Procrastination is also one item and is specific to ChatGPT ("caused by ChatGPT use"). If either is rejected, the decision becomes E1 or no_eligible_correlate.

codes.sample: 200 public-school teachers in Santo Domingo de los Tsáchilas, Ecuador, reporting on their students' AI use. The paper describes both semi-structured interviews and a survey of dichotomous and multiple-choice items.
codes.ai_system: AI tools in general (virtual assistants, text generators, automated platforms) used by students for academic tasks
codes.dependence_measures: None validated. Teachers answered single items, reported only as percentages, about how often students use AI (87%), whether creativity has declined (74%), and whether students trust AI more than their own knowledge (81%). No item explicitly asks about dependence, addiction or inability to stop. The authors call frequent use "dependencia tecnológica".
codes.note: This is a descriptive teacher survey. The methods section calls it both qualitative and quantitative. It reports only percentages and no correlations. No eligible correlate was measured (the outcomes were creativity, critical thinking and autonomy). E5 (qualitative design) would also fit, but the main problem is that there is no dependence measure: the AI item asks only about frequency of use.

codes.sample: No human participants. The units of analysis are AI providers: consumer pricing tiers of OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, Mistral, DeepSeek, Qwen, Character.AI and Microsoft Copilot, plus Google Trends defection-search around five dated 'squeeze' events.
codes.ai_system: Consumer LLM chatbots and AI companions in general (ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, Mistral, DeepSeek, Qwen, Character.AI, Copilot)
codes.dependence_measures: None at the individual level. 'Reliance' is inferred from commercial features (free-tier limits, tier ladders, caps, portability, metering changes) and from relative Google Trends search interest. The author says so directly: 'pricing measures the machinery built to capture dependency, not dependency itself.' There is no self- or informant-report scale.
codes.possible_duplicate: The paper calls itself the third part of the author's 'reliance trilogy' (institutional, generational, consumer). The other two papers are by the same author (NM AI Research) and may also be in the search results, but this paper shares no participant sample with them.
codes.note: This is a working paper that profiles AI providers' pricing and market data. It has no survey and no psychological correlates, so I1, I3 and I4 all fail. E5_design (non-empirical/theoretical) could also be argued, but E1 fits best. The text includes a section of instructions addressed to AI summarisers; I treated it only as part of the paper's content and it did not affect this screening decision.

codes.sample: No empirical sample; narrative/theoretical review paper.
codes.ai_system: AI in general (virtual assistants such as Siri/Alexa, AI in healthcare and mental health care)
codes.dependence_measures: None. AI dependency is only discussed conceptually; no quantitative dependence measure was administered.
codes.note: A narrative review/commentary about AI in healthcare, trust, physical and mental health, and AI dependency. It has no methods, participants, measures or results section; the abstract says it 'explores the advantages and drawbacks of AI dependency' using literature only (e.g., 'AI Dependency' section, p. 76).

codes.sample: 150 second-semester engineering students (6 intact classes; ~75 experimental, ~75 control) and 4 English lecturers, Universitas Muhammadiyah Tangerang, Indonesia. Quasi-experimental mixed-methods design.
codes.ai_system: Generative AI writing tools in general (ChatGPT, Gemini, and similar platforms) used for academic English writing
codes.dependence_measures: Ad hoc 'AI-generated text dependence questionnaire' (5-point Likert): "frequency of AI use, reliance on AI for idea generation... paragraph writing... final draft production, lack of revision after AI use, difficulty writing without AI, and perceived need for AI in writing tasks" (p. 6). Pre/post means reported (Table 2).
codes.note: Other measures: writing performance, originality/similarity, academic integrity, learner agency (incl. self-regulation and confidence subdimensions), perceptions. None is an eligible correlate. The correlation analysis described in the methods (p. 7) was never reported; only Welch t-tests on gain scores.

codes.sample: Study 1: 142 university students (incl. graduate students) at Qufu Normal University, China, who had used generative AI (63 M, 79 F; mean age 24.32). Study 2: 132 students in an experiment; Study 3: 160 students in a 2×2 experiment.
codes.ai_system: Generative AI in general (ChatGPT, DeepSeek); ChatGPT in the experiments
codes.dependence_measures: Generative AI Dependence Scale (Tang et al., 2023; 3 items, α = 0.79, 5-point Likert, e.g., "I depend on generative AI to handle or assist with academic research/study tasks"). Study 1 used it as a trait measure. In Studies 2–3 it was only a manipulation check after AI dependence was manipulated experimentally.
codes.note: Study 1 linked AI dependence only to creativity (r = −0.20) and critical thinking (r = −0.44); neither is eligible. Study 2 measured self-efficacy of unstated type (3 items), but only against the manipulated condition, not the dependence scale. Its means are in Table 2, which was not in the text received. The reviewer may want to check it.

codes.sample: 438 Turkish university students (24.9% male; mean age 21.65, SD 3.65; range 18–50), convenience sample, cross-sectional online survey.
codes.ai_system: AI in general (generative AI/chatbots discussed); dependence on AI not tied to one tool
codes.dependence_measures: Scale for Dependence on Artificial Intelligence (Morales-García et al., 2024), 5 items, 5-point Likert; Turkish adaptation by Savaş (2024); α = .75 in this study. Only the total score is used.

correlations.exposure: AI dependency (Scale for Dependence on AI, total)
AI dependency (Scale for Dependence on AI, total)
correlations.correlate_instrument: Ten-Item Personality Inventory (TIPI), extraversion subscale, 2 items, α=.65

codes.possible_duplicate: None apparent.
codes.note: Psychological distress is reported only as the DASS-21 total. No separate depression, anxiety or stress correlations are given. TIPI measured all Big Five traits, but only extraversion is reported. The note says "*p < .01, ** p < .001", which is unusual. The moderation analysis (PROCESS) gives multivariable B values only, and these are not usable.

codes.sample: 1,047 undergraduate Basic Education students, Universidad Pedagógica Veracruzana, Mexico; 78.6% female (823), 21.4% male (224); cross-sectional Google Forms survey.
codes.ai_system: Generative AI tools in general (ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini mentioned)
codes.dependence_measures: INPADE Dependence on GenAI subscale (DEP): initially 10 items, final 6 items, 5-point Likert, α = .890, ω = .892, e.g., 'Me he vuelto dependiente de las herramientas de IA'. The CFA also reports two-factor DEP submodels (DEH, USO).
codes.possible_duplicate: Same authors published a related scale (Torres-Gastelú & Torres-Real, 2025, Ciencia Latina 9(2)) on perception of AI in higher education. It may come from the same student population, but this is not confirmed.
codes.note: The only correlate is intention to pay (INA), which is not an eligible correlate. Its only link to dependence is an SEM path (β = .297). Item 16 ('Prefiero dejar mis tareas al final porque confío en que la IA me ayudará') sounds like procrastination, but it is part of the dependence scale, not a separate measure. No psychological correlates and no correlation matrix.

codes.sample: Not available in retrieved text. Title indicates Indonesian university students (mahasiswa Indonesia); sample size not reported in the retrieved portion.
codes.ai_system: AI in general ("Artificial Intelligence Dependency"); the specific tools cannot be confirmed from the retrieved text.
codes.dependence_measures: Not verifiable. The title names "Artificial Intelligence Dependency" as the predictor. The reference list cites Zhang et al. (2024) and Wu et al. (2026, AI dependence scale), but the instrument actually used is not described in the retrieved text.
codes.possible_duplicate: Likely an Indonesian undergraduate thesis (skripsi, 2026). Check for a related journal article by the same author; no overlap can be confirmed from the reference list.
codes.note: The retrieved full text contains only the reference list (Daftar Pustaka, pp. 80-89). The methods and results chapters are missing. Based on the title, the thesis probably studies the effect of AI dependency on academic self-efficacy, which is an eligible correlate, and a simple regression or r may be reported. Retrieve the full thesis to check for a zero-order r or a single-predictor beta.

codes.sample: None. This is a theoretical/conceptual paper with no participants or empirical data.
codes.ai_system: Generative AI tools in arts education (Midjourney, DALL-E, Stable Diffusion, Suno, Udio, ChatGPT, Gemini)
codes.dependence_measures: None. 'Cognitive dependence' on AI is only discussed conceptually, drawing on cognitive load theory, cognitive offloading and Bloom's taxonomy. No quantitative measure is administered.
codes.note: Full text reviewed (pp. 198-207). The abstract describes the work as theoretical: it systematises mechanisms, proposes pedagogical strategies and a three-level conceptual model, and offers 'a theoretical basis for future empirical research'. The conclusions call empirical testing a future direction. No data, scales or statistics are reported.

codes.sample: 89 prospective mathematics teachers (students), Universitas Negeri Semarang, Indonesia; chosen by simple random sampling
codes.ai_system: AI in general for academic work (ChatGPT, Gemini, Claude and similar are named)
codes.dependence_measures: A 20-item AI dependence questionnaire ("instrumen ketergantungan kecerdasan buatan"), modified from an existing instrument. It has five aspects: usage, feelings, usefulness, ease of access, and dependence. Cronbach's alpha = 0.785.
codes.note: This paper only tests the psychometrics of the scale: item-total Pearson correlations (Table 2) and Cronbach's alpha. No other psychological variable was measured, so none of the eligible correlates (depression, anxiety, stress, loneliness and the rest) can be paired with AI dependence. The only correlations reported are item-total values, which do not count.

codes.sample: None. This is a conceptual paper with no participants or empirical data.
codes.ai_system: AI systems in professional work in general (AI substitution and mediation of professional tasks)
codes.dependence_measures: None. 'AI dependency' is discussed only in theory, as an organisation or system losing its independent human capability. There is no self-report or informant-report measure.
codes.note: Excluded on design: conceptual paper. P.1: "Conceptual research paper. Numerical examples are illustrative unless explicitly identified as empirical." P.10: "This paper is conceptual." No data, dependence measure or psychological correlates. 'Dependency' means organisational skill loss, not individual psychological dependence, so E3 would also apply.

codes.sample: 145 students (2024 and 2025 cohorts) at STIKes Muhammadiyah Bojonegoro, a health sciences college in Indonesia. They were recruited by voluntary response sampling: 158 responses were collected and 13 duplicates removed. The design was a cross-sectional survey.
codes.ai_system: "AI technology" in general (chatbots, virtual assistants and other learning AI tools), used for study
codes.dependence_measures: An ad hoc 4-item "Dependency on AI" (X5) subscale on a 5-point Likert scale, part of a 25-item AI utilization questionnaire. Its item-total correlations ranged from 0.783 to 0.912 and Cronbach's alpha was 0.892 (Table 1, p. 2234). Mean = 10.772, SD = 3.244.
codes.note: The only outcome is "learning independence" (5 items: planning, effort, assignments, self-evaluation, responsibility), which is not an eligible correlate. No zero-order r is reported either: dependence appears only in a 5-predictor multiple regression (beta = -0.176). If learning independence counted as self-control, the reason would be E4.

codes.sample: No primary sample. Secondary descriptive synthesis of published meta-analyses and one RCT (Barcaui 2025, 120 undergraduates), as cited.
codes.ai_system: Generative AI / ChatGPT in education
codes.dependence_measures: None. 'Dependence' is discussed only conceptually (AI-assisted vs AI-dependent learning). No dependence scale was administered.
codes.note: Methods p.2: 'This study uses a secondary research design. No survey, interview, questionnaire, experiment, or primary data collection was conducted.' This is a narrative review of meta-analyses on learning outcomes. It has no dependence measure and no eligible psychological correlates.

codes.sample: No empirical sample. Conceptual threat-model paper with no participants or data collection.
codes.ai_system: External conversational AI / LLMs used in organizations (general)
codes.dependence_measures: None. 'Evaluative dependence' and overreliance are discussed only conceptually and formally (e.g., criterion-weight vectors, frame-transfer equations). No self-report dependence scale is administered.
codes.possible_duplicate: Cites a related conceptual paper by the same author: Nekludoff (2026), 'When the assistant becomes the norm...', doi:10.5281/zenodo.22793609. Neither paper appears to have data.
codes.note: Theoretical/conceptual paper. The Limitations section (p. 24) states: 'this paper proposes a threat class and threat model. It does not estimate the real-world prevalence'. The Research Agenda section (p. 23) states: 'The threat model proposed here is conceptual and requires empirical validation.' No psychological correlates were measured.

codes.sample: 350 undergraduate programming students (IT and Engineering, HNDIT/HNDEng) at SLIATE institutes, Sri Lanka; 56.6% male; mostly aged 21–23; Years 2–3. Cross-sectional online survey, multi-stage purposive sampling.
codes.ai_system: AI tools in programming education in general (generative coding assistants, chatbots, e.g., ChatGPT, GitHub Copilot)
codes.dependence_measures: Unproductive AI Usage (UAIU): ad hoc 5-item, 5-point Likert scale "capturing over-reliance on AI, copying without understanding, dependency, shortcut usage, and lack of critical evaluation" (α = 0.83; CR = 0.87; AVE = 0.59; M = 3.21, SD = 0.77).

correlations.correlate_instrument: Ad hoc 18-item mindfulness measure (general items on a 6-point frequency scale, reverse-coded; α = 0.91)
correlations.quote: Table 5. Correlation matrix. ... Mindfulness 0.49 0.15 0.52 0.56 0.48 0.50 1 (row Mindfulness, column UAIU = 0.15)

codes.possible_duplicate: None identified. The study is part of a wider PhD programme (Waidyarathna, University of Kelaniya), so a thesis or other articles may use the same SLIATE sample. Raw data are on OSF (doi:10.17605/OSF.IO/XCWZT).
codes.note: The sign of r is uncertain. The text calls UAIU correlations "negative" but prints them unsigned, and betas shown as −0.18 in the abstract appear as 0.18 in the body, so minus signs may be lost. The OSF raw data could settle this. Red flags: implausibly round numbers and hypothesis labels that don't match between sections.

codes.sample: 404 adult regular companion-chatbot users (weekly use ≥1 month) recruited via CloudResearch Connect; ages 18–73, mostly US (93.6%), 59.7% men.
codes.ai_system: Companion chatbots (Snapchat MyAI 31.6%, Character.ai 30.4%, Replika 22.6%, others)
codes.dependence_measures: Adapted Generalized Problematic Internet Use Scale (GPIUS2; Caplan 2010) measuring problematic chatbot use (shortened/adapted; α = .91 cited for original scale).
codes.possible_duplicate: Extended version with appendix on arXiv (https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.21596), same sample of 404. Appendix Figure 6 has the correlation matrix with the original variable names.
codes.note: Eligible correlates were measured: loneliness (ULS-8), self-esteem (B-RSES), perceived social support (MSPSS) and Big Five incl. neuroticism (BFI-10). The Spearman matrix (Figure 1, p.4) is an image with no values in the extracted text. The text reports only GPIUS2–usage correlations (r=0.303, 0.337) and multivariable betas (GPIUS2→loneliness 0.166). Check the figure for annotated values.

codes.sample: 36 Diploma in English for Professional Communication (LG120) students at UiTM Cawangan Johor, Malaysia, who had taken Literature (ALS103); purposive sample.
codes.ai_system: AI tools in general, used for literature appreciation assignments
codes.dependence_measures: None. The text says "perceptions and dependency", but C1–C8 are single perception items (helps understanding, generates ideas, improves writing, saves time, builds confidence, helps close reading, reduces critical thinking, is beneficial). Other sections cover adoption reasons, frequency and trust. No item asks about dependence or addiction.
codes.note: Personality was a self-declared category (introvert/extrovert/ambivert/omnivert) from an online quiz, not a Big Five scale. Analyses: a chi-square test (personality × adoption reasons) and ANOVAs on C1–C8 (Tables 3–4). Group means and SDs are reported, but the AI measure is perceived benefits, not dependence. E1 applies despite the "dependency" wording.

codes.sample: 622 university students (57% male, aged 18–25) from 9 comprehensive universities in China, surveyed online via Wenjuanxing in May 2025 (676 collected, 54 excluded).
codes.ai_system: Generative AI (GAI) tools in general used for academic tasks (e.g., ChatGPT mentioned)
codes.dependence_measures: GAI dependency: 5 items adapted from Acosta-Enriquez et al. (e.g., "I find it hard to do my academic tasks without GAI tools"), 5-point Likert; retained items GAID1–4, GAID6; CA = 0.876, CR = 0.910, AVE = 0.670.

correlations.correlate_instrument: 5 items adapted from Rustam & Tentama (4 retained: AS1–AS4), CA = 0.953
6-item academic anxiety scale adapted from Finch et al. (4 retained: ACA1–ACA4), CA = 0.876

codes.possible_duplicate: None identified.
codes.note: Table 3 gives zero-order correlations. Performance expectations and desire thinking are not eligible correlates. Academic anxiety is counted under anxiety, which the reviewer should confirm. Table 7 path coefficients (e.g., AS→GAID 0.803) and Table 5 HTMT values (0.875) are not zero-order and were not used. Table 3 does not say whether it uses PLS latent scores or observed scale scores.

codes.sample: 1,589 Chinese adolescents from six primary, middle and high schools in 5 provinces, surveyed November 2025 (765 boys, 824 girls; mean age 14.62 ± 1.65). A supplementary discriminant-validity analysis used n = 1,676 from the same survey.
