codes.ai_system: Generative AI in general (examples given: ChatGPT, Kimi, Siri, Copilot, Doubao); human-AI interaction
codes.dependence_measures: AI-related affective dependence scale: 5 items adapted from the craving dimension of the Emotional Dependence Scale (Sirvent-Ruiz et al., 2022), with the target changed to AI. One factor; α = 0.946; CR = 0.890; AVE = 0.620; S-CVI/Ave = 0.96. The authors describe it as emotional/psychological reliance on AI, not AI addiction.

correlations.quote: Anxiety was also positively correlated with AI dependence (r = 0.166, p < 0.001)

correlations.correlate: Short-form video addiction (proxy for problematic social media use; check)
correlations.correlate_instrument: Short-form video addiction scale (8 items implied; instrument not named)
correlations.quote: The correlation between the two total scores was modest (r = 0.219, p < 0.001)

codes.possible_duplicate: The discriminant-validity check uses data 'from the same school-based survey' that also measured short-form video addiction. The same author group (Liu Y, Xiao T, Wang J) publishes often from school surveys, so check other papers for overlap with this sample.
codes.note: The primary correlate is anxiety (GAD-2), r = 0.166. Emotional abuse (r = 0.214) and physical activity (r = −0.044) are not eligible correlates. Network edges are partial correlations and mediation betas are adjusted, so neither is usable. Whether short-form video addiction counts as problematic social media use is up to the reviewer. The scale measures emotional dependence on AI (I1).

codes.sample: N = 684 undergraduate and postgraduate students who use Gen-AI for academic tasks, from six public and private higher education institutions (country not stated; authors are in Lahore, Pakistan). Data collected October 2025 to February 2026; pilot study N = 60.
codes.ai_system: Generative AI platforms / Gen-AI tools in general, used for academic tasks
codes.dependence_measures: Passive Gen-AI Dependency (PGD): "Measured using a 5-item scale adapted from automated tool dependency inventories, assessing complete delegation of ideation, synthesis, writing, and problem-solving to AI" (5-point Likert scale).
codes.note: Only eligible correlate: academic self-efficacy. Reported only as PLS-SEM path PGD->ASE (β = -0.421, t = 10.332). Strategic Cognitive Offloading also predicts ASE (R2 = 0.435), so this is not a single-predictor beta. Discriminant validity is HTMT only (max 0.741). No correlation matrix, Fornell–Larcker table, or group means.

codes.sample: 149 users of the Xuanhe AI platform were recruited, and 108 valid participants were retained. They were aged 16–28 (M = 21.15, SD = 1.802), 78.7% were male and most were Chinese undergraduates. Ten of them were also interviewed.
codes.ai_system: Xuanhe AI, a Chinese role-playing LLM chatbot platform (four characters: Asuka, Hu Tao, Yandere Girlfriend, Satoru Gojo)
codes.dependence_measures: Media Dependency Scale: 6 items rated on a 7-point scale, 'adapted from the Facebook Addiction Scale', completed for each of the four chatbots (alpha .752–.891). This counts as an eligible addiction-type exposure measure.
codes.possible_duplicate: arXiv preprint 2411.17157 of the same Chinese CHI '24 paper. No other overlapping sample was identified.
codes.note: The only other variables measured were demographics, perceived anthropomorphism (HRIES) and user satisfaction with the chatbot (3 items). Satisfaction with a chatbot is not life satisfaction or well-being. No depression, anxiety, loneliness or other eligible correlate was measured. The results are reported only as multivariable regressions with demographic controls (Tables 2–5).

codes.sample: N = 208 university students in India (Lovely Professional University author), aged 18–28 (M = 21.26, SD = 1.77); 79.8% female (166 F, 42 M). All participants used AI tools for academic work. Online survey; the paper says sampling was "random".
codes.ai_system: Generative AI tools used for academic tasks (writing, research, editing)
codes.dependence_measures: Generative AI Dependence Scale (GAIDS; labelled "GAI" in the tables). Total score M = 27.308, SD = 8.1235, range 11–55. The paper does not report item count, citation or reliability. The abstract mentions subscales (AI opinion, AI study, AI creativity), but no subscale results are reported in the text.
codes.possible_duplicate: None identified.
codes.note: Mind-wandering (MWQ; r = .231 with GAI, Table 5) is not an eligible correlate. The abstract gives correlations of "-.15 to -.33" for subscales (AI opinion/study/creativity) with self-esteem, but these are not reported in the full text; only the total-score r = -.169 can be extracted. Quality concerns: several references look fabricated, and the interpretation of Table 5 contradicts itself.

codes.sample: 417 Chinese undergraduates aged 18–24 (M = 21.21, SD = 1.48; 70.3% female). Stratified random sample from one normal university in Southwest China; cross-sectional online survey.
codes.ai_system: Generative AI / AI tools in general, used for academic purposes
codes.dependence_measures: AI Dependence Scale for Chinese Undergraduates (AIDep-22; Wu et al., 2026). 22 items on a 5-point scale, alpha = .93. Four dimensions: emotional dependence, functional dependence, cognitive dependence and loss of control. Only the global score is correlated with the other variables.

correlations.correlate_instrument: Academic Procrastination Scale-Short Form (APS-S; Yockey, 2016), 5 items
correlations.quote: Academic procrastination was positively correlated with AI dependence (r = .475, p < .001).

codes.possible_duplicate: The AIDep-22 comes from a validation paper by Wu et al. (2026) that also used Chinese undergraduates. It is not clear whether that paper used the same sample, so the reviewer should check.
codes.note: Table 4 prints the r rounded as .47. No AIDep-22 subscale correlations are reported. AI self-efficacy (AISES) is self-efficacy specific to AI, not general or academic self-efficacy, so it was not extracted as an eligible correlate (r = −.361 with AI dependence, in case the reviewer counts it). AI literacy (r = −.283) is not an eligible correlate.

codes.sample: No participants. A conceptual policy framework with one hypothetical worked example (Kenya, Appendix A), not an empirical sample.
codes.ai_system: National AI infrastructure in general (compute, data centres, foundation models accessed via APIs) used in public services; no individual users.
codes.dependence_measures: None at the individual level. The proposed National AI Sovereignty Index (NASI) is a qualitative diagnostic for national infrastructure dependency. Its dimensions include Public Sector Dependency and Foreign Exposure Risk, rated High/Partial/Minimal control. It is not a self- or informant-report measure of psychological dependence.
codes.note: Theoretical paper with no data: 'presented as a foundational framework intended for iterative empirical refinement' (p.1); NASI is 'a structured framework for assessment rather than a finalized quantitative metric' (p.4). 'Dependency' here means national infrastructure dependence, not psychological dependence on AI, so E3 would apply too. No psychological correlates measured.

codes.sample: Turkish educators (teachers and academics). Qualitative interviews with n=32; EFA sample n=330 (236 academics, 94 teachers); CFA sample n=216.
codes.ai_system: "AI tools" in general, mostly generative AI such as ChatGPT
codes.dependence_measures: AI Dependency Scale for Educators: newly developed, 32 items, 5-point frequency scale (never to always). Two subscales: Dependency in Educational Processes (18 items) and Dependency in Academic Processes (14 items). Total score ranges from 32 to 160.
codes.note: This is a scale development and validation study (EFA, CFA, reliability). The only correlations reported are within the scale itself (Table 8: subscales vs total r=.932/.881, between subscales r=.649) and the split-half r=.961. No external or psychological correlates were measured (no convergent or criterion validity variables), so none of the eligible correlates are present.

codes.sample: Students with disabilities in Indian higher education who had used generative AI in the previous term. Recruited by purposive and snowball sampling. The text never states N; it is 200 by summing Table 2 (78 male + 120 female + 2 other). 63.5% undergraduates.
codes.ai_system: Generative AI tools in general (e.g., ChatGPT), used for learning
codes.dependence_measures: AI dependence (AID): a 5-item reflective scale on a 5-point Likert format; source and item wording not given. α = .881, CR = .913, AVE = .677; M = 3.21, SD = 0.91 (Tables 1, 4, 6). Cognitive offloading (CO, 5 items) is a separate construct.
codes.note: The only eligible correlate is learning self-efficacy. The AID–LSE link appears only as an HTMT ratio (.43, Table 7, p.11), which does not count. Fornell–Larcker is described in words (p.10) but no correlation matrix is printed; otherwise only PLS-SEM paths. Data-quality concerns: abstract uses future-tense methods, subgroup results 'going to be presented', N never stated.

codes.sample: 237 active Indonesian university students from several universities who had used generative AI (ChatGPT, Gemini, Claude, Copilot) for at least the past 3 months, aged 18 or older, recruited by purposive sampling through Google Forms (p. 4).
codes.ai_system: Generative AI in general (ChatGPT, Gemini, Claude, Copilot and similar apps)
codes.dependence_measures: Generative AI Dependency Scale, 11 items, 5-point Likert (cites Goh et al., 2025); ω = 0.944, α = 0.945; M = 30.64, SD = 11.28 (pp. 4–5).
codes.note: Only correlate: difficulties in emotion regulation (DERS), not an eligible correlate; r = 0.674, BF10 = 3.822 × 10^29 (Table 4, p. 6). Anxiety, stress, loneliness and self-esteem are only suggested for future research, not measured. Reviewer may check whether emotion dysregulation could count as a related construct; under the listed criteria it does not.

codes.sample: 300 Mexican adolescents (52.0% female): 150 from a technical upper-secondary school (CBTIS 146, Tijuana) and 150 from a technical middle school (Sec. Téc. #59, Tlajomulco, Jalisco). Split into three AI-tutoring groups (n = 100 each). 14-week pre-post intervention, Feb–Jun 2026.
codes.ai_system: Generative AI tutors: ChatGPT, Gemini, Copilot and DeepSeek, used in emotional-tutoring, guided-metacognition and personalised-feedback programmes
codes.dependence_measures: "Dependencia de IA percibida" (perceived AI dependency), scored on a 1–5 Likert scale at week 1 and week 14. The text gives no item content, number of items, source or reliability, so it is unclear whether it is multi-item or ad hoc.

correlations.correlate_instrument: Likert scale (1-5) of academic anxiety; details not reported
correlations.quote: La dependencia de IA percibida correlacionó positivamente con la ansiedad académica (r = .412, p < .01)

codes.possible_duplicate: The paper calls itself the "componente complementario de un estudio mixto más amplio con predominio cualitativo" (a complementary part of a larger, mainly qualitative mixed-methods study). Other reports from the same project may exist.
codes.note: Academic anxiety is counted under anxiety; please confirm. Timepoint of the r is not stated. Emotional self-regulation (r = -.124) is not an eligible correlate and was left out. Integrity concerns: submitted about a month after fieldwork ended, a reference contains a placeholder, some cited sources may not exist, and instrument details are missing.

codes.sample: 228 undergraduate students from three private universities in Cebu, Philippines (age 19–24, M = 21.46; 64.5% female); non-probability quota sampling; online survey, July–August 2026.
codes.ai_system: AI tools in general (academic use)
codes.dependence_measures: Artificial Intelligence Dependence Questionnaire (AIDQ; Akinwale et al., 2025): 12 items on a 4-point scale measuring excessive use of and overreliance on AI tools among undergraduates. Only the total score is used (M = 2.5, SD = 0.601).

correlations.correlate_instrument: General Academic Self-Efficacy Scale (GASE; van Zyl et al., 2022), 5 items
correlations.quote: AI dependence demonstrated a statistically significant, negative correlation with academic self-efficacy (r = -.220, p < .001)

codes.possible_duplicate: No clear duplicate. A related study, Antogop et al. (2026, IJRISS 10(3)), looked at self-efficacy and AI dependence among Cebu college students. It has different authors and appears to use a different sample. Worth checking.
codes.note: Academic self-efficacy is the only eligible correlate. Academic motivation (AMS-C 28 SDI) is not on the eligible list; its correlation with AIDQ (r = -.143, n = 228) is not reported here. The regression beta (-0.169) is multivariable, so it is excluded. The SDI descriptives (M = 3.5, SD = 0.401) look odd, but this does not affect the extracted r.

codes.sample: N = 205 young adults aged 18–30 in urban India (88 male, 117 female), university students and young professionals who use AI systems such as ChatGPT, Gemini and Replika; purposive sampling.
codes.ai_system: AI companions/chatbots (Replika, Character AI, ChatGPT, Gemini; voice assistants)
codes.dependence_measures: Adapted Emotional Dependence Questionnaire (adapted from Schmidt & Bartholomew, 2018, and parasocial/attachment scales), "10–12 items" on emotional reliance, attachment and comfort from AI companions, 5-point Likert. The number of items and the obtained alpha are not reported ("expected to exceed 0.70").

correlations.exposure: Emotional dependence on AI companions (adapted EDQ)
correlations.correlate: Social connectedness (NOT on eligible list; possible inverse proxy for loneliness – reviewer to decide)
correlations.correlate_instrument: Social Connectedness Scale–Revised (Lee, Draper, & Lee, 2001), 8 items
correlations.quote: neither Technology Readiness (r = -.110, p > .05) nor Social Connectedness (r = .107, p > .05) yielded a significant correlation with Emotional Dependence

codes.possible_duplicate: None identified. This may be the published version of an M.A. psychology dissertation (first author is an M.A. student, Amity University Punjab).
codes.note: Correlates measured: technology readiness, social connectedness and anthropomorphism (IDAQ); none is on the eligible list. SC r = .107 is listed in case the reviewer accepts it as an inverse loneliness proxy. Quality concerns: methods are in future tense like a protocol and plan N ≈ 100, but N = 205 is reported; reliabilities are cited from the literature or "expected".

codes.sample: 370 secondary school students (4th–5th grade) from eight schools in Tacna, Peru. The sample was split into two groups of 185 (one for EFA, one for CFA). 53.5% were female; ages 15–17, mean 16.6 (SD 0.92).
codes.ai_system: AI tools in general for academic tasks (e.g., ChatGPT, Claude, Grammarly, Wolfram Alpha)
codes.dependence_measures: SAID questionnaire (newly developed, 13 items, 1–5 Likert) on AI dependence in academic tasks, with three dimensions: Trust in AI (3 items, ω=0.71), Informational exclusivity with AI (6 items, ω=0.81) and AI literacy (4 items, ω=0.72).
codes.possible_duplicate: None identified.
codes.note: Scale-development study only (EFA/CFA, reliability). No other constructs were measured; the authors say concurrent and discriminant validity were not analysed (p.10). Reviewer: E1 is also arguable, since the SAID items mostly measure trust, how often AI is used, and AI literacy rather than dependence symptoms. Either way, not eligible.

codes.sample: 400 full-time undergraduates (259 female, 141 male; age 18–24, M = 21.17) from one normal university in Southwest China, stratified sampling, online survey Sept–Nov 2025.
codes.ai_system: AI tools in general (generative AI used for academic purposes)
codes.dependence_measures: AI Dependence Scale (AIDep-22; Wu et al., 2026), 22 items, 5-point; subscales emotional, functional and cognitive dependence and loss of control; only the total score is correlated (α = 0.93).

correlations.correlate_instrument: Artificial Intelligence Anxiety Scale (AIAS; Wang & Wang, 2022), 21 items
correlations.location: Table 2; Results, Descriptive statistics and correlation analysis
correlations.quote: AI anxiety was significantly and positively related to AI dependence (r = 0.528, p < 0.001)

codes.possible_duplicate: None identified. The AIDep-22 comes from Wu et al. (2026), which appears to be a separate scale-development study, so it should be checked for possible sample overlap.
codes.note: The only eligible correlate is AI anxiety, which counts as AI-related anxiety (fear of AI). AI self-efficacy (AISES) correlates r = –0.492 with AI dependence, but it is AI-specific rather than general or academic self-efficacy, so the reviewer should decide whether it counts. AI literacy (r = –0.530) is not an eligible correlate. The PROCESS β = 0.53 includes control variables, so it was not used.

codes.sample: Snowball sample of working professionals in major Chinese cities (Shanghai, Beijing, Suzhou), recruited through an online survey on WJX; 138 people took part and 84 remained after data cleaning and screening (only AI chatbot users were kept).
codes.ai_system: Generative AI chatbots used for mental health or emotional support (e.g., DeepSeek)
codes.dependence_measures: Emotional Dependence (DEP) on AI chatbots: a multi-item 5-point Likert scale adapted from the Bergen Social Media Addiction Scale. Sample item: "I find it difficult to stop using the AI chatbot when I feel down." [20]
codes.note: The dependence measure counts, but the other constructs are perceived usefulness, ease of use, trust, help-seeking intention, single-item help-seeking shame (self-stigma), and prior therapy experience. None of these is an eligible correlate. Only PROCESS regression coefficients are reported; there is no correlation table.

codes.sample: 310 College of Education students (1st–4th year), University of Cabuyao, Philippines; simple random sampling; online survey sent through group chats.
codes.ai_system: AI tools in general (AI-assisted technology for academic tasks: chatbots, paraphrasing, grammar and writing tools)
codes.dependence_measures: Ad hoc, researcher-made AI-dependence items rated on a 4-point Likert scale, adapted from Capinding (2024) and Chan (2023). Four aspects: Reasoning/Logical (2 items), Analytical (3), Grammar-Checking (3) and Writing Construction (2). Scored as weighted means (Tables 5–8). Validated by three experts.
codes.note: AI-dependence aspects were correlated (Pearson r, Tables 9–12) only with academic-integrity subscales (cheating, plagiarism, direct source duplication, paraphrasing). None is an eligible correlate. No depression, anxiety, stress, loneliness, self-esteem, procrastination etc. was measured. Some items describe use or reliance rather than dependence.

codes.sample: 150 university students in Pakistan (80 male, 70 female; 99 undergraduate, 51 postgraduate); convenience sample, online Google Forms survey; cross-sectional.
codes.ai_system: AI tools in general (ChatGPT, Grammarly, Quillbot named as examples)
codes.dependence_measures: AI Dependence scale: 5 items, 5-point agreement scale, α = .865 (ad hoc); example item: "I feel I cannot complete academic tasks without AI." (Table 2, p. 3 / Page 5608).
codes.note: AI Dependence was correlated only with AI Assistance (r = .306) and Critical Thinking (r = .173). Neither is an eligible correlate. Some references look doubtful (e.g., arXiv 2604.27349; a Frontiers article numbered 12742215), so the reviewer may want to check quality.

codes.sample: None. There are no human participants. This is a theoretical, mathematical computer science paper.
codes.ai_system: None studied as something people use. The paper is about removing AI or ML components from a rendering and token-generation pipeline.
codes.dependence_measures: None. In this paper, "AI dependency" means a software pipeline relying on AI inference infrastructure, not a psychological dependence on AI.
codes.note: This is a theoretical paper on deterministic token generation (the FNV-64 hash formula) for game rendering, with formal proofs and C++ code and no empirical human data. It is excluded under E5 as a theoretical paper. It would also meet E3, because "dependence" is used in a technical or infrastructure sense ("without dependence on AI inference infrastructure").

codes.sample: 383 Italian university students (273 F, 110 M; mean age 22.0, SD 2.41), recruited by convenience sampling from 35 universities. 332 had used GenAI in the past 3 months; n per task-specific item ranged from 212 to 308. Cross-sectional online survey, March–April 2026.
codes.ai_system: Generative AI in general (e.g., ChatGPT) used for academic tasks
codes.dependence_measures: Six ad hoc single items, one per academic task, asking how often (1 = Never to 5 = Always) the student uses AI-generated output 'without making substantial revisions' (passive acceptance/reliance). The authors say these items do not form a scale. They measure frequency of a behaviour, not dependence, addiction or inability to stop as such.
codes.note: Only correlates measured: Critical Thinking Disposition (CTDS) and Decision Fatigue (DFS). Neither is an eligible correlate; decision fatigue is not perceived stress or psychological distress. No correlation matrix, only hierarchical multivariable regression betas. E1 is also arguable, since the 'reliance' items measure how often unmodified output is used, not dependence.

codes.sample: 200 students who use AI tools for academic purposes (104 male, 96 female), convenience sample, online Google Forms survey; country not stated explicitly (authors are at SCMS School of Technology and Management, Kerala, India).
codes.ai_system: AI tools in general (chatbots, virtual assistants, automated content generators) used for academic purposes
codes.dependence_measures: None. The constructs measured were Self-Efficacy (10 items), Perceived Usefulness (5), Perceived Ease of Use (5), Information Quality (10) and Usage of AI (10), all on 5-point Likert scales (TAM/DeLone & McLean). The abstract mentions 'concerns related to dependency on AI tools', but no dependence scale was administered.
codes.note: This is a TAM-style AI adoption/usage study. 'Usage of AI' is a usage/acceptance measure, not a dependence measure. Self-efficacy was measured as technological self-efficacy toward AI, and only multivariable regression betas are reported (β = 0.137 for self-efficacy). No correlation matrix is given. Even if a dependence measure had been present, the report would fail I4.

codes.sample: 727 students at Nueva Ecija University of Science and Technology, Gabaldon campus, Philippines (survey sent to 1635 via Google Forms, starting Dec 5, 2023); qualitative item development with 4-6 students and 6 educators; 15 content-validity raters.
codes.ai_system: AI tools in general for reading, writing and numeracy (AI writing assistants, summarisers, paraphrasers, ChatGPT-type tools, AI calculators)
codes.dependence_measures: Students' AI Dependency in 3R's questionnaire (new, ad hoc): 33 items in three subscales: Dependence on AI in Reading (10 items, alpha .89), Writing (11 items, alpha .91), Numeracy/Arithmetic (12 items, alpha .90).
codes.possible_duplicate: Same author earlier published an instrument on AI's impact in higher education with an AI-dependency facet (Capinding 2024, Int J Educ Methodology 10(2):197-211). That looks like a different instrument and sample. Later papers using this 3Rs scale may report correlates.
codes.note: Psychometric validation only (Aiken's V, EFA, Rasch, Cronbach's alpha); no other construct measured. Many items describe use or helpfulness rather than dependence, and some cover non-interactive AI (calculators, recommenders), so E1 is also arguable.

codes.sample: No original sample. The paper is a narrative/"systematic" review of secondary sources (MIT Media Lab, BMJ, Nature, Stanford and Psychiatric Times reports, 2023–2025) plus four brief clinical case vignettes.
codes.ai_system: AI language models and chatbots in general (ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini) and AI companions (Replika)
codes.dependence_measures: None. No quantitative dependence scale was given to participants. Screening questions are proposed (p. 11) but no data were collected with them. Limitations state: "Standardized AI dependency assessments lacking" (p. 12).
codes.note: Review/theoretical paper with case vignettes (Methods: "Systematic review of documented clinical cases, neuroimaging studies, and psychiatric reports", p. 1). No primary data or correlations. All figures (e.g., 9.5% emotional dependency) are cited from other sources, and several references appear unverifiable.

codes.sample: 236 medical students (years 1–4) at Bilecik Şeyh Edebali University, Türkiye; cross-sectional online survey, November 2025; mean age 20.02±1.65; 49.2% male.
codes.ai_system: AI tools in general (95.8% used ChatGPT, 55.5% Gemini, 10.6% Canva AI/Notion AI)
codes.dependence_measures: Scale for Dependence on Artificial Intelligence (DAI; Morales-García et al., 2024; Turkish adaptation by Savaş, 2024): 5 items on a 5-point Likert scale, total score 5–25. Sample mean 11.04±4.08.

correlations.correlate_instrument: Academic Self-Efficacy Scale (Jerusalem & Schwarzer; Turkish version by Yılmaz et al.)
correlations.quote: A weak negative correlation was found between DAI and ASES scores (r=-0.235, p<0.001)

correlations.correlate_instrument: Multidimensional Scale of Perceived Social Support (Zimet; Turkish revised form by Eker et al.), total score
correlations.quote: a moderate negative correlation was found between DAI and MSPSS scores (r=-0.376, p<0.001)

codes.possible_duplicate: None identified. This is a single-author article. A different medical-student sample appears in ref 13 (Korkmaz & Toraman 2026), which is not the same study.
codes.note: The correlations are zero-order Pearson r values reported in the text; there is no correlation matrix. No r values are given for the MSPSS subscales. The Table 3 regression B values are multivariable and do not count. The other eligible correlates were not measured.

codes.sample: Undergraduates in an intermediate Python course (Data-Oriented Programming), University of Michigan, Fall 2023. Anonymous end-of-course survey n = 158 (N = 153 in the over-reliance regression); mid-course self-efficacy survey n = 158 of 203; 10 interviews.
codes.ai_system: LLMs in general (ChatGPT, GPT-4, Copilot, university-hosted GPT-3.5/4, Llama 2) used for programming homework
codes.dependence_measures: One binary self-report item on perceived over-reliance on LLMs ('Yes, I have felt over-reliant' / 'No, I have never felt over-reliant'). Other AI measures are only use counts (LLM citations on homework, reported number of homework assignments with LLM use) and Likert attitude items about how over-reliance could affect learning or careers.
codes.possible_duplicate: arXiv preprint 2406.06451 of the same ICER '24 paper (doi 10.1145/3632620.3671098).
codes.note: Borderline I1: the only dependence-like measure is one binary item on felt over-reliance on LLMs. Its link with end-of-course programming self-efficacy is reported only as a multivariable regression (Table 5: Std. β = -.233, also controlling for LLM usage and major). No zero-order r is derivable. Table 8 odds ratios cover use motives and are adjusted.

codes.sample: 210 higher-education students who use AI tools often for coursework, recruited by convenience sampling (country not stated; the author is affiliated with Trujillo, Peru).
codes.ai_system: Artificial intelligence tools in general / generative AI (e.g., ChatGPT) used in academic activities
codes.dependence_measures: An ad hoc 5-point Likert questionnaire, 'Dependencia de IA' (cognitive delegation, task automation), checked by expert judgement and a pilot; α = 0.82. The text does not give the number of items.
codes.note: Pearson matrix (Table 3, p.48): AI dependence vs academic self-regulation r = -0.41**; vs depth of learning r = -0.52**. Academic self-regulation (planning, monitoring, metacognitive control) is not on the list of eligible correlates. It is not self-control or self-efficacy, so check whether it could count as self-control. Self-efficacy is discussed in theory only and was not measured.

codes.sample: 411 Turkish university students (341 women, 70 men), aged 18–49 (M = 22.34, SD = 4.49), recruited online via Google Forms.
codes.ai_system: Generative AI tools in general (ChatGPT 92.5%, Copilot, NotebookLM, Claude, Genspark)
codes.dependence_measures: Turkish Generative AI Dependency Scale (GAIDS; Goh et al., 2025): 11 items, 3 subscales (Cognitive Preoccupation, Negative Consequences, Withdrawal), α = .88 overall. Also the Artificial Intelligence Chatbot Addiction Scale (AICAS; Zhang et al., 2025, Turkish version): 8 items, α = .91. This second scale is a dependence measure, not a correlate.

correlations.correlate_instrument: Young's Internet Addiction Test – Short Form (YIAT-SF), Turkish version

codes.possible_duplicate: None identified. This is a Turkish adaptation sample, separate from the original GAIDS development study (Goh et al., 2025) and from the Turkish AICAS adaptation (Yıldız-Durak & Balıkçı, 2025).
codes.note: The only eligible correlate is problematic internet use (YIAT-SF). The GAIDS–AICAS correlations (total r = .72) link two AI-dependence measures, so I did not report them as correlates. None of the primary correlates (depression, anxiety, stress, loneliness and so on) was measured. The total n is 411; the text does not report n for each correlation separately.

codes.sample: None. This is a conceptual/argumentative paper with no empirical sample.
codes.ai_system: AI language tools in general (machine translation apps such as Google Translate, multilingual AI chatbots)
codes.dependence_measures: None. 'Dependency' / 'relying too much on AI' is discussed only conceptually; no quantitative measure was administered.
codes.note: Short theoretical essay (pp. 1068-1070) about AI language tools and linguistic diversity, drawing on sociolinguistics and language ecology. It has no methods, data, participants or statistics. The full text appears complete (abstract through references).

codes.sample: 51 Indian college students aged 18–25 (58.8% female, 41.2% male), purposive sampling, cross-sectional (pp. 4–5).
codes.ai_system: AI tools in general / generative AI (ChatGPT, Google Gemini, Microsoft Copilot mentioned)
codes.dependence_measures: Dependence on AI Scale (DIA; Morales-García et al., 2024), reported only as five subscales: Vulnerability, Relevance, Social Motivation, External Validation, Obsolescence (5-point Likert; p. 5). No total score is reported.
codes.note: DIA subscales were correlated only with K-DOCS creativity domains (Table 3, p. 8). The other measure, QAIUM (AI-use motivation), is not an eligible correlate either. Its expectancy subscale is AI-specific ability belief, not general or academic self-efficacy, and was correlated only with creativity. No DIA–QAIUM correlations are reported.

codes.sample: 580 Chinese undergraduate art and design students (aged 18–25, M = 20.58; 49.5% male), recruited from multiple universities by purposive sampling; online survey (Wenjuanxing), May–June 2026; all had used at least one generative AI tool for creative tasks.
codes.ai_system: Generative AI tools in general (e.g., Midjourney, Stable Diffusion, ChatGPT) used for creative tasks
codes.dependence_measures: AI Dependence Scale adopted from Zhang X. et al. (2025), i.e. the AI Chatbot Dependence Scale: 8 items, unidimensional, 7-point Likert; Cronbach's α = 0.906, AVE = 0.548, CR = 0.906. Translated and back-translated.

correlations.correlate: Challenge stressors (academic stress: coursework demands, time pressure)
correlations.correlate_instrument: Challenge-Hindrance Stressor Scale (Cavanaugh et al., 2000; Rodell & Judge, 2009), adapted to art coursework; 8 items
correlations.location: Table 4, p. 8; text p. 7; also Table 3, p. 7
correlations.quote: Challenge stressors were significantly and positively correlated with AI dependence (r = 0.515, p < 0.01)

correlations.correlate: Hindrance stressors (academic stress: unclear requirements, lack of resources)
correlations.correlate_instrument: Challenge-Hindrance Stressor Scale (Cavanaugh et al., 2000; Rodell & Judge, 2009), adapted; 5 items
correlations.location: Table 4, p. 8; text p. 7; also Table 3, p. 7
correlations.quote: Hindrance stressors were significantly and positively correlated with AI dependence (r = 0.530, p < 0.01)
Creative self-efficacy was significantly negatively correlated with AI dependence (r = −0.288, p < 0.01)

codes.possible_duplicate: None identified.
codes.note: Eligible only if challenge/hindrance stressors count as academic stress (paper: both "fall under the category of academic stress"). Creative self-efficacy is domain-specific, not general/academic, so the reviewer should decide. Positive experiences is not an eligible correlate. Table 3 values match Table 4 Pearson r. No combined stress score.

codes.sample: 386 Spanish adult LLM users recruited via Prolific, all with Spanish origin and current residence in Spain (M age = 27.99, SD = 6.08; 55.18% male). Each participant used LLMs almost daily and/or reported significant dependence. 80.8% named ChatGPT as their primary LLM.
codes.ai_system: Each participant's primary LLM (ChatGPT 80.8%, Gemini, Copilot, DeepSeek, others)
codes.dependence_measures: LLM-D12-SP (Spanish Large Language Model Dependency Scale), 12 items on a 6-point scale, with two subscales: Instrumental Dependency (6 items, α = .86) and Relationship Dependency (6 items, α = .85); total α = .89.
codes.possible_duplicate: Same scale and team as the UK LLM-D12 (Yankouskaya et al., 2025) and Arabic (AlShakhsi et al., 2025) validations; Spanish sample appears separate. The Research Square preprint (rs-8940489) and the Discover Psychology article are probably the same report.
codes.note: Eligible correlates: internet addiction (IAT-7) and AI Fear (ATAI). Reported only as standardised betas from a 5-predictor regression (e.g., Internet Addiction β = 0.253 and 0.265; Table 5), no zero-order r. Raw data on OSF (osf.io/3b7ea) would allow computing r. NFC and IA row labels appear swapped in Table 6.

codes.sample: 428 valid Chinese Replika users (496 collected), recruited via Douban, Xiaohongshu, Weibo and similar platforms, Oct–Nov 2023; 71.5% female; 61.7% aged 18–25.
codes.ai_system: Replika (AI companion chatbot)
codes.dependence_measures: "Users' media dependence on Replika": 6 items (C1–C6), adapted from Kwon et al.'s (2013) Smartphone Addiction Scale and Chen et al.'s (2003) Chinese Internet Addiction Scale, with "smartphone/internet" replaced by "Replika"; 5-point Likert; α = 0.923; M = 3.2936, SD = 1.05839.

correlations.exposure: Users' media dependence on Replika (6-item, adapted SAS/CIAS)
correlations.correlate: Real-life interpersonal communication problems (social avoidance/distress, loneliness); possible social anxiety proxy
correlations.correlate_instrument: 5-item ad hoc scale adapted from ICDS (Zheng) and SADS (Watson & Friend), alpha = 0.815
correlations.quote: Users' media dependence on Replika | Pearson correlation | 1 | 0.741** | 0.674** ... N | 428

codes.possible_duplicate: None identified.
codes.note: The dependence measure is eligible. The only correlate is a combined 5-item interpersonal communication scale (from ICDS and SADS) that mixes social avoidance/distress, loneliness and self-disclosure, so it is not clearly social anxiety or loneliness. The reviewer must judge. Items are coded 1 = strongly agree, but the authors say a higher score means more dependence.

codes.sample: Convenience sample of 58 students at ATU Letterkenny, Ireland (33 international, 25 from the Republic of Ireland); survey run on Survey Monkey (p. 4).
codes.ai_system: ChatGPT
codes.dependence_measures: Ad hoc survey on "academic dependence on ChatGPT", described as 17 items but also as twenty-four items, rated on a 5-point Likert scale (e.g., "without Chat GPT I would struggle to complete my assignments on time"). Only correlations between items are reported (R = 0.9424; R = 0.8371).
codes.note: Mostly a conceptual paper with a short preliminary-data section (p. 4). It has ad hoc ChatGPT dependence items but reports only correlations between those items. No eligible correlate was measured. Item count is inconsistent (17 vs 24). Fallback reason: E5_design (paper is mainly theoretical).

codes.sample: 395 adult AI chatbot users (had used one in the past 6 months) recruited through the Wenjuanxing sample service in China; 47.09% male, most aged 26–35, 83.8% with a bachelor's degree; cross-sectional online survey.
codes.ai_system: AI chatbots in general (e.g., ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, Character.AI)
codes.dependence_measures: 8-item AI Chatbot Dependence Scale (AICDS; Zhang et al., 2025), unidimensional, rated 1–7; covers reliance for information, emotional support and everyday decisions; α = 0.905. The authors read scores as degree of reliance, not addiction or problematic use.

correlations.quote: Social anxiety was positively correlated with AI chatbot dependence (r = 0.623, p < 0.001)

codes.possible_duplicate: No obvious overlap. The AICDS comes from Zhang et al. (2025), which is probably a separate scale-development sample. Worth checking for other papers by Sun/Li/Yang using the same 2025–2026 Wenjuanxing sample of 395.
codes.note: Psychological resilience (CD-RISC-10; r = −0.525 with AICD) is not on the list of eligible correlates. Table 9's single-predictor β for SA→AICD is 0.623, the same as r. The authors stress that the AICDS measures reliance, not problematic use. The text has no page markers, so table labels are used as locations.

codes.sample: 528 Peruvian university students (280 female, 248 male), aged 18–37 (M = 19.00, SD = 3.84), from various majors, with 3–6+ months of experience using AI tools for academic work; online survey, April–May 2024.
codes.ai_system: AI tools in general (artificial intelligence tools used for academic purposes)
codes.dependence_measures: Artificial Intelligence Dependence Scale (DAI; Morales-García et al., 2024c): 5 items, unidimensional, 5-point Likert, α = 0.87, ω = 0.87. Total score only.

correlations.correlate_instrument: Anxiety Toward the Use of AI Scale (2 items, ad hoc, 0–3 format, α = 0.85)
correlations.quote: anxiety toward AI use is positively correlated with dependence on AI (r = 0,71, p < ,01)

correlations.correlate: Self-efficacy in AI use (AI-specific; may not count as general/academic self-efficacy)
correlations.correlate_instrument: GSE-6AI (6 items, adapted from the General Self-Efficacy Scale, α/ω = 0.91)
correlations.quote: self-efficacy with the use of AI has a significant positive correlation with anxiety toward AI use (r = 0,43, p < ,01) and with dependence on AI (r = 0,61, p < ,01)

codes.possible_duplicate: Same author group (Morales-García et al.) and the same Peruvian student population as the DAI scale validation paper (2024c, Frontiers in Education) and the GSE-6AI validation paper (2024a). The data here were collected April–May 2024, so the sample is probably new, but check for overlap.
codes.note: AI anxiety is an ad hoc 2-item scale and fits the 'AI-related anxiety' correlate. AI self-efficacy is specific to AI use, so the reviewer should decide if it counts. Table 2 means/SDs appear assigned to the wrong variables, but the r values match the text. The regression 'β' values are unstandardised and come from a multivariable model.

codes.sample: 1108 full-time Chinese employees aged 21–60 (618 male, 490 female; M age 40.63) from internet, pharmaceutical, publishing companies and high schools; three-wave one-year longitudinal design (T1 June 2024, T2 Dec 2024, T3 June 2025).
codes.ai_system: AI products/AI tools in general (artificial intelligence used at work)
codes.dependence_measures: AI dependence at T1: 8 items adapted from the Smartphone Addiction Scale – Short Version (Kwon et al., 2013; Luk et al., 2018), e.g., "I rely too much on AI", "I feel anxious and upset when I cannot use artificial intelligence"; 5-point scale; total score; α = 0.90.

correlations.correlate: T2 work self-efficacy (gender group A: upper triangle)
correlations.correlate_instrument: 6 items adapted from General Self-Efficacy Scale (Schwarzer & Jerusalem), work context

correlations.correlate: T2 work self-efficacy (gender group B: lower triangle)
correlations.correlate_instrument: 6 items adapted from General Self-Efficacy Scale (Schwarzer & Jerusalem), work context

codes.possible_duplicate: None detected in the text. The AI dependence items follow S. Huang et al. (2024), which is a different study.
codes.note: Borderline: the only correlate is WORK self-efficacy (General Self-Efficacy Scale adapted to work), not strictly general/academic. If it does not count, the reason is no_eligible_correlate. Table 1 correlations are split by gender, but the table never says which triangle is male or female. No pooled r. Work engagement is not eligible.

codes.sample: 132 first-year BSHM (hospitality management) students, IBA College of Mindanao Inc., Valencia City, Bukidnon, Philippines, AY 2025–2026 (the methods say stratified sampling; the abstract says convenience sampling)
codes.ai_system: AI tools in general (chatbots, grammar checkers, problem-solving platforms) used for numeracy, reading and writing tasks
codes.dependence_measures: AI Dependency questionnaire "patterned from" Capinding (2024), contextualised, with subscales Reading Dependency, Writing Dependency and Numeracy Dependency plus an overall score. Cronbach's alpha 0.871 for the instrument as a whole.
codes.note: The only correlate is critical thinking (Kobylarek et al., 2022), which is not an eligible correlate. Pearson r with critical thinking: Reading 0.11, Writing 0.22, Numeracy 0.21, Overall 0.423 (Tables 3–4, p. 4). No eligible psychological correlate was measured.

codes.sample: 310 first-year students at one Japanese high school (I High School), Information class. Single-group pre/post/6-month follow-up teaching practice. Note: the abstract dates it to 2025, the body to 2024.
codes.ai_system: Generative AI in general (生成AI)
codes.dependence_measures: Generative AI Dependence Tendency Scale for high-school/university students (Tsuruta, Ishikawa & Tanaka, 2024): 22 items, 5 factors (mental dependence, anxiety about AI answers, long-time use, use while doing other things, face-to-face communication anxiety), 4-point scale. The Internet Addiction Tendency Scale for high-school students (39 items, 5 factors) was also given.
codes.possible_duplicate: Same author's Generative AI Dependence Tendency Scale development paper (AI時代の教育論文誌, 6, 2024, pp. 40-45) and earlier intervention reports by Tsuruta may involve related samples. No overlap is evident.
codes.note: Problematic internet use (internet addiction tendency) was measured alongside generative AI dependence at three time points. Only subscale means/SDs by time point and repeated-measures ANOVA F values are given (Tables 3 and 5). No correlation between AI dependence and internet addiction is reported or derivable. No other eligible correlates were measured.

codes.sample: 290 US young adults aged 18–25 who use AI chatbots at least weekly (Microsoft intern newsletter + Prolific), June–August 2025; 74 self-identified as dependent, 216 as non-dependent.
codes.ai_system: General-purpose AI chatbots (e.g., ChatGPT)
codes.dependence_measures: A single self-report AI dependence item rated 1–5 (agreement with feeling dependent on AI chatbots), plus selected items from the Problematic ChatGPT Use Scale (Yu et al. 2024), the Affective Dependence Scale (Sirvent-Ruiz et al. 2022) and the AI Dependence Scale (Huang et al. 2024 / Zhou & Zhang 2024). Analyses are item-level Spearman correlations with the single self-report item.

correlations.exposure: Self-reported AI chatbot dependence (single Likert item)
correlations.correlate: Coping/emotion-regulation motive (single item: 'I use AI chatbots to manage my feelings') - borderline
correlations.correlate_instrument: Motivation items adapted from Huang et al. 2024 / Wolf & Maier 2024
correlations.quote: I use AI chatbots to manage my feelings 0.35 2 1

codes.possible_duplicate: An extended arXiv version describes the same sample: Milton et al. 2026, arXiv:2608.07592. It reportedly includes the non-significant results and more details on the scales.
codes.note: Mainly qualitative. Spearman rhos are given only for usage, motive, attitude and dependence items. No listed correlate was measured. Borderline: the single motive item 'manage my feelings' (rho = .35) could count as a coping motive. If the reviewer accepts it, change the decision to eligible. The extended arXiv paper may have more data.

codes.sample: None. This is a theoretical/philosophical essay with no participants or data collection.
codes.ai_system: AI systems / large language models in general (ChatGPT, GPT-4 mentioned), discussed only in concept
codes.dependence_measures: None. 'Yapay zekâ bağımlılığı' (AI dependence) and 'epistemic laziness' are discussed only as concepts, with no quantitative measure or scale.
codes.possible_duplicate: None identified.
codes.note: This is a theoretical philosophy-of-science paper drawing on Popper, Kuhn, Goldman, Bandura, Clark & Chalmers and Borgmann. It proposes the concepts 'algorithmic learning', 'Cognitive Convergence Trap' and a 'critical dependence model'. It has no methods, sample, measures or statistics. The full text was retrieved and confirms there is no empirical component.

codes.sample: 502 Chinese international students in higher education abroad (US, UK, Australia, Canada, South Korea, other); 45.2% male; mostly aged 18–29. Three-wave longitudinal survey (T1 June 2025, T2 Sept 2025, T3 Jan 2026), convenience plus snowball sampling; only complete, matched cases were analysed.
codes.ai_system: Generative AI tools for academic writing, translation and language tasks (China-based 32.3%, international 67.7%)
codes.dependence_measures: Generative AI dependency (GAD): 9 items adapted from Goh et al. (2025) Generative AI Dependency framework/scale, 7-point Likert, α = .957; measured at T1.

correlations.correlate: Reduced self-efficacy (rSE, T2; reverse-worded academic self-efficacy, higher = lower self-efficacy)
correlations.correlate_instrument: 10 reverse-worded items adapted from Pintrich & De Groot (1990) self-efficacy scale; α = .942

codes.possible_duplicate: None identified. The GAD scale comes from Goh et al. (2025, Computers in Human Behavior Reports), which uses a different sample. Data are deposited on Mendeley (r43pgy8ych/2).
codes.note: Eligibility rests only on rSE counting as academic self-efficacy; reviewer should confirm. rSE is a reverse-worded MSLQ self-efficacy adaptation about confidence without AI; higher rSE = lower self-efficacy, so flip the sign (≈ −.345). The r is cross-wave (GAD T1, rSE T2). Skill degradation and psychological capital are not eligible correlates.

codes.sample: 102 college students (years 1–3; described as non-English majors) in China. Seven of them were also interviewed (mixed methods).
codes.ai_system: Generative AI used in English writing (general generative AI tools)
codes.dependence_measures: Self-developed 20-item, 5-point Likert questionnaire on generative AI use behaviours in English writing. It has 4 dimensions: dependence tendency (依赖倾向, Q1–Q5), substitutive behaviour (Q6–Q10), cognitive inertia (Q11–Q15) and withdrawal reactions (戒断反应, Q16–Q20). Pilot Cronbach's alpha = .982. Only descriptive statistics are reported (Table 2).
codes.note: The paper has an AI-dependence measure, but no eligible correlate was measured. The only quantitative results are descriptive means and SDs for the 4 dimensions (Table 2). Writing anxiety and self-confidence come up only as items within the withdrawal dimension or in the interviews, not as separate measured constructs. No correlation analysis is reported.

codes.sample: 397 female employees of fitness centres in the Marmara region, Turkey; convenience sample, online Google Form (subgroup ns add up to 392).
codes.ai_system: Artificial intelligence technologies in general ("yapay zekâ teknolojileri")
codes.dependence_measures: Artificial Intelligence Dependence/Addiction Scale (Yapay Zekâ Bağımlılık Ölçeği, YZBÖ), from Morales-García et al. (2024), Turkish adaptation by Savaş (2024). It has 5 items on a 5-point Likert scale; reported alpha is .82 in the method section and .856 in Table 2.
codes.note: The only correlate is quality of working life (Macit et al. 2019; commitment, efficiency, development, atmosphere, management). This is a work-specific measure of how employees see their workplace, not well-being. Table 7 (p.4): r=-,221 with AI dependence. If the reviewer counts it as well-being, this r could be used. The other comparisons are demographic only.

codes.sample: 450 undergraduates from FUTO (n=228) and IMSU (n=222), Imo State, Nigeria; stratified random sampling. A qualitative arm (15 curriculum leaders, 6 counsellors, 20 high-dependence students) is not relevant.
codes.ai_system: Generative AI tools (ChatGPT, Google Bard/Gemini, AI writing assistants)
codes.dependence_measures: AI dependence scale "adapted from previous studies on technology over-reliance (Kazemi & Ahmadi, 2024)", 5-point Likert, Cronbach's alpha = 0.87; mean 3.72/5 (FUTO M=3.89, SD=0.91; IMSU M=3.54, SD=1.02).
codes.note: Only correlate: learning autonomy (Zimmerman SRL-based). AI dependence r(448)=-0.43 overall; independent problem solving r=-0.49; self-regulation r=-0.38; effort investment r=-0.32 (pp.7-8). Self-regulation subscale is borderline (not self-control/self-efficacy). Stress/AI anxiety only qualitative. Integrity concerns: likely inaccurate refs, response rate 92.4% vs N=450, 3.1% never use AI.

codes.sample: No primary sample. This is a literature review and theory-building paper: the authors searched WoS, PubMed, CNKI and Wanfang for 2014–2026 and included 43 core articles ("纳入43篇核心文献").
codes.ai_system: Generative AI tools in general (ChatGPT, 文心一言/Ernie Bot); discussed conceptually only
codes.dependence_measures: None administered. The paper only describes existing scales from other studies: Goh et al. (2025) Generative AI Dependency Scale and Wu et al. (2026) AIDep-22.
codes.note: A literature review that proposes a chain mediation model. It has no original data or correlations. Cited primary studies worth screening: Goh et al. 2025 (GAID scale; FOMO, procrastination), Wu et al. 2026 (AIDep-22), Lan et al. 2026, Tian & Zhang 2025, Ye et al. 2025, Deng & Deng 2025.

codes.sample: 92 Chinese EFL undergraduates at one university who completed all assessments (47 AMP-Agent, 45 AMP; 100 enrolled). Nine-week randomized active-control study with measurements at T1, T2 and T3.
codes.ai_system: Doubao LLM-based adaptive metacognitive prompting (AMP) writing system; dependency items ask about GenAI use in general
codes.dependence_measures: Yu and Yan's (2026) 17-item Generative AI Dependency Questionnaire: Cognitive-Behavioral (6 items), Functional (6) and Emotional (5) subscales. Cronbach's α for the total was 0.783/0.806/0.843 at T1/T2/T3.
codes.note: The only other measures are self-regulated learning (Ji et al. 2025 scale), writing performance (Jacobs rubric) and behavioural transitions. None is an eligible correlate; SRL is not self-control or self-efficacy. No correlations are reported, only ANOVA group contrasts. Supplementary tables S1–S10 were not in the text received.

codes.sample: Undergraduate students at Aljufra University, Libya (2024–2025); convenience sample. The abstract gives N = 200, but the Methods report 222 completed responses out of 263 distributed.
codes.ai_system: Generative AI tools in general (ChatGPT, Gemini, Claude mentioned)
codes.dependence_measures: An ad hoc "AI dependence" section of a structured questionnaire, using a 5-point Likert scale. The item content is not reported. Cronbach's alpha of 0.88 is given only for the whole instrument. Mean = 3.89, SD = 0.76.
codes.note: AI dependence was correlated only with motivation (r = 0.36) and academic achievement (r = -0.48) in Table 2. Ease of use, perceived usefulness, digital literacy and ethical awareness were also measured. None of these is an eligible correlate. The paper reports N inconsistently (200 vs 222).

codes.sample: 46 medical and health sciences educators in Palestine (22 semistructured interviews plus 4 focus groups with 24 participants), from nursing, pharmacy, optometry, medicine, medical laboratory sciences and dental disciplines.
codes.ai_system: Generative AI tools in general (e.g., ChatGPT) used for teaching, research and administration
codes.dependence_measures: None quantitative. AI dependency was explored only through qualitative interviews and focus groups and analysed thematically in NVivo. The only numbers are counts of participants who mentioned each theme (e.g., procrastination under 'Motivational decline', 31/46).
codes.note: Methods: "A qualitative research design was used, using semistructured interviews (n=22) and focus group discussions (n=24)". This is a qualitative study with no quantitative dependence scale. Anxiety, procrastination and self-efficacy appear only as themes, with no correlations reported.

codes.sample: Distance-learning students, Faculty of Administrative Sciences, Universidad Central del Ecuador; the paper states n=261 were surveyed, but the frequency tables only add up to 50 respondents.
codes.ai_system: AI tools in general (AI-powered educational platforms)
codes.dependence_measures: No dependence or addiction scale. The ad hoc items cover weekly hours of AI use, use frequency (Never/Sometimes/Always), "Do you think relying on AI tools has affected your confidence?" (Yes/No), ability to write an essay without AI, a perceived drop in problem-solving, and exam results without AI. No item asks directly about dependence or inability to stop.
codes.note: The AI exposure is only use time/frequency plus perceived-effect items. Anxiety and isolation are mentioned in the abstract but were not measured. The paper says Pearson correlations were run, but no coefficients are reported, only narrative percentages. Even if the "relying on AI" item counted as dependence, no eligible correlate has a zero-order statistic (that would be E4).

codes.sample: University students from public and private universities in Punjab, Pakistan. Phase 1: 30 interviews and a pilot of 75. EFA sample N=300 (also reported as N=350 elsewhere in the text). CFA sample n=250. Purposive sampling; data collected November–December 2025.
codes.ai_system: AI tools in general (ChatGPT, Sora, Copilot and others are mentioned), used for study by students
codes.dependence_measures: Komal & Qureshi AI Dependency Scale (KQAIDS 2025): 14 items rated on a 5-point scale, alpha=.74, with three factors (emotional dependency, relatedness thwarted, competence thwarted). Generative AI Dependency Scale (GAI-DS), used for discriminant validity.
codes.note: The only correlations reported are in Table 4 (p.10, N=300): KQAIDS with the AI Literacy Scale r=.11* and KQAIDS with the GAI-DS r=.03. Neither is an eligible correlate: AI literacy is not on the list, and the GAI-DS is another dependence measure. No depression, anxiety, loneliness or other eligible psychological correlate was measured.

codes.sample: Turkish-context undergraduate students (country not explicitly stated in the text), surveyed online. Three independent groups: EFA n=429, CFA n=490, large-scale implementation n=803 (494 female, 309 male). All were GAI users.
codes.ai_system: Generative AI tools in general (GAI tools; free vs paid versions)
codes.dependence_measures: Generative Artificial Intelligence Addiction Scale (GAI-AS): 18 items, 5-point Likert, newly developed. Four subscales (Salience, Excessive Dependency, Mood Modification, Functional Impairment) plus a total score; total α=0.90.
codes.note: The GAI-AS was compared only with gender, grade level, GAI version and frequency of use. The only correlations reported are among the GAI-AS subscales. The authors say criterion validity was not tested against other scales. No eligible psychological correlate was measured. Mood-modification items mention escapism, but these are part of the AI-dependence scale itself, not a separate measure.

codes.sample: 396 Chinese GenAI users (526 collected; 130 with no GenAI experience or low-quality responses removed); 48.5% male; 97% aged 19-35; 86.1% bachelor's degree or above. Anonymous online survey, cross-sectional.
codes.ai_system: Generative AI (GenAI) in general
codes.dependence_measures: Problematic GenAI Use (PGAIU), 5 items on a 7-point Likert scale, adapted from Hu et al. (2023) (problematic conversational AI use); α = .883, CR = .885, AVE = .606.

correlations.correlate: Fear of missing out (FoMO), adapted to the GenAI context
correlations.correlate_instrument: FoMO, 5 items, adapted from Przybylski et al. (2013) and Chen (2025); 7-point Likert
correlations.quote: Table 3. Discriminant validity of the measurement model. ... PGAIU 0.457 0.517 0.593 0.591 0.778 (FoMO column = 0.517)

codes.possible_duplicate: None identified.
codes.note: The only eligible correlate is FoMO. It is framed as AI-contextualised FoMO (fear of falling behind on productivity), adapted from Przybylski and Chen (2025). The r = 0.517 is a latent correlation from the CFA Fornell–Larcker table (Table 3). Social comparison orientation, AI flow and perceived irreplaceability are not eligible correlates. Table 5 reports SEM paths only, which do not count.

codes.sample: 240 university teachers (123 male, 117 female; aged 28-60) in Rawalpindi and Islamabad, Pakistan; inclusion required at least 1 year of teaching experience and regular use of AI in academic tasks. Cross-sectional survey.
codes.ai_system: AI applications/tools in general used for academic tasks (planning, decision support, content generation)
codes.dependence_measures: Dependence on AI Scale (DAI), "a 5-item scale which assess the reliance on AI", Cronbach's alpha = .87 (p. 6).
codes.note: Has an eligible dependence measure (DAI), but the only correlates were cognitive load (NASA-TLX workload) and rational/intuitive decision styles (Decision Style Scale). None is on the eligible list; workload was not counted as perceived stress. No correlation table, only regression and moderation coefficients, so it would also fail E4.

codes.sample: Employed adults and students who use LLMs, recruited online: China n = 563 (Credemo/Wenjuanxing), Germany n = 360 and UK n = 567 (Prolific); total N = 1,490. Mean ages 26.68, 31.06 and 28.94.
codes.ai_system: Large Language Models in general (e.g., ChatGPT, DeepSeek)
codes.dependence_measures: Adapted LLM-D12 (Yankouskaya et al., 2025): instrumental dependency (6 items) and relational dependency (6 items), 6-point Likert scale.
codes.possible_duplicate: Part of a broader multi-country project on LLM dependency (Ali/Yankouskaya/Liebherr group). The samples may overlap with the LLM-D12 scale paper (Yankouskaya et al., 2025b, ACM TWeb) or other papers from the same project.
codes.note: Only correlate is workaholism (working excessively/compulsively), not an eligible correlate. Per-country Pearson r are shown only in Figure 2 (no text); the text gives Fisher z tests and pooled regressions. Personality and other measures from the broader survey are mentioned but not reported. The OSF data (osf.io/vcpzr) may hold eligible variables.

codes.sample: 81 medical university students in Ukraine (Ternopil National Medical University); 54.9% women; aged 16–22; 52.4% were 3rd-year students; cross-sectional online survey.
codes.ai_system: Generative AI in general: general-purpose text LLMs, image generators, coding assistants, and role-play/communicative bots (e.g., Character.ai)
codes.dependence_measures: An author-developed block of 10 statements on problematic AI use, in 3 groups: cognitive offloading/loss of autonomy, emotional attachment, and loss of control/hiding use. Students were classified as risk group vs adaptive use (37.0% vs 63.0%). The analysis is item by item; no total score is reported.
codes.possible_duplicate: None identified. The author's earlier work (ref 9, Chornomydz & Klantsa 2025) is a theoretical paper.
codes.note: Item-level Spearman ρ (n=81) only, e.g. 'anxiety when AI is unavailable' with uncritical acceptance (+0.433), 'blank page fear' (+0.344), 'AI understands me better' (+0.390). That anxiety is a withdrawal-like part of dependence, not general anxiety or fear of AI. Other correlates (use time, gender, bot type, cognitive laziness) are not eligible. Reviewer may judge this differently.

codes.sample: Exp 1: 338 US junior-level business students (convenience sample). Exp 2: 563 US Amazon MTurk workers (mean age 31.7, 78% male). Both were 2 × 2 between-participants randomised experiments.
codes.ai_system: Generative AI in general (GenAI tools); the stimuli were health summaries generated by GPT-4o
codes.dependence_measures: Learned dependency on GenAI, self-report on a 5-point Likert scale. Exp 1 used a 6-item scale adapted from media/technology reliance research [42] (α=0.782). Exp 2 used a 17-item scale: the 6 Exp 1 items plus 11 items adapted verbatim from Goh et al [26] (α=0.932).
codes.note: The dependence measure is eligible, but the only correlate is trust in AI-generated health information, which is not on the eligible list. Trust–dependency latent r is 0.697 (Exp1) and 0.643 (Exp2). Controls were demographics only. No depression, anxiety, stress, loneliness or other eligible correlate was measured.

codes.sample: N = 392 EFL undergraduates in mathematics courses at three public universities in Eastern and Southern China. All were active generative AI users (ChatGPT, ERNIE Bot or similar), recruited by purposive sampling through an online survey.
codes.ai_system: Generative AI tools in general (ChatGPT, ERNIE Bot or similar platforms) used for academic tasks
codes.dependence_measures: Perceived AI Dependency: an 8-item scale adapted from Zhang et al. (ref 41), rated on a 5-point Likert scale (α = 0.90, CR = 0.92, AVE = 0.59; M = 3.82, SD = 0.91). A separate 8-item Generative AI Usage scale (Abbas et al.) measures frequency and depth of use, so it is not a dependence measure.

correlations.correlate_instrument: Reading self-efficacy scale adapted from Pei & O'Brien (15 items; difficulty, enjoyment, processing)
Reading self-efficacy scale adapted from Pei & O'Brien
Technostress scale adapted from Wang et al. (ADT 7 items, NST 6 items)
Technostress scale adapted from Wang et al.

codes.possible_duplicate: None identified.
codes.note: Eligible only if reading self-efficacy counts as academic self-efficacy; reviewer should confirm. Technostress is an ICT-misfit construct, not perceived stress, so it is listed only for judgement. Table 2 (Pearson) and Table 5 (Fornell-Larcker) give identical values. A technology-anxiety marker was measured, but its correlation with dependency is not reported.

codes.sample: Secondary school students in Karachi, Pakistan, from public and private schools. Reported N = 250, but the text says "Out of the 100 respondents" and the regression df (1, 98; total 99) imply n ≈ 100. 76% female, aged 13–16+.
codes.ai_system: AI tools in general (ChatGPT, Gemini, Copilot mentioned)
codes.dependence_measures: AI Dependency Score: the mean of 5 Likert items on "perceived dependency or risk (over-reliance, reduced original thinking)" (p. 6). The questionnaire was adapted from the Kazmi, Ahmad & Siddique (2025) ChatGPT Reliance Scale.
codes.note: The only outcome is a Creativity Score: 10 items on ideation, creative thinking and creative self-efficacy, averaged into one score. Dependency vs creativity: R = .041, β = .041 (Table 4.8/4.10). Creative self-efficacy is not general or academic self-efficacy, and it is not reported separately anyway. No eligible correlate was measured. The sample size is inconsistent (N = 250 vs df = 98).

codes.sample: 250 Arab adults recruited via Prolific (mean age 28.27, SD 6.08; 47.6% male), all frequent or reliant LLM users; Arabic version of the scale; test-retest subsample n=50.
codes.ai_system: LLMs in general (mostly ChatGPT, then Gemini and DeepSeek; respondents rated their own "primary LLM")
codes.dependence_measures: Arabic LLM-D12 (Yankouskaya et al.): Instrumental Dependency (6 items, α=.85), Relationship Dependency (6 items, α=.90), total score (α=.90); 6-point Likert scale.
codes.possible_duplicate: Arabic validation of the LLM-D12 first developed in a UK sample (Yankouskaya et al., 2025, ACM TWEB, doi 10.1145/3765895). Different sample, so not a duplicate, but related work by the same team.
codes.note: Internet addiction (IAT-7) and AI fear (ATAI Fear) were measured, but their links to the LLM-D12 subscales appear only as betas from a 5-predictor multivariate regression (Table 4, p.12; e.g., internet addiction β=0.271), which Table 4 notes control for all other predictors. No correlation matrix. Raw data on OSF (10.17605/OSF.IO/Q9GZT) could yield r.

codes.sample: 1000 students from five vocational high schools in central Taiwan (56% male, 44% female), surveyed October–December 2025 after a 60-minute "AI Emotional Dependence Survey" lesson in the Health and Nursing course.
codes.ai_system: Generative/conversational AI in general (ChatGPT given as an example), used as an AI chatbot for emotional support
codes.dependence_measures: Ad hoc 3-item "Emotionally Dependent Behavioral Intention" (EDBI) scale, 7-point Likert (B1 "Without AI, I would feel like I've lost someone to listen to"; B2 "I may continue to rely on AI for companionship"; B3 "...regard AI as a source of emotional support"). Alpha 0.70, CR 0.83, AVE 0.61. It is framed as an intention, so it only borderline meets I1.

correlations.correlate: Emotional support needs (ESN) - borderline; not a listed eligible correlate
correlations.correlate_instrument: Ad hoc 3-item ESN scale (need for support when stressed/in a bad mood; one loneliness item)

codes.possible_duplicate: None identified.
codes.note: The only psychological construct is ESN (need for emotional support; items cover stress and one loneliness item). It does not measure loneliness, stress or perceived support. A latent r between EDBI and ESN (0.31) is available if ESN is accepted. All other constructs are TAM-type. The reviewer could also exclude under E1, since EDBI measures intention.

codes.sample: Study 1: convenience online survey, 129 respondents, of whom 102 were analysed (73 women, 71.6%; ages 15–55, M = 22.82; mostly university students; 97.1% use ChatGPT). Study 2: qualitative open-ended questionnaire, 11 respondents (10 analysed).
codes.ai_system: Generative AI assistants/chatbots (mainly ChatGPT; also Gemini, Copilot, MetaAI, DeepSeek, Grok, Perplexity)
codes.dependence_measures: Ad hoc 5-point Likert 'Apego' (attachment) scales. Emotional Attachment (AE), 3 items, e.g. 'Si paso un tiempo sin usar mi asistente de IA, lo echo de menos'; α = .394. Functional Attachment (AF), 4 items, e.g. 'Necesito la IA para realizar ciertas tareas', 'Se me hace complicado realizar ciertas tareas sin ayuda de la IA'; α = .795. The thesis frames these as emotional/functional dependence.
codes.possible_duplicate: None identified (undergraduate thesis, Universidad Pública de Navarra, 2025).
codes.note: AE and AF are correlated (Table 15) only with utilitarian functions, hedonic functions, trust in AI and perceived emotional authenticity, none of which is an eligible correlate. Loneliness is discussed but not measured. Item FH2 ('manera de desconectar') touches on escapism, but it belongs to a hedonic-enjoyment scale, not an escapism measure.

codes.sample: 504 full-time working adults in Shanghai, China, who use AI tools regularly in daily work. Purposive online sample (Wenjuanxing), Feb–May 2025; 56.15% male, 76.59% under 35.
codes.ai_system: AI tools in general, used in daily work tasks (including generative AI)
codes.dependence_measures: AI Dependency (AI_Den): 5 items adapted from Morales-García et al. (Dependence on AI scale). AI Addiction (AI_ADD): 12 items adapted from Pawlikowski et al. (short Internet Addiction Test). AI Overreliance (AI_OL): 11 items adapted from Maral et al. All rated on a 7-point Likert scale.

correlations.correlate_instrument: Anxiety, 8 items adapted from Oei et al.
Anxiety, 8 items adapted from Oei et al.
Anxiety, 8 items adapted from Oei et al.
FOMO, 8 items derived from Budnick et al.
FOMO, 8 items derived from Budnick et al.
FOMO, 8 items derived from Budnick et al.

codes.possible_duplicate: None identified.
codes.note: Values are PLS-SEM construct correlations (Fornell-Larcker table); Table 6/7 betas are multivariable paths, not used. Anxiety scale (Oei et al., 8 items) may be general or AI-related anxiety; check Appendix 1. Technostress correlations (AI_ADD .437, AI_Den .463, AI_OL .531) not counted as eligible stress. Cognitive overload is not an eligible correlate.

codes.sample: 1,157 graduate students (553 male, 604 female; master's and doctoral) from universities in Shaanxi, Shandong, Fujian and other Chinese provinces; online survey, cross-sectional.
codes.ai_system: Generative AI (GenAI, e.g., ChatGPT) used for academic and research tasks
codes.dependence_measures: 18-item AI dependence scale adapted from Li et al. (37), with two dimensions (functional dependence and existential dependence), rated on a 5-point Likert scale; α = 0.913, CR = 0.943, AVE = 0.483. Only the total score is correlated in Table 1; no subscale correlations are reported.

correlations.correlate_instrument: Research anxiety scale, 4 items, adapted from Wang et al. (34) (based on PANAS / Rodell & Judge); α = 0.828
correlations.location: Table 1; Descriptive statistics and correlation analysis section
correlations.quote: Research anxiety was significantly and positively correlated with performance expectancy (r = 0.332, p < 0.01), GenAI dependence (r = 0.524, p < 0.01)

correlations.correlate: Time pressure (possible academic stress proxy – reviewer to judge)
correlations.correlate_instrument: Time pressure scale, Maruping et al. (31), 3 items; α = 0.746
correlations.location: Table 1; Descriptive statistics and correlation analysis section
correlations.quote: time pressure was significantly and positively correlated with research anxiety (r = 0.717, p < 0.01), performance expectancy (r = 0.441, p < 0.01), GenAI dependence (r = 0.507, p < 0.01)

codes.possible_duplicate: The paper cites Li and Jiang (10), who found that time pressure was positively associated with graduate students' GenAI dependence. This could be the same research group, and the samples might overlap. Please check authorship and sample overlap.
codes.note: Eligibility depends on whether domain-specific "research anxiety" (worry or frustration over unfinished research tasks) counts as anxiety or academic stress. Time pressure may not qualify as a stress proxy. Other correlates are not eligible. In Table 1 the diagonal is √AVE and the off-diagonal values are Pearson r. The PROCESS betas are not zero-order.

codes.sample: None. This is a descriptive-analytical paper based on library studies and published articles, with no participants or data collection.
codes.ai_system: AI-generated responses / smart answer-generating tools in general (school students)
codes.dependence_measures: None. 'Cognitive dependence' on AI-generated responses is discussed conceptually only; no quantitative scale or item was administered.
codes.note: Abstract (p.2): 'The research method of this article is descriptive-analytical and is based on library studies and credible scholarly articles.' The paper is a Persian-language conceptual/theoretical essay on managing students' cognitive dependence on AI, with teaching recommendations. It reports no empirical data, measures or correlations.

codes.sample: 1105 volunteer participants (Türkiye), predominantly undergraduate and graduate students; mean age 22.88 (SD = 5.28, range 18–54); 77.4% female; online convenience sample via Google Forms.
codes.ai_system: AI tools in general (AI used for information, learning, problem solving, etc.)
codes.dependence_measures: Artificial Intelligence Dependency Scale (Morales-García et al., 2024; Turkish adaptation by Savaş, 2024): 5 items, 5-point Likert, one dimension (e.g., "I feel vulnerable when I don't have access to AI."); α = .81 in this sample.

correlations.correlate_instrument: Self-Doubt Scale (Oleson et al., 2000; Turkish adaptation by Duru & Balkıs, 2014)

correlations.correlate: Fear of failure (not a listed correlate)
correlations.correlate_instrument: Fear of Failure Scale (Conroy et al., 2002; Turkish adaptation by Balkıs & Duru, 2019)
correlations.quote: Fear of failure was also positively correlated with self-doubt (r = .67, p < .01) and AI dependency (r = .35, p < .01).

correlations.correlate: Neophobia / fear of innovation (general novelty; not fear of AI)
correlations.correlate_instrument: Neophobia Scale (Turkish adaptation by Karataş Yücel, 2021), 8 items
correlations.quote: neophobia was positively correlated with ... AI dependency (r = .24, p < .01)

codes.possible_duplicate: None identified.
codes.note: The exposure is eligible, but the correlates are neophobia, fear of failure and self-doubt, and none is on the list. Self-doubt is close to low self-efficacy or self-esteem; if the reviewer counts it, the report is eligible, with zero-order r = .346 in Table 2. Neophobia is fear of novelty in general, not AI-related anxiety. All correlations are listed for the reviewer to judge.

codes.sample: 164 Bachelor of Secondary Education students at a higher education institution in Davao de Oro, Philippines, selected by stratified random sampling (p. 9).
codes.ai_system: AI tools in general, used for academic tasks (generative AI)
codes.dependence_measures: A 22-item AI dependence questionnaire on a five-point scale (M = 2.68, SD = 0.72). It measured "the extent to which students rely on AI tools when carrying out academic tasks" (pp. 9, 12). The scale's source and name are not given.
codes.note: Correlates were only self-regulated learning (SRL) and a researcher-made critical-thinking test; neither is eligible. SRL is not self-control or self-efficacy, but the reviewer may want to confirm this. The only r reported is SRL–critical thinking (.56). No zero-order r with AI dependence is given, and the moderation results are only described in words.

codes.sample: 200 undergraduate students from several universities in Pakistan (100 male, 100 female), most aged 18-22 (55.5%). All used AI academic tools at least 3 times a week. Convenience sample recruited online through Google Forms.
codes.ai_system: AI academic tools in general (ChatGPT, Grammarly, paraphrasing software) used for writing, reading and numeracy
codes.dependence_measures: Students' AI Dependency in 3R's Questionnaire (Capinding, 2024). 33 items on a 4-point scale, with subscales for Writing (11 items), Reading (10) and Numeracy (12); total α = .91. Only the total mean score is correlated with other variables. No subscale correlations are reported.

correlations.correlate: Fear of negative evaluation (social anxiety component)
correlations.correlate_instrument: Brief Fear of Negative Evaluation Scale (Leary, 1983), 12 items
correlations.quote: AI dependence showed a significant positive relationship with the Fear of Negative Evaluation, r = .36, p < .001

codes.possible_duplicate: None identified.
codes.note: Eligible only if the BFNE counts as social anxiety; the authors call FNE "a core element of social anxiety". Impostor syndrome (r = .37) is not an eligible correlate. Many 3R's items measure use rather than dependence. If FNE is not accepted, the reason should be no_eligible_correlate.

codes.sample: Students from three universities in China and one in Malaysia: 15 interviewees (another passage says 30), a pilot of n = 50, an EFA sample of n = 130, and a CFA sample of n = 279.
codes.ai_system: Digital technologies in general (digital devices, smartphones, internet, digital platforms), with some items about AI-driven devices or platforms.
codes.dependence_measures: There is no AI-dependence measure. The 37-item Digital Burnout Scale has a 'Behavioral Addictions' subscale (X31–X35). Its items cover entertainment software and digital devices generally; only X33 mentions AI. It is a subscale of a digital burnout scale, not a measure of dependence on AI.
codes.note: Scale-development study of digital burnout. The exposure is general digital use, not dependence on AI. No separate eligible correlate was measured; anxiety, loneliness and FOMO appear only as item content. The only associations are HTMT ratios between subscales (Table 6). If the subscale were accepted as the exposure, the report would still fail on no_eligible_correlate.

codes.sample: 180 active Indonesian university students who had used AI-based applications (convenience sample, online Google Form); pilot readability test with 10 students.
codes.ai_system: AI-based applications in general (ChatGPT, Gemini, Grammarly, Claude, other AI apps)
codes.dependence_measures: Indonesian adaptation of the AI Dependency Scale: 15 items, 5-point Likert, with three dimensions (cognitive, emotional, behavioral dependency). The text gives the original instrument as Goh et al. (2025) in one place and Sultana et al. (2025) in another. The only analysis is a three-factor CFA.
codes.note: Psychometric adaptation study only. The only correlations reported are latent correlations between AI dependence subscales (cognitive–emotional .934, cognitive–behavioral .949, emotional–behavioral .955, p.8). No external psychological correlates were measured; the authors list convergent validity against internet or smartphone dependence as future work (p.11).

codes.sample: 639 university students in Java, Indonesia, recruited by convenience sampling through an online survey run January–March 2026 (683 responses collected, 44 excluded for straight-lining).
codes.ai_system: AI tools in general used for academic or learning activities (ChatGPT named as an example), measured as generative AI dependency
codes.dependence_measures: Generative AI Dependency Scale (Goh et al., 2025), 11 items in three dimensions: salience & compulsive use, negative consequences, and withdrawal. It was modelled as a higher-order construct in PLS-SEM (p. 128: "The AI dependency variable was measured using 11 items of the Generative AI Dependency Scale developed by Goh et al. (2025)").
codes.note: The only correlates measured were cognitive fatigue (Yang et al., 2026), engagement with AI, and critical thinking disposition (Sosu, 2013). None of these is on the eligible list, and cognitive fatigue is not perceived or psychological stress. Even if a correlate had counted, only HTMT ratios (Table 2) and PLS-SEM path coefficients (Table 4) are reported. There is no zero-order correlation matrix.

codes.sample: 166 first-year Vietnamese EFL students (English majors) in the English Writing Skills 1 course at Hanoi University of Industry; 114 female (68.7%) and 52 male (31.3%); online survey given in week 9.
codes.ai_system: Generative AI writing tools in general: ChatGPT (most often used), Google Translate, Grammarly, Gemini and QuillBot.
