codes.dependence_measures: AI Dependency (B4): an ad hoc 5-item Likert scale (α = 0.71) that "assessed the extent to which students relied on AI assistance during writing tasks" (M = 3.35, SD = 0.58).
codes.possible_duplicate: None identified.
codes.note: Table 4 (p.7) correlates AI Dependency only with AI frequency, AI purposes, AI use across writing stages, perceived writing improvement and AI Concerns (r = 0.37**). AI Concerns covers risks such as accuracy, plagiarism and ethics, not fear of AI or AI anxiety, so I treated it as ineligible. The reviewer may want to confirm this. No other eligible psychological correlate was measured.

codes.sample: 1,139 Chinese university students (undergraduate and graduate) from 20 provinces; 59.4% female; mean age 20.51 ± 2.65 years; cross-sectional online survey (Wenjuanxing).
codes.ai_system: Generative AI in general (GenAI tools such as ChatGPT, DeepSeek, Kimi); the LLM Dependence Scale with "LLMs" reworded as "GenAI"
codes.dependence_measures: Large Language Models Dependence Scale (LDS; Li et al.), adapted to "GenAI": 18 items, 5-point scale, two dimensions (functional dependency, existential dependency); total α = 0.71, subscale α = 0.84 and 0.89. Only the total score was correlated.

correlations.correlate_instrument: Self-Control Scale (Tangney; Chinese revision by Tan), 19 items
correlations.location: Results, Descriptive statistics and correlation analysis; Table 1
correlations.quote: After controlling for age and gender, Pearson correlation analysis... negatively correlated with GenAI dependence (r = −0.19, p < 0.001)

codes.possible_duplicate: No obvious duplicate. The LDS comes from Li et al. (scale development paper, different samples).
codes.note: Only value is a partial r controlling for age and gender (Table 1 titled "partial correlations"); SEM gives only path coefficients. If the reviewer accepts this partial r as near zero-order, code r = −0.19 with self-control (N = 1139) as eligible. Meaning in life and academic engagement are not eligible correlates. The LDS sample items quoted are trust items.

codes.sample: No primary sample. This is a literature survey. It describes datasets from other studies (e.g., the 2017 KISA survey of 29,712 Korean participants), but the authors collected no data themselves.
codes.ai_system: None as the exposure. The paper covers machine learning, data mining and deep learning used to detect or predict smartphone addiction.
codes.dependence_measures: No measure of dependence on AI. The paper only mentions smartphone addiction scales from the studies it reviews (S-scale, Smartphone Addiction Scale, Smartphone Dependency Test, Modified Social Media Addiction Scale).
codes.note: The abstract says: "This paper offers a comprehensive survey of machine learning, data mining and deep learning techniques employed to detect and predict smart phone addiction." This makes it a review with no original data (E5). It would also fail E3, because AI is used here to detect or predict addiction, and the addiction studied is to smartphones, not to AI.

codes.sample: University students in Pakistan (SZABIST Islamabad authors); N=300, aged 18-37; online cross-sectional survey. Table 1 header says N=250, and its gender counts (137+164) add up to 301, but the text, Table 2 and df=298 all point to N=300.
codes.ai_system: AI in general (AI tools/technologies, e.g. ChatGPT, chatbots, virtual assistants)
codes.dependence_measures: AI Dependency Scale: 5 items on a 5-point Likert scale covering emotional dependence, fear of falling behind in tasks, need for AI validation and worries about AI replacing human abilities. Higher scores mean more dependence. Only a total score is reported.

correlations.quote: AN .257 .067 .217 3.84** ... In Step 2, anxiety showed a standardized coefficient (β= .217, p < .01) ... (R² = .047, F= 14.7, df=298)
ST .238 .065 .208 3.67** ... Stress demonstrated a standardized coefficient (β= 2.08, p < .01) ... (R² = .043, F= 13.5, df=298)
DP .259 .072 .205 3.61** ... depression showed a standardized coefficient (β= .205, p < .01) ... (R² = .42, F= 13.0, df=298)

codes.possible_duplicate: None identified.
codes.note: Called 'stepwise', but each predictor looks like its own one-predictor regression: beta = R = √R², and t (3.84, 3.67, 3.61) and F (14.7, 13.5, 13.0) match a bivariate r at n=300, df=298. So the betas can be read as zero-order r. No correlation table. Typos: '2.08' for .208; R²='.42' for .042. Reviewer should check this reading; if rejected, use E4.

codes.sample: No participant sample. The authors searched documentation from GenAI developers and AI conference proceedings (2022–2025) by keyword and reviewed the literature.
codes.ai_system: GenAI assistants in general (ChatGPT, Gemini, Claude, Llama, Qwen, DeepSeek, Grok), discussed conceptually
codes.dependence_measures: None. The authors did not give a dependence or addiction scale to anyone. They only summarise other studies (e.g., Gerlich 2025; Zhou & Zhang 2024; Marriott & Pitardi 2024; Fang et al. 2025).
codes.note: Position/review paper (FAccT '26). Its only data are keyword counts of AI-safety topics in industry documents and conference papers; no new participant data or correlations. Cited primary studies may be worth screening: Zhou & Zhang 2024 (GenAI addiction), Marriott & Pitardi 2024 (Replika addiction, loneliness), Fang et al. 2025 (emotional dependence, loneliness).

codes.sample: N = 521 people recruited by snowball sampling at King Abdulaziz University, Saudi Arabia. Mostly undergraduates (89.4%); the rest were postgraduates, faculty and staff. 80.2% female; age 18–58 years (M = 21.92, SD = 3.75).
codes.ai_system: AI tools / AI-driven digital resources in general (generative AI in academic and daily tasks)
codes.dependence_measures: AI-Dependency Scale: 15 items, 5-point Likert, total score Ai-Dep. It has three subscales from EFA/CFA: Direct Interaction Reliance (DIR), Practical/Applied Dependency (PAD) and Cognitive/Affective Reliance (CAR). Second-order CFA fit was acceptable; omega total = 0.95.

correlations.quote: Anxiety was modestly associated with Ai-Dep (r = 0.228)

correlations.correlate_instrument: Digital stress test, FoMO subscale (5 situational items)
Digital stress test, Social Acceptance Anxiety subscale
Digital stress test, total of 25 items (adapted from Xie et al.)

codes.possible_duplicate: This is a Research Square preprint. The page says a Version of Record was published in BMC Psychology on 5 Sep 2026 (doi:10.1186/s40359-026-05496-0). That is the same sample, so the two should be linked and counted once.
codes.note: Anxiety is AI-related anxiety, not general anxiety. QoL (higher = better) correlates positively with Anxiety (0.343) and dependence, and the text's "weaker" QoL claim and positive anxiety–digital-stress claim don't match Table 3 (it shows negatives): possible scoring error. FoMO/SAA/stress are subscales of a custom situational test. Network partial correlations not used.

codes.sample: 394 young adults living in Mumbai City who use Generative AI, recruited by purposive sampling through Google Forms. Ages: 41.37% were 18–20, 26.65% were 21–24, 27.41% were 25–30 and 4.57% were over 30. Most were undergraduates (53.55%) or working (29.70%).
codes.ai_system: Generative AI tools in general (ChatGPT, Gemini, Microsoft Copilot and similar applications)
codes.dependence_measures: Ad hoc 4-item 'Generative AI Dependence' scale on a 5-point Likert scale (M = 3.58, SD = 1.01, α = 0.794). Example item: 'Completing certain academic/professional tasks without Generative AI can be difficult'. A separate single item on AI substitution behaviour was also reported.
codes.note: Only productive struggle (3 items) and independent skill development (4 items) were measured; neither is an eligible correlate. Dependence was linked only to productive struggle, by simple regression (R = 0.101, β = 0.104, p = 0.045, Table 10, p. 8). No depression, anxiety, stress, loneliness, self-efficacy, procrastination or other eligible correlate was measured.

codes.sample: 47 Astana IT University students studying programming (Google Forms survey), plus a semi-structured interview with 1 student (Kazakhstan).
codes.ai_system: AI tools for programming: ChatGPT, Copilot, Gemini, Cursor Cloud, and others
codes.dependence_measures: None. The survey asked about which AI tools students used, what they used them for, and how they saw AI's effect on learning, and reported only percentages. 'Potential reliance on AI' came up only as a topic in the one interview, which was qualitative.
codes.note: Descriptive student report that gives only percentages, e.g. '54.3% noted that artificial intelligence is very effective at reducing stress'. Stress was a perceived benefit, not a stress measure. There is no dependence or addiction scale and no correlations. 'Reduction in independence' comes from interview and survey impressions only.

codes.sample: 250 university students in Pakistan (undergraduate and postgraduate; social sciences, business, computer science, education), chosen by simple random sampling; 56% male.
codes.ai_system: AI tools in education in general (generative AI, ChatGPT, AI writing tools, intelligent tutoring systems)
codes.dependence_measures: A self-report 'AI Reliance Score' / 'AI Overreliance' / 'AI dependency level' from a structured questionnaire written for this study. Items, number of items and reliability are not reported. Dependency was also grouped into 3 levels for the ANOVA.
codes.note: The only outcomes measured were academic usage efficiency (r = 0.68, Table 2), creativity (single-predictor regression β = -0.52, Table 3) and analytical abilities (ANOVA F = 18.67, Table 4). None of these is an eligible correlate. The dependence measure is poorly described, so it is borderline for I1 as well. Report quality is low (for example, unrelated references are cited).

codes.sample: 200 undergraduate students aged 18-25 (mean age 20.78; 62.5% female) in BS (Hons) programmes at four public and private universities in Lahore, Pakistan, all using AI tools for academics. Purposive sampling, cross-sectional design.
codes.ai_system: AI tools for academic work in general (ChatGPT 94.5%, Grammarly, DeepSeek, Quillbot, Copilot, Perplexity, SciSpace)
codes.dependence_measures: AI Dependency subscale of the Academic Self-Efficacy and AI Dependency Assessment Scale (ASAIDAS; Acosta-Enriquez et al., 2025): 5 items on a 5-point Likert scale (e.g., "I have difficulty performing tasks without AI support"); M=15.6, SD=3.75, α=0.81 (Table 2).

correlations.correlate_instrument: ASAIDAS academic self-efficacy subscale (7 items, α=0.82)

codes.possible_duplicate: No overlapping publication found. The scale is taken from Acosta-Enriquez et al. (2025), which uses a different sample.
codes.note: No primary correlates measured. Academic self-efficacy is a subscale of the same ASAIDAS instrument (shared method). BFI-10 α=0.24. Table 3 prints some impossible values (e.g., -2.83, -3.65, -6.26, 1.85), and column positions were inferred from the PDF extraction, so values should be checked against the PDF. Imposter phenomenon (r=0.48) is not an eligible correlate.

codes.sample: 300 young adults aged 18-30 from Chennai, South India, who use AI tools often; purposive sampling; offline/online questionnaires.
codes.ai_system: Generative AI tools in general (chatbots, AI writers, search assistants; e.g., ChatGPT, Gemini, Google Bard)
codes.dependence_measures: Generative AI Dependency Scale (GAIDS; Goh & Hartanto, 2025), 10 items, 5-point Likert, total score used (M = 30.22, SD = 10.73). Labelled 'Reliance on AI (RAI)' in tables.
codes.note: There is a dependence measure (GAIDS), but the only correlates are critical thinking disposition (CTDS; r = -.902) and problem-solving ability (PSI total; r = -.958), Table 2, p. 8. Neither is an eligible correlate. The PSI has a problem-solving confidence facet, but only the PSI total is reported, so no self-efficacy r is available. The correlations are implausibly high.

codes.sample: Indian university students aged 18–25. Cronbach's alpha pilot n = 80; test–retest n = 42 matched; EFA n = 240 (77.5% female, M age = 20.8). The abstract says the scale was given to 300 students.
codes.ai_system: AI tools in general used for academic purposes (generative AI, AI study tools)
codes.dependence_measures: Academic AI Usage Scale (AAIUS), 24 items, 5-point Likert. It includes a 9-item 'AI Dependence' subscale (alpha = .864), e.g., 'I struggle to complete academic work without AI assistance.' The other subscales are Academic Support (11 items) and Academic Skills (4 items).
codes.possible_duplicate: The study was done as part of a Master's dissertation at CHRIST University, Bengaluru (Chakraborty), so the dissertation may describe the same sample.
codes.note: Scale development preprint (content validity, EFA, alpha, test–retest). It has an AI Dependence subscale, but no psychological correlate was measured and there is no convergent validity analysis. The supplementary files hold only KMO, CVR/CVI and item reliability statistics. Self-efficacy is mentioned only as future research.

codes.sample: None. This is a proposed study only: a planned target of 600–800 Indian adults aged 18–29 who used conversational AI in the past 3 months. No participants were recruited.
codes.ai_system: Conversational AI / generative AI in general (planned)
codes.dependence_measures: Planned only: an existing conversational AI dependence measure, e.g., an adaptation of the Indian CAIDSS (Verma, 2025), to be validated for the Indian context. No data were collected.
codes.possible_duplicate: None known. If a results paper from this protocol appears later (Bose, Indian young adults, conversational AI dependence), screen it separately.
codes.note: This is a study protocol/proposal with no results. p.13: "Because this manuscript represents a proposed empirical study, no numerical findings are claimed." Planned correlates are loneliness (UCLA), distress (DASS-21), perceived social support (MSPSS) and well-being (WHO-5), but no correlations are reported.

codes.sample: 122 post-graduate management students (61 MBA, 61 PGDM) in India; 50.8% male, 48.4% female; mean age 24.10 (SD 2.96); convenience sample, cross-sectional survey (p. 3, 5).
codes.ai_system: Generative AI tools in general (ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, etc.) used for academic work.
codes.dependence_measures: Cognitive Dependence (CD): ad hoc 5-item, 5-point Likert scale, "5 items about students' dependence on AI for tasks" (p. 4); α = 0.981. No item content is given.
codes.possible_duplicate: None identified.
codes.note: CD is correlated only with GAI usage (r=0.947), learning effectiveness (0.943) and critical thinking confidence (-0.950) (Table 2, p. 6). None is an eligible correlate. Borderline: CT confidence (own critical thinking without AI) is not general or academic self-efficacy. Metadata year 2024 conflicts with the PDF header (July 2026).

codes.sample: No primary participants. This is a systematic evidence map of 268 reports (263 study families), 150 of them T1a human-participant reports in health professions education. Ethics section: "This study analysed only study-level data from publicly available reports."
codes.ai_system: AI in health professions education in general (generative AI, ChatGPT, AI decision support), as mapped across the included reports
codes.dependence_measures: None collected. The review codes dependence-related claims and assessments (over-reliance, cognitive offloading, automation bias, delegation of decision authority, weakened reasoning ability, skill degradation) at the level of each report. No participant-level dependence scale was given.
codes.note: Systematic evidence map (PRISMA-ScR, PROSPERO CRD420261390138). No correlations with psychological correlates; no pooling. Cited primary studies to check: ref 22, Cui & Zhang 2026, Front Psychol (AI dependence, AI literacy, critical thinking in nursing interns); ref 23, Wu et al., Front Psychol (AIDep-22 AI dependence scale, Chinese undergraduates).

codes.sample: Chinese adults recruited via Credamo. Sample 1: n=30 interviewees. Sample 2: n=300 (EFA). Sample 3: n=297 (CFA and validity correlations). Retest subsample: n=100 university students, retested at 4 weeks.
codes.ai_system: Generative AI tools in general (e.g., ChatGPT)
codes.dependence_measures: New 19-item GAI Dependence Scale on a 7-point scale. Subscales: Intensity of Use, Content Dependency, Withdrawal Symptoms, Negative Consequences. Also a 6-item AI Dependence Scale adapted by Zhang et al. (2024) from the Bergen Facebook Addiction Scale.
codes.note: Table 3 (n=297) only correlates the GAI dependence total and subscales with the 6-item AI Dependence Scale (the other dependence measure) and with Behavioral Intention (acceptance/UTAUT). Neither is an eligible correlate. No psychological correlates were measured. The supplementary material holds only demographics (Table S1).

codes.sample: No empirical sample. This is a theoretical overview of what Uzbek psychologists have written.
codes.ai_system: Artificial intelligence in general (conceptual discussion only)
codes.dependence_measures: None. Emotional dependence on AI is only discussed conceptually; no measure or data are reported.
codes.note: Conference paper giving a narrative/theoretical review of Uzbek scholars (Barotov, Karimova, Nishonova and others). Quote: "the relationship between individuals and technological environments is not discussed directly through the concept of 'emotional dependence on artificial intelligence.'" No methods, participants or statistics. The text ends within the references; the body looks complete.

codes.sample: Three-wave time-lagged survey; matched sample of 623 Chinese university students (bachelor, master, PhD) who use generative AI tools. A qualitative component used 15 educator interviews.
codes.ai_system: Generative AI tools for learning (e.g., ChatGPT, Copilot)
codes.dependence_measures: AI Over-Reliance: 5 items adapted from Acosta-Enriquez et al. (2025), 5-point Likert, α = 0.870. Example items: "I find it difficult to perform academic tasks without AI support"; "I find it difficult to control how much I rely on AI for my studies".
codes.note: Correlates measured: AI literacy, critical AI evaluation, self-regulated learning (AI-specific), effective AI use, polychronicity and sustainable learning performance. None of these is on the eligible list. Even if one were treated as eligible, only HTMT values (Table 5) and PLS-SEM path coefficients (Table 6) are reported, with no correlation matrix, so E4 would also apply.

codes.sample: 112 active university students at a private campus in West Jakarta, Indonesia (35 male, 77 female), aged 19-26 (mean 24), using AI in learning; cross-sectional online survey.
codes.ai_system: AI tools in general used for learning (ChatGPT, Perplexity, Gemini, "Gbt")
codes.dependence_measures: AI Dependency Scale (Hoffmann et al., 2024), 5 items, adapted into Indonesian; alpha = .724 in this sample.

correlations.correlate_instrument: Self-Regulation Questionnaire short form (Brown et al., 1999; Indonesian adaptation Tresnadiani & Taufik, 2020), 9 items
correlations.quote: Dependency on AI showed a significant correlation with self-regulation (SR), r = .317**.

codes.possible_duplicate: None identified.
codes.note: Reviewer decision needed: is general self-regulation (SRQ short form) an acceptable proxy for self-control? If not, the report is no_eligible_correlate. Sign anomalies: SR correlates positively with AID and negatively with critical thinking (-.345), and the text says men scored higher on SR while Table 3 shows women higher. SR scoring may be reversed; verify the sign.

codes.sample: Undergraduate computer science students enrolled in object-oriented programming courses (N=12); within-subject lab study comparing a standard generative AI chat interface with a guided prototype (p. 3, Section 5.1).
codes.ai_system: Generative AI coding assistants / chat-based LLM (e.g., ChatGPT) vs. a task-centered guided AI prototype for Java courses
codes.dependence_measures: None. 'Cognitive dependency' is targeted conceptually. The only outcome related to it is observed copying of code ('blind code duplication') during an experimental task. Other instruments were the System Usability Scale, an expert heuristic evaluation, and a code-understanding quiz with think-aloud (p. 3, Section 5.2). There is no self-report dependence scale.
codes.note: This is an HCI design and usability study of an interface meant to reduce dependence on AI. Over-reliance was only observed as behaviour during the task (copying code), and no self-report dependence measure was used. No eligible psychological correlates (e.g., depression, anxiety, stress) were measured. No statistics are reported, only descriptive 'preliminary results'.

codes.sample: 80 Computer Studies students and 10 faculty members at Saint Francis College Guihulngan, Negros Oriental, Philippines; purposive sampling (p. 2–3).
codes.ai_system: AI tools in general (ChatGPT, grammar applications, content generators)
codes.dependence_measures: None quantitative. A study-made needs-assessment questionnaire asked how users "felt about AI in their studies". Responses were tallied and averaged, and open answers were coded. Results are given only as narrative themes ("Reliance on AI and Its Effect on Independent Learning"). No dependence scale and no scores are reported.
codes.note: This is a system-development (Prototype Model) paper about a web portal. The needs assessment is reported only as qualitative themes (p. 4). There is no quantitative AI-dependence measure, no eligible psychological correlate and no statistics. E1_no_dependence_measure would also apply.

codes.sample: 528 Peruvian medical students (described as university students), aged 18–37 (M = 20.31, SD = 3.8); 53.0% female. Convenience sample, split into an EFA subsample (n = 226) and a CFA subsample (n = 302). Cross-sectional design.
codes.ai_system: AI platforms or tools in general (the introduction mentions ChatGPT, GPT-4, Copilot and Dall-E 2)
codes.dependence_measures: Scale for Dependence on Artificial Intelligence (DAI/DIA): 5 items, unidimensional, 5-point Likert scale, adapted from DSM-5 dependence criteria (alpha = omega = 0.87). This is a newly developed scale.
codes.possible_duplicate: This is the scale development paper for the DAI by Morales-García et al. (2024). Later papers that use the DAI may come from the same research group or sample; check any Morales-García / Universidad Peruana Unión reports that use this scale.
codes.note: Psychometric validation only: EFA, CFA, reliability and gender invariance. No other construct was measured, so no convergent or discriminant correlations exist. Only item descriptives, item-total r, loadings and fit indices are reported. Item 5 (fear that AI replaces one's skills) is an item inside the scale, not a separate fear-of-AI measure.

codes.sample: 428 college students from five universities in eastern China (196 female, 232 male); convenience sample; two-wave time-lagged online survey, Sept–Nov 2025.
codes.ai_system: Generative AI (GenAI) tools in general, used for academic tasks
codes.dependence_measures: GenAI dependence (AID): 5-item scale adapted from Zhang et al. (2024), 5-point Likert, α = 0.906 (e.g., "I feel anxious when I am unable to use GenAI to complete learning tasks"). Measured at wave 2.

correlations.exposure: GenAI dependence (AID, Zhang et al. 2024 scale)
correlations.correlate_instrument: 7-item academic self-efficacy scale adapted from Nielsen et al. (2018) and Acosta-Enriquez et al. (2025)
correlations.location: Table 1 (CFA and correlation analysis results); Results text
correlations.quote: Academic self-efficacy was significantly negatively correlated with ... GenAI dependence (r = −0.422, p < 0.01)

correlations.exposure: GenAI dependence (AID, Zhang et al. 2024 scale)
correlations.correlate_instrument: 5-item academic stress scale adapted from Zhang et al. (2024)
correlations.location: Table 1 (CFA and correlation analysis results); Results text
correlations.quote: Academic stress was significantly positively correlated with perceived usefulness of GenAI (r = 0.448, p < 0.01) and GenAI dependence (r = 0.411, p < 0.01)

codes.possible_duplicate: No obvious duplicate. The dependence and academic stress scales come from Zhang et al. (2024), which is a separate study. Single author (CZ, Jinling Institute of Technology); worth checking for other reports from the same 2025 dataset.
codes.note: Correlations come from a Fornell–Larcker-style table, but the text says they are Pearson correlations. Time-lagged design: self-efficacy and stress at wave 1, dependence at wave 2, three weeks apart. Perceived usefulness (r = 0.399) is not an eligible correlate. The SEM betas are not zero-order and were not used.

codes.sample: 453 undergraduate sports majors (295 male, 158 female) from three universities in Jiangxi Province, China. Snowball sampling via Wenjuanxing, March–April 2025. 78.8% were aged 18–21.
codes.ai_system: Generative AI tools in general (e.g., ChatGPT, Midjourney) used for learning and training
codes.dependence_measures: Generative AI Dependence Scale adapted from Hou, Zhu, Sudarshan, Lim & Ong: 16 items, 5-point Likert, four dimensions (reflective, cautious, thoughtless and collaborative use; alphas .774/.833/.857/.878; overall alpha .736). It is modelled as a higher-order construct, with the dimension scores serving as its indicators in PLS-SEM.

correlations.correlate_instrument: Self-Efficacy Scale adapted from Fangzhou, Lin & Lai (3 items)
correlations.quote: SE | 0.693 | 0.687 | 0.372 | 0.848 (row SE, column Generative AI dependency)

codes.possible_duplicate: None identified. The dependence scale comes from Hou et al. (ref 86), which is a separate sample.
codes.note: The only candidate correlate is self-efficacy framed around AI ("complete required tasks more effectively with the help of generative AI"), which is not clearly general or academic self-efficacy. Exposure is debatable: reflective/cautious-use items are not dependence. Flow and creativity are not eligible. No subscale correlations.

codes.sample: No primary sample. This is a narrative literature review (it calls itself a "meta-analytic review") of studies on college students published 2022–2026.
codes.ai_system: Generative AI tools in general (ChatGPT, Gemini, AI-assisted learning platforms), discussed only through the studies reviewed
codes.dependence_measures: None administered. The authors summarise AI dependence findings from other studies, e.g., Ahmad & Arshad 2025 and Tian & Zhang 2025.
codes.note: Methods, p. 9: "Qualitative analysis of selected studies was performed." No pooled effect sizes and no primary data; ethics statement (p. 17) says no human subjects were involved. Primary studies it cites (Ahmad & Arshad 2025; Tian & Zhang 2025) may be worth checking as separate records.

codes.sample: 186 university students (63.4% female; 89.2% aged 16–24) at one branch campus of a private university in Puerto Maldonado, Peru, 2024-II cycle. Methods say non-probabilistic convenience sampling, but the abstract says probabilistic sampling.
codes.ai_system: AI tools in general for academic tasks (virtual assistants, content generators, tutoring applications)
codes.dependence_measures: Artificial Intelligence Dependence Scale (Morales et al., 2024): 5 items on a single factor, 1–5 response scale, total score (M=13.08, SD=3.742). The original authors report α=0.870; no alpha is reported for this sample.

correlations.exposure: AI dependence (Artificial Intelligence Dependence Scale, total)
correlations.correlate_instrument: Academic Situations Specific Perceived Self-Efficacy Scale (ASSPSE; 10 items; Domínguez, 2016)
correlations.quote: Table 7 presents the correlation between academic self-efficacy and AI dependence. A Pearson correlation of -0.299 is observed

codes.possible_duplicate: No specific overlap identified. The Estrada-Araoz group has published several studies on AI dependence in Peruvian students, so check those for an overlapping sample.
codes.note: Academic self-efficacy is the only eligible correlate. Comparisons by sex and age (Tables 5–6) are not eligible correlates. Dependence item 5 (fear that AI will replace one's skills) overlaps with AI-related anxiety. The paper contradicts itself on sampling method, and no reliability is reported for this sample.

codes.sample: 316 active students at Indonesian universities who had used AI for academic work, recruited by purposive sampling; cross-sectional design.
codes.ai_system: AI in general for academic activities (AI dependency)
codes.dependence_measures: AI Dependence Scale (AIDep-22; Wu et al., 2026)
codes.note: Only front matter retrieved (abstract, contents, lists of tables and appendices). The only correlate is academic perfectionism (CAPS), which is not eligible. Tables and appendices list only the two instruments. Covariates seem demographic (gender, education level). If the full text shows an eligible covariate, re-check.

codes.sample: None reported. This is a correction notice; the original study was of graduate students in sport sciences (Firat University, Türkiye), but the notice gives no sample details.
codes.ai_system: Artificial intelligence (general), per the original article's title; the correction itself does not describe it.
codes.dependence_measures: The correction gives none. The original article's title mentions 'dependence on artificial intelligence', but the measure is not described here.
codes.possible_duplicate: This is a corrigendum to Yavuz, Karahüseyinoglu & Kirdemir (2026), Front. Psychol. 17:1873886, doi:10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1873886. The original article should be screened as a separate record.
codes.note: The correction only replaces the Funding statement ('An incorrect Funding statement was provided...'). It has no data, measures or results, so it counts as a correction or erratum notice without data. Also, 'creative thinking dispositions' from the original title is not on the eligible-correlate list, so the original article may not qualify either unless it measured other correlates.

codes.sample: 40 participants recruited by convenience sampling (the authors are undergraduate psychology students at Mount Carmel College, Bengaluru, India); no demographics reported.
codes.ai_system: AI conversational agents / chatbots (ChatGPT, Character.AI and Replika are mentioned)
codes.dependence_measures: There is no quantitative dependence measure. AI use was assessed with an open-ended survey on "frequency of use, purpose of use, perceived emotional understanding, trust in AI, and comfort in sharing personal experiences" (p. 272). "Emotional dependency" was identified only through Braun and Clarke thematic analysis.
codes.note: Loneliness was measured with the Loneliness Inventory (Meenakshi & Krishnan, 2010). It was compared with AI engagement only descriptively, via high/moderate/low groups and themes; no statistics, means or r are given. E5 is a possible alternative reason (the dependence part is qualitative). Even if dependence counted, it would fail E4: no zero-order statistic.

correlations.quote: Table 1: Hypothesis tested using Pearson correlation ... Academic Self-Efficacy 22.97 3.04 -.107* 1

codes.possible_duplicate: The AIDQ comes from a validation paper by overlapping authors: Akinwale, Ojakorotu & Oloko (2025), IJSPSY 5(3), 45–50. It may use the same or an overlapping University of Lagos student sample. Please check.
codes.note: Academic motivation (r = .436) is not an eligible correlate. Inconsistencies: AIDQ item count (13 vs 12); self-efficacy instrument (Chemers vs Nielsen); a mean of 22.97 against a stated 9–63 range; F(1, 562) with n = 400; differing R² values. The correlation's n was not stated and is assumed to be 400.

codes.sample: None. This is a theoretical/conceptual essay with no participants or empirical data collection.
codes.ai_system: AI in general (algorithmic recommendation, AI-generated content, AI question-answering tools, virtual assistants) in online science communication
codes.dependence_measures: None. AI dependency is described only conceptually as "functional and emotional reliance the public develops on artificial intelligence technologies" (p. 1); it is never measured quantitatively.
codes.note: Conceptual/theoretical paper with no Methods, sample, measures or statistics. It analyses how AI dependency reshapes public engagement with science (participants, forms, content, logic), discusses challenges, and proposes strategies. Some cited references (e.g., Zhang et al. 2024 IJETHE; Salah et al. 2024 AIholic) may be eligible empirical studies for citation screening.

codes.sample: 347 undergraduate students (300 female, 47 male) at a comprehensive university in China, all with prior AI use in learning
codes.ai_system: AI learning tools / generative AI in general
codes.dependence_measures: AI dependency: 5 items adapted from Andreassen et al. (2016), Zhai et al. (2024), Zhang S. et al. (2024) and Morales-García et al. (2024) University Students' AI Dependency Scale (e.g., "I feel less confident completing academic tasks without AI assistance"). It was used only as a moderator in PROCESS Model 14.
codes.note: Other measures: AI attitude, AI usage motivation (intrinsic, identified, external) and AI-assisted creativity. None is an eligible correlate. AI dependency is not in the Table 2 correlation matrix. Self-efficacy appears only inside the dependency item wording and was never measured on its own. Dependency results are interaction terms only, so E4 would also apply.

codes.sample: No participants were sampled. The paper proposes a secondary analysis of a public synthetic Kaggle dataset ('Academic Outcomes & AI Dependency Analysis Dataset', 8,000 records, 26 variables). A Yamane sample size of 381 is calculated, but no data are analysed.
codes.ai_system: AI tools in education in general (generative AI / conversational assistants)
codes.dependence_measures: 'AI Dependency – level of reliance on AI for academic tasks', taken as a variable from the synthetic Kaggle dataset. No instrument is described and no scores are reported.
codes.note: Proposal with no results: the t-test table is 'intentionally left as a reporting template' (every cell reads 'To calculate'). No eligible correlate is planned either; outcomes are academic performance, conceptual understanding, problem solving, critical thinking and skills. The authors say the dataset is synthetic.

codes.sample: The abstract says 300 university students took part ("Tadqiqotda 300 nafar talaba ishtirok etdi"; "The study involved 300 university students"), in Uzbekistan (Gulistan State University author). No demographics, procedure or descriptive statistics are given.
codes.ai_system: Artificial intelligence in general, especially generative AI and conversational chatbots
codes.dependence_measures: The abstract (p. 3–4) lists an "Emotional Dependence on Artificial Intelligence Scale" ("Sun'iy intellektga nisbatan hissiy qaramlik shkalasi"). It gives no source, items or reliability, and reports no scores. The paper describes 5 conceptual components (emotional, cognitive, behavioral, communicative, reflective), but these are theoretical, not reported subscales.
codes.possible_duplicate: The author, Oqmurzayev D.J., is a doctoral student at Gulistan State University. The same N=300 sample may appear in a later empirical article or in his dissertation, which could report the correlations. Worth checking.
codes.note: Full article retrieved (pp. 440–445). Abstract names eligible correlates (loneliness/UCLA-3, social anxiety/SIAS, Rosenberg self-esteem) but no statistics are reported anywhere. Results are conceptual and the conclusion calls the work a "nazariy-metodologik tahlil" (theoretical-methodological analysis). E5 is a defensible alternative reason.

codes.sample: 120 undergraduate Informatics Engineering students at Universitas Indraprasta PGRI, Jakarta, Indonesia, enrolled in Linear Algebra and experienced with AI/generative AI for academic purposes; purposive sampling; cross-sectional online survey, January–June 2026.
codes.ai_system: AI / generative AI tools in general, used for academic tasks (e.g., conversational AI for solving Linear Algebra problems)
codes.dependence_measures: AI Dependency (KD): ad hoc scale, 6 indicators on a 5-point Likert scale, measuring "the extent to which students relied on AI in completing academic tasks and solving problems". KD6 was dropped (loading 0.406), leaving KD1–KD5; alpha = 0.954, CR = 0.964, AVE = 0.844 (p. 26, 29).
codes.possible_duplicate: None identified.
codes.note: The study has a dependence measure, but the only other constructs are AI literacy and computational thinking skills, and neither is an eligible correlate. Table 5 (Fornell–Larcker) gives only the highest inter-construct correlation for KD: 0.629, with AI literacy. Self-efficacy and academic stress appear only as cited literature and were not measured in this study.

codes.sample: 23 college students (7 male, 16 female; 8 Korean and 15 international) in an English-medium instruction course at Kyung Hee University, Korea.
codes.ai_system: ChatGPT, used for English language learning and essay writing
codes.dependence_measures: None. A researcher-made questionnaire covered perceptions of ChatGPT (purposes, benefits, drawbacks, effect on learning). Dependence appears only as a multiple-choice drawback option ("Depending too much on ChatGPT can limit students' independent thinking...", 73.9%). It is a general perceived drawback, reported as a frequency, not a self-report of dependence.
codes.note: The Big Five Inventory (44 items) was measured. In Tables 2–3 it is correlated only with perception items (speaking, vocabulary, enjoyment, 'good tool', etc.), not with any dependence or over-reliance measure. The over-reliance drawback item is reported only descriptively (Table 6, p.9). There is no dependence exposure, so E1 applies.

codes.sample: None. This is a letter to the editor that proposes a scale; no participants were recruited ("No datasets were generated or analysed during the current study").
codes.ai_system: AI in general (large language models, virtual companions)
codes.dependence_measures: AI Addiction Scale (AIAS-21) was proposed but not administered. It has 21 items rated on a 5-point Likert scale, with 3 items for each of 7 dimensions: compulsive use, craving, tolerance, withdrawal, preoccupation, continued use despite harm, and functional impairment.
codes.note: This is a correspondence piece (letter to the editor) with no data. The author says: "No datasets were generated or analysed during the current study" and "the scale has not been validated in the general population." No correlates were measured. Later validation studies of the AIAS-21 may be eligible.

codes.sample: 241 Chinese university students who are high-frequency AI users (121 male, 120 female), online Wenjuanxing survey, July 2025. 30 at-risk students (24 mild-risk, 6 moderate-risk) took part in a 6-month uncontrolled pre-post exercise intervention.
codes.ai_system: "AI tools and services" in general: conversational AI, generative AI and algorithmically curated systems
codes.dependence_measures: Self-developed "AI Usage Status" module, adapted from the IAT and CIAS-R. 16 items on a 5-point scale, total score 16–80, α=.93. Four subdimensions: difficulty in usage control, emotional dependence, cognitive offloading and social dependence. Risk cut-offs: normal 16–39, mild 40–55, moderate 56–71, severe 72–80.

correlations.exposure: AI Usage Status risk group (at-risk ≥40, n=91 vs normal, n=150)
correlations.correlate: Perceived negative impact of AI use on emotional state (borderline; not a standard well-being/distress measure)
correlations.correlate_instrument: Ad hoc 'Real-life Impact' module, emotional state domain (max 15)
correlations.quote: Emotional wellbeing was also impacted, as at-risk users averaged higher scores (M = 9.27, SD = 2.89) than normative users (M = 5.60, SD = 2.02)

codes.possible_duplicate: None identified
codes.note: No validated eligible correlate was measured. The only borderline item is the ad hoc "emotional state" rating. It asks how much AI use harmed the person's mood, which is an impairment rating within the addiction framework, not a well-being or distress scale. Its group means and SDs could be converted to r if the reviewer counts it. Exercise intensity is not an eligible correlate.

codes.sample: 981 US adults recruited on CloudResearch who completed a 4-week RCT (2,539 enrolled); mean age 39.9 (SD 11.6); 51.8% female. Participants were randomised to a 3×3 design (modality × task) and asked to use ChatGPT GPT-4o at least 5 minutes a day.
codes.ai_system: OpenAI ChatGPT (GPT-4o), in text, neutral-voice or engaging-voice mode (Advanced Voice Mode)
codes.dependence_measures: Emotional dependence: the 'craving' subscale of the Affective Dependence Scale (ADS-9), adapted to refer to the chatbot (1–5). Problematic use: the Problematic ChatGPT Use Scale (PCUS) (1–5). Both were measured weekly; the week-1 score was the baseline and week 4 the final score.

correlations.quote: Final Loneliness row of key-outcome block: 1.0, -0.472, 0.105, 0.185 (columns: Final Loneliness, Final Socialization, Final Emotional Dependence, Final Problematic Use); 'Values in cells represent Spearman correlation coefficients.'

The extracted heatmap cells are scrambled and cannot be matched to rows and columns, so the original figure needs checking. Only BH-significant cells are shown. codes.sample: 190 Grade XII students (culinary and hospitality programmes) who actively used AI in learning, chosen by purposive sampling from a population of 413 at SMK Negeri 9 Padang, Indonesia, in the 2025/2026 odd semester.
codes.ai_system: AI tools in general for learning (examples given: ChatGPT, Photomath, Grammarly)
codes.dependence_measures: An ad hoc Likert-scale questionnaire on AI dependency, built from indicators of AI dependency. Validity came from expert judgement and factor analysis, and Cronbach's alpha was above 0.70. Mean = 43.46, SD = 9.89 (p. 1, 3).
codes.note: The study does measure AI dependency, but the only correlate is critical thinking, which is not on the list of eligible correlates. The reported result is r = 0.066, p = 0.365 (p. 3: "Pearson's correlation analysis was performed, yielding an r-value of 0.066 with a significance level of p = 0.365"). No other psychological variables were measured.

codes.sample: 342 valid online questionnaires from undergraduates at "X University" (Qinghai, China); year 1 12%, year 2 68%, year 3 18%, year 4 3%. Unstructured interviews were also done.
codes.ai_system: Generative AI tools in general (Doubao 87%, DeepSeek 59%, Kimi, ERNIE Bot and others)
codes.dependence_measures: Custom Likert items on functional, cognitive and judgmental dependence, e.g. "I have developed a habitual reliance on AI tools when organizing research materials" and "When encountering complex problems, I tend to consult AI-generated answers before thinking independently". Results are given only as response percentages.
codes.note: Purely descriptive (frequencies only). The other sections cover demographics, AI use frequency and duration, perceived impacts of AI, and views on institutional rules. No eligible psychological correlate was measured and no correlations are reported. Even if one had been, the ad hoc dependence items would be borderline for I1.

codes.sample: Four studies of full-time employees. Study 1: US Prolific experiment, N=172. Study 2: China Credamo experiment, N=165. Study 3: US Prolific two-wave survey, N=218. Study 4: China EDP three-wave field survey, N=285. Only Studies 3 and 4 measured self-efficacy alongside AI dependence.
codes.ai_system: AI systems/tools at work in general (intelligent algorithms, generative AI tools); in the experiments, a conversational algorithm interface
codes.dependence_measures: Employee AI dependence: 3-item scale adapted from Tang et al. (2023), 5-point. Example item: "I depended on AI to manage or assist with work-related tasks." Alpha = 0.96 (S1 manipulation check), 0.90 (S2), 0.79 (S3), and given in Table 6 for S4. It is framed as perceived work reliance on AI, not problematic use.
codes.note: S3 and S4 measured job self-efficacy as a control (Spreitzer 1995, 3 items, alpha .87); its eligibility as a correlate is borderline. The correlation tables (Table 4 for S3, Table 6 for S4) are cited but their contents are not in the retrieved text, so no r values can be taken. Check the PDF tables. Also judge whether Tang's work-reliance construct fits I1.

codes.sample: Chinese undergraduates from one comprehensive university in Southwest China. Sample 1 (EFA) N=400 (70.2% female). Sample 2 (CFA and criterion validity) N=400 (64.8% female; age 18–24, M=21.17). Pilot n=30. Combined N=800 was used for the demographic analyses.
codes.ai_system: AI tools in general, used for academic purposes (generative AI such as ChatGPT)
codes.dependence_measures: AI Dependence Scale (AIDep-22), newly developed: 22 items on a 5-point Likert scale. Subscales: emotional dependence (5 items), functional dependence (6), cognitive dependence (5) and loss of control (6), plus a total score. Total α=0.87.

correlations.correlate_instrument: Academic Self-Efficacy Scale (Pribeanu et al., 2023), SEA subscale

codes.possible_duplicate: None identified.
codes.note: The only eligible correlate is academic self-efficacy (Table 7, sample 2, N=400). The correlation type is not stated, but Pearson is assumed. SSE (social) and CSE (computer) are ASE subscales; the reviewer may decide whether these count as academic self-efficacy. Table 8 betas are multivariable and were excluded. The usage-behaviour correlations are not eligible correlates.

codes.sample: 292 final-year Information Systems students (commuters who use AI tools), Universitas Pamulang, Indonesia; purposive sampling.
codes.ai_system: Generative AI tools / AI assistants used for thesis writing (unspecified)
codes.dependence_measures: "AI Assistant Dependency (X5)" is labelled as dependency, but no items, scale or source are given. It is also called "AI Usage (X5)" with "larger numerical ranges" than the Likert variables X1–X4, and its means reach 54,076 (Table 7). This suggests usage intensity, not a dependence scale.
codes.note: No eligible correlate was measured: the only other variables are distance, travel time, task load, psychosomatic fatigue and graduation status/batch. No correlation matrix is reported, only RF feature importance and mean AI usage by distance/fatigue (Table 7). If X5 counted as dependence, the reason would be no_eligible_correlate. Results are inconsistent (RF accuracy 100% vs 13.56%).

codes.sample: 367 tertiary students (graduate, postgraduate, MPhil/Diploma/PhD) from various disciplines in Bangladesh; purposive sampling; 56% male; aged 18–29; data collected May–Aug 2025.
codes.ai_system: AI tools in general (95% use AI text generators such as ChatGPT and Gemini; also video, image and audio AI tools)
codes.dependence_measures: AI Dependency (AID): 5 items adapted from Morales-García et al. (2024) Dependence on AI scale (e.g., "I feel unprotected when I do not have access to AI"), 5-point Likert; 4 items retained in model (CA = 0.834, CR = 0.889, AVE = 0.667).

codes.note: Correlates are 21st-century skills, none on the eligible list. Self-confidence (social, fear of judgement) is borderline, possibly self-esteem. No correlation or Fornell–Larcker table, only HTMT and PLS paths. SC has AID as sole predictor, so β=0.614 should equal the construct-score correlation (inferred). If SC is accepted, decide on that β; otherwise E4.

codes.sample: 208 Indonesian university students who had actively used ChatGPT for at least the past month (purposive sampling); 100 male, 108 female; mean age 19.98 (SD = 1.38).
codes.ai_system: ChatGPT
codes.dependence_measures: None. The only AI measure is an ad hoc ChatGPT Usage Intensity Scale (5-point Likert) covering frequency, duration and purpose of use: "Intensitas penggunaan ChatGPT diukur dengan kuesioner skala Likert 5 poin mencakup frekuensi, durasi, dan tujuan penggunaan."
codes.note: "Dependence" is mentioned only in the abstract and discussion. The measure covers frequency, duration and purpose of use (use intensity, so E1). For reference: loneliness (UCLA-LS v3) correlated with intensity, Spearman rho = 0.807, n = 208 (Tabel 5). Not extracted, because the exposure is not a dependence measure.

codes.sample: 452 university students (undergraduate and graduate) from one large university in China, matched across two waves 4 weeks apart (580 at T1); 58.0% female; ages 18–28, mean 21.4 (SD 2.8); all used GenAI for academic work at least weekly.
codes.ai_system: Generative AI tools in general (e.g., ChatGPT), used for academic purposes
codes.dependence_measures: Problematic Use of Generative AI (T2): 7-item scale adapted from the Problematic Internet Use Questionnaire (PIUQ; Demetrovics et al., 2008), covering loss of control and preoccupation; 5-point Likert; α = 0.90. Sample item: "I find it difficult to stop using Generative AI even when I know I should focus on other things."

correlations.exposure: Problematic Use of GenAI (T2), 7-item adapted PIUQ
correlations.correlate_instrument: 5-item Perceived Academic Stress scale adapted from PSS (Cohen et al., 1983), T2, α = 0.87

codes.possible_duplicate: None identified.

Correlates left out as not eligible: need for cognition, positive affect, AI literacy, avoidance motivation. Possible integrity issues: the text says the highest r is 0.56 but the table's highest is 0.55, and it says all correlations were significant although −0.05 is not.

codes.sample: 30 third-year computer engineering students at Bulacan State University, Philippines, 2nd semester AY 2023-2024, chosen by simple random sampling (10 per section across 3 sections).
codes.ai_system: AI tools in general (ChatGPT, AI code generation/debugging, paraphrasing, documentation tools)
codes.dependence_measures: Ad hoc 8-item 5-point Likert 'Dependency on AI' questionnaire (e.g., 'I will rely on AI-based code generation...', 'I rely on AI-powered documentation generation'); overall mean 3.5. Most items describe use rather than dependence. Also 6 items on 'factors influencing dependency' (time saving, clarity, availability, trend).
codes.note: The only correlate is academic performance (GWA), which is not on the eligible list, and no correlation statistic is reported. The study is descriptive only (item means, GWA frequencies). The 'factors' items are perceived benefits (e.g., saving time), not escapism or coping motives. Could also be excluded as E1, because the 'dependency' items mostly measure use rather than dependence.

codes.sample: 222 bachelor's and master's students at the University of Dar es Salaam, Tanzania, chosen by stratified sampling (p. 4).
codes.ai_system: AI tools / generative AI in general (e.g., ChatGPT)

The AD items are mostly about use and trust, so E1 could also apply. The text has inconsistencies: it calls a positive β a 'negative effect', and p = .020 does not fit t = 16.663.

codes.sample: 299 university students at Universidad de La Guajira, Colombia, surveyed April 2–27, 2026 (2026-1 academic period). The test set had n = 90.
codes.ai_system: Generative AI tools in general. ChatGPT was mentioned most often, followed by Gemini and Copilot.

Scores range from 2 to 10 and were grouped as Low (2–5), Medium (6–8) and High (9–10). The items ask about perceived cognitive erosion and do not ask directly about dependence.
codes.possible_duplicate: The text mentions 'a preliminary version of the study with a smaller sample', so there may be an earlier report on an overlapping sample.
codes.note: Predictors were sociodemographic, tech-access, usage and perception variables (comprehension, time savings, performance). No eligible psychological correlate was measured. Only ML metrics and feature importances are reported, with no zero-order statistics. E1 could also apply: the index measures perceived loss of critical thinking and autonomy rather than dependence.

codes.sample: No original sample. The text summarises a secondary source: "469 preservice mathematics teachers" (Zhang et al., 2025, Scientific Reports).
codes.ai_system: AI tools in general (as described in the summarised study)
codes.dependence_measures: The report itself contains no measure. It mentions the "AI dependency" measure used in the summarised study (Zhang et al., 2025) but gives no scale details or statistics.

It reports no original data and no statistics, so I classed it as E5_design (it works like a commentary). The summarised study links AI dependency to 21st-century skills and "self-confidence". codes.sample: 66 active Statistics students (2023–2025 cohorts) at Universitas Negeri Medan, Indonesia; purposive sampling; 43 female (65.2%), 23 male (34.8%); all had used ChatGPT at least 3 times in the past month.

One literacy item, "Able to write without GPT assistance", and the discussion of "self-efficacy" (p. 6) touch on writing confidence, but no general or academic self-efficacy scale was used. codes.note: The author calls this a qualitative descriptive study ("metode kualitatif dengan pendekatan deskriptif", p. 3). Results are frequency percentages and open-ended answers only. There is no quantitative dependence measure (E1 would also apply), no eligible psychological correlate (only critical-analysis ability and confidence), and no correlations.

codes.sample: No participants or primary data. This is a conceptual/architectural paper on the Model Context Protocol in FinTech enterprises.
codes.ai_system: Anthropic's Model Context Protocol (MCP) for enterprise AI in financial services. It is discussed as an architecture; no users studied.

codes.note: This is a theoretical/architectural paper with no empirical data and no psychological measures, so E5_design is the primary reason. E3_out_of_scope would also apply, because "dependency" is used in the software-engineering sense (e.g., "reducing AI dependency conflicts"), not as dependence on AI.

codes.sample: 704 Hungarian adults (557 women, 147 men), aged 18–60 (M = 27.8), mostly graduate and postgraduate university students; frequency of AI use available for n = 260.

codes.sample: No human participants. The units are 52 open-source LLM GitHub repositories, 482 Python packages, 890 package vulnerabilities from Snyk.io and 100 merged vulnerability-related pull requests.
codes.ai_system: Open-source LLM code repositories (e.g., LLaMA, ChatGLM, Qwen, StarCoder) analysed as software artefacts, not as interactive systems people use.
codes.dependence_measures: None in the psychological sense. Here "dependency" means the third-party Python packages an LLM codebase relies on (from requirements.txt/setup.py and import statements). The study measures dependency usage frequency and vulnerability counts, not human dependence on AI.
codes.note: Software-dependency security study with no humans or psychological measures. Its only correlations (Spearman 0.1471; Pearson 0.966/0.985) link package or repository metrics. E1 also applies (no human dependence measure), but E3 ("dependence" in another sense) fits best.

codes.sample: 274 active students of the Office Administration Education Study Program, Universitas Negeri Surabaya (population 868), Indonesia; non-probability sampling; online questionnaire.
codes.ai_system: AI / artificial intelligence technology in general for academic tasks
codes.dependence_measures: Artificial Intelligence Dependency (AID), 5 items (AID1–AID5), 5-point Likert scale, Cronbach's alpha 0.904; source not stated (looks like the Morales-García et al. 2024 dependence on AI scale, which is cited).
codes.possible_duplicate: Possibly the same sample as an undergraduate thesis (skripsi) by Dina Yuliana, UNESA (not verified).
codes.note: Correlates: academic stress, academic self-efficacy. Only PLS paths (Tab 7), HTMT (Tab 4: AS–AID .896, ASE–AID .836), item cross-loadings. No correlation/Fornell–Larcker table. Derivable algebraically (reviewer's call): ASE–AID ≈ -0.754 (-0.302 + -0.452); AS–AID ≈ 0.581+(-0.302)(-0.779) ≈ 0.813; this rebuilds R²=.703. ASE->AS -0.779 is a single-predictor beta but has no AI dependency.

codes.sample: Study 2: 572 usable US adult AI friendship app users recruited via Prolific (346 male, 210 female, 10 nonbinary, 6 undisclosed; age 18–85, mostly 20–45). Study 1 (netnography: 321 Reddit posts plus 21 interviews) is qualitative only.

codes.possible_duplicate: None identified. Table 1 reports "594 total users" (Study 1 plus Study 2), but the quantitative sample is 572.

'Fear of judgment' (0.555) means being judged by the AI, not social anxiety, so it was not coded. The AI well-being correlate is app-specific, not general well-being; reviewer should decide.

codes.sample: Indian undergraduate students; online Google Form survey; N=165 (129 female, 33 male, 3 non-binary), aged 17-22. The abstract says N=150.
codes.ai_system: ChatGPT
codes.dependence_measures: New 10-item scale from UTAUT2 items. Two factors: User Attitude (expected effort, enabling circumstances) and Intentional Behaviour (educating value, habit, intention). Even if the scale counted as a dependence measure, no eligible psychological correlate was measured, so the paper would still be excluded (no_eligible_correlate).

codes.sample: Not available in the retrieved text. The title refers to university students (Russian authors: Аникин А.Н., Басалаева Н.В., Захарова Т.В., Левшунова Ж.А., Шелкунова Т.В.).

codes.sample: 218 criminology students at a higher education institution in Ozamiz City, Misamis Occidental, Philippines, recruited by stratified random sampling; all used at least one AI tool.
codes.ai_system: AI tools in general (ChatGPT, Gemini, Grammarly, Copilot) used for academic tasks

It has three subscales: Frequency of AI Usage, Purpose of AI Use, and Perceived Reliance on AI Outputs. Only subscale correlations are reported; no total-score correlation is given.
codes.possible_duplicate: The data-handling section mentions a "final thesis", so a Misamis University graduate thesis by Laroza (supervised by Naparota) on the same sample may exist.

codes.sample: 532 Indonesian university students took part and 500 AI users were analysed (EFA n = 200, CFA n = 300). Of the 532: 305 female, 227 male; bachelor's, D4 and master's students from several universities, recruited online by quota sampling.
codes.ai_system: Generative AI tools used for academic tasks in general, e.g., ChatGPT and DeepSeek
codes.dependence_measures: AI Task Completion Dependency Scale, newly developed here. It started with 13 items and ended with 10, rated on a 4-point Likert scale. It has three factors: functional dependency on AI, reflective attitude and independent use, and regulation and critical evaluation of AI.
codes.note: This is a psychometric scale-development study (EFA, CFA, Rasch, gender DIF). No other psychological variables were measured: there was no convergent validity against depression, anxiety, stress or other constructs. The only results reported are item descriptives, factor loadings, CR/AVE, Rasch statistics and DIF. Anxiety comes up only in the introduction as background.

codes.sample: 45 Moroccan final-semester undergraduates in Applied Foreign Languages, Ibn Zohr University (Oct 2024–Mar 2025). They produced 360 English-to-Arabic translations, and 10 students were interviewed.
codes.ai_system: Neural machine translation and LLM tools (Google Translate, ChatGPT)
codes.dependence_measures: None. "AI dependence" appears only in the title. The study measures translation error frequencies with an MQM-based taxonomy (κ = 0.84). Semi-structured interviews give qualitative reports of AI tool use. No scale or item measures dependence, over-reliance or problematic use.
codes.note: This is an error-analysis study of translation quality with follow-up qualitative interviews. AI influence on errors is inferred from pattern matching, not measured. No psychological correlates were measured (no depression, anxiety, stress or similar). E5_design was also considered, but the study has quantitative error data, so E1 is the primary reason.

codes.sample: 242 emerging adults in Pakistan (mostly undergraduates in Islamabad/Rawalpindi; 68.2% female; mean age 20.32, SD 2.30) who had used an AI chatbot several times in the past 3 months. Cross-sectional survey, Oct–Dec 2025.

codes.sample: 1,295 Chinese university students with programming experience involving GenAI, recruited by convenience sampling through WeChat/QQ. Randomly split into an EFA group (n = 661) and a CFA group (n = 634). Data collected 31 Dec 2025 to 3 Jan 2026.

codes.sample: 94 Radiologic Technology students (1st to 3rd year) at the University of Perpetual Help College of Manila, Philippines. 32 male, 62 female; most aged 16-20.
codes.ai_system: ChatGPT

It has three 5-item sections: Frequency of Usage, Purpose of Usage, and Impact on Independent Learning. Items include "I usually depend on Chatgpt more than textbooks". The authors say experts validated it. No reliability statistics are given.

Procrastination appears only as one item in the effects scale ("ChatGPT makes me procrastinate less"). It is not a measure, and no correlation with it is reported. The reviewer could check whether this scale meets I1, since it is partly about frequency and purpose of use.

codes.sample: N = 312 undergraduate and graduate students from four universities in Uzbekistan (60.6% female, age 18-32, M = 22.4, SD = 3.1). Qualitative strand: 28 students and 16 faculty members.
codes.ai_system: AI tools in general (ChatGPT, Grammarly, Google Bard/Gemini, DeepSeek)
codes.dependence_measures: No dependence measure. The AI measure is the AI Usage Patterns Scale (AUPS), 15 items, written for this study, which "measured the frequency, purpose, and nature of AI tool engagement" (p. 4). Table 2 correlates "AI Usage Frequency" only. "Over-reliance" appears in the framing and as a descriptive figure (62.8% accept AI output unmodified), not as a scale.
codes.possible_duplicate: None identified.

Quality concerns: the paper names "three validated instruments" but lists four. The Discussion and Conclusion cite SEM and cognitive offloading results that are never reported.

codes.sample: 84 Islamic Religious Education (PAI) students at Universitas Islam Nahdlatul Ulama Jepara, Indonesia (population 475, intakes 2022–2025); online Google Forms questionnaire with yes/no items.
codes.ai_system: Generative AI chatbots in general (ChatGPT used by 72.6%, also Gemini, Perplexity, etc.)
codes.dependence_measures: No dependence scale. Students were sorted into "AI Dependency" or "AI Assisted Learning" from single yes/no use-pattern items (e.g., using AI without editing, writing articles with AI without filtering, using AI to outline tasks or find references, checking official indexers). None of these items asks about dependence, addiction or inability to stop.
codes.note: Descriptive percentages only; p.5: "This analysis does not involve inferential statistics". No eligible correlate measured. The closest is one yes/no item on concern that AI lowers critical thinking (81% yes), which was not correlated with anything. Even if the use-pattern items counted as a dependence measure, the report would fail as no_eligible_correlate / E4.

codes.sample: 402 Indian college students aged 18-25 (292 female, 102 male, 8 other), recruited online through purposive sampling; undergraduate, postgraduate, diploma and doctoral students.

codes.dependence_measures: None. The AI measure is the Academic AI Usage Scale (AAIUS; Chakraborty & Subramani, 2025), 24 items, α = .86: "measured how students employ AI tools for learning." The authors describe it as a usage measure: "The study, however, looked mainly at how frequently and when students used AI, not at how they engaged with it" (p. 32).

If the reviewer decides the AAIUS counts, Table 2 (pp. 17-18, N=402) gives Pearson r: AI usage vs Academic Procrastination r = 0.23 (p<0.001); AI usage vs Academic Self-esteem r = 0.08 (p = 0.098). codes.sample: 312 university students who used ChatGPT, from Universitas Muhammadiyah Kotabumi and Universitas Muhammadiyah Metro, Lampung, Indonesia. Purposive sampling, online survey (Google Forms).

It covers six indicators: preference for instant answers, excessive use intensity, reduced self-study efforts, emotional need for AI, difficulty quitting, and substitution of thought processes. Total M = 3.42, SD = 0.56.
codes.note: Only one correlate: self-regulated learning (12 items covering planning, monitoring and evaluation, based on Zimmerman). It is not on the eligible list (not self-control, self-efficacy or procrastination). Its r with dependency is -0.466 in Table 6 (p.6), but -0.468 in the abstract and Table 7.
