codes.sample: 386 Spanish-resident adult LLM users recruited via Prolific (M age = 27.99, SD = 6.08; 55.18% male); online survey; analysed sample limited to daily users and/or self-perceived dependent users.
codes.ai_system: Each participant's primary LLM: ChatGPT 80.8%, Gemini 7.3%, Copilot 4.1%, DeepSeek 3.6%, others.
codes.dependence_measures: LLM-D12-SP, the Spanish Large Language Model Dependency Scale (12 items, 6-point Likert), with two subscales: Instrumental Dependency (6 items, α=.86) and Relationship Dependency (6 items, α=.85). Total α=.89.
codes.possible_duplicate: Related LLM-D12 validations by the same group: UK/English (Yankouskaya et al., 2025, ACM Trans Web) and Arabic (AlShakhsi et al., 2025, arXiv 2508.17063). Those used different samples. This Spanish sample appears to be unique.
codes.note: Two eligible correlates were measured: internet addiction (IAT-7) and AI fear (ATAI Fear). Their associations with the dependency subscales are reported only as multivariable betas with 5 predictors (Table 5, p.19), e.g. IA→Instrumental β=0.253 and IA→Relationship β=0.265. There is no correlation matrix. Raw data are on OSF (osf.io/3b7ea), so r could be computed from there.

codes.sample: 358 Japanese university students aged 18-24 with prior LLM use (mean age 20.13, SD 1.26; 41.1% men, 57.8% women). Online survey (Google Forms), Oct-Dec 2025.
codes.ai_system: Large language models in general (the participant's self-identified Primary LLM, e.g., ChatGPT, DeepSeek, Gemini, Copilot)
codes.dependence_measures: Japanese LLM-D12 (Yankouskaya et al. 2025b), 12 items rated 1-6, two subscales used separately: Instrumental Dependency (6 items) and Relationship Dependency (6 items). Alpha = .85 and .86.
codes.possible_duplicate: Same author group as the English, Arabic, German and Spanish LLM-D12 validations. Those used different language samples, so this is probably not a duplicate.
codes.note: Eligible correlates measured: IAT-7 (problematic internet use) and ATAI Fear (AI anxiety). Only standardized betas from a multivariate regression with 5 predictors are given (Table 3). No correlation matrix. The only zero-order r is between the subscales (.613). Raw data are on OSF (view-only link), so r values could be derived.

codes.sample: 1580 university students in Vietnam (47.8% female), convenience sample, online Google Form survey, December 2025 to February 2026.
codes.ai_system: AI in general for academic study (generative AI tools); no specific chatbot named.
codes.dependence_measures: AI dependency: 5 items adapted from Acosta-Enriquez (e.g., "Are you overly reliant on AI to complete your academic assignments?", "Do you find it difficult to control the amount of time you spend using AI?"), 5-point Likert scale; α = 0.918, CR = 0.938, AVE = 0.752.

correlations.correlate_instrument: 6 items adapted from Zhang et al. (ASE1-ASE6), α = 0.902
4 items adapted from Zhang et al. (AST1-AST4), α = 0.871

codes.possible_duplicate: This is a Data in Brief dataset paper (Mendeley DOI 10.17632/2rrz65cxp9.1). The same Vietnamese sample of 1580 students may also appear in a substantive PLS-SEM article by the same authors (Pham Viet, Nguyen et al.).
codes.note: The correlations are PLS-SEM construct-score correlations from the Fornell–Larcker table. "AS" in Table 3 most likely means academic self-efficacy (coded ASE in Table 2). The positive AID–self-efficacy r is reported as printed. Critical thinking and performance expectations were not extracted because they are not eligible correlates. HTMT values were also ignored.

codes.sample: 26 Indonesian EFL university students (second- and third-year) at Universitas Negeri Malang who were taking or had completed an academic writing course. Selected by purposive sampling; 31 were recruited and 5 outliers were removed.
codes.ai_system: ChatGPT, used for academic writing
codes.dependence_measures: A 15-item "dependence on AI scale" by Morales-García et al. (2024), adapted to ChatGPT, with a 1–4 Likert scale and five components: vulnerability, relevance/performance, updated image, external validation, and obsolescence. Reliability was reported as 0.933. The paper labels it "Overdependence" (OV).
codes.note: The only correlate is academic motivation (12-item version of the Academic Motivation Scale), which is not an eligible correlate. Pearson r = -0.154 (p = 0.454, N = 26) with overdependence; Table 7 labels this variable "Frequency of Usage," which conflicts with the paper's text. No depression, anxiety, stress, or other eligible correlate was measured.

codes.sample: No empirical sample. Appendix B proposes a hypothetical RCT with about 150 medical students, but it was not run.
codes.ai_system: LLMs (e.g., GPT-4o Mini) and AI decision-support systems in general, discussed conceptually
codes.dependence_measures: None. Over-reliance is defined conceptually and would be identified behaviourally by a proposed 'reliance drill' (AI advice with deliberate errors). There is no self-report dependence scale.
codes.note: Conceptual/position paper with no data: 'this paper proposes the reliance drill... We conclude by arguing that reliance drills should become a standard risk management practice.' No psychological correlates were measured. Even if it were empirical, over-reliance would be behavioural only (E1).

codes.sample: 430 students from public universities in northern Peru (Piura 120, Tumbes 60, Lambayeque 100, La Libertad–Trujillo 110, Cajamarca 40) who had used generative AI for academic purposes; data collected Nov–Dec 2025.
codes.ai_system: Generative AI tools in general (e.g., ChatGPT, Gemini, Claude, Copilot) used for academic tasks
codes.dependence_measures: AI dependence (AID): 5-item reflective scale on a 5-point Likert (e.g., "Me resulta difícil realizar tareas académicas sin usar inteligencia artificial"; "Siento que dependo cada vez más de la inteligencia artificial para estudiar"), α = 0.925, AVE = 0.744. Adapted from Acosta-Enriquez et al. (2025).

correlations.correlate_instrument: 5-item academic self-efficacy scale (AS1–AS5), adapted from Acosta-Enriquez et al. 2025
correlations.quote: TABLA II VALIDEZ DISCRIMINANTE FORNELL–LARCKER ... AID -0.318 0.318 0.863 (AID row, AS column = -0.318)

codes.possible_duplicate: The questionnaire is adapted from Acosta-Enriquez et al. (2025, Comput. Educ. AI 8:100381), which also studied self-efficacy and AI dependence in Peruvian students. This sample (Nov–Dec 2025) looks different, but the overlap should be checked.
codes.note: The only zero-order value is the latent Fornell–Larcker correlation. The abstract's β = −0.707 is a PLS path coefficient and does not count. The values are internally consistent: r(AS,PE) = .55, r(AS,AID) = −.318 and r(PE,AID) = .318 reproduce β = ±.707 and R² = .45. Caveat: some self-efficacy items mention AI (e.g., AS1), so the two constructs may overlap in content.

codes.sample: N = 102 adults (51 men, 51 women), aged 20–40, students and working professionals from Rawalpindi and Islamabad, Pakistan; purposive sampling, online and face-to-face; cross-sectional.
codes.ai_system: Generative AI tools in general (ChatGPT, Google Gemini, Microsoft Copilot, Claude)
codes.dependence_measures: Generative AI Dependency Scale (GAIDS; Goh et al., 2025), 11 items, 5-point scale, summed total score (subscales cognitive preoccupation, negative consequences, withdrawal not analysed separately); α = .90

correlations.correlate_instrument: Melbourne Decision Making Questionnaire (MDMQ), procrastination subscale, 5 items, α = .74
correlations.quote: Procrastination −.339*** < .001 ... AI dependency was significantly and negatively correlated with ... procrastination (r = −.339, p < .001)

codes.possible_duplicate: None identified. Uses the GAIDS from Goh et al. (2025), but the Pakistani sample is independent.
codes.note: Only eligible correlate is MDMQ decisional procrastination (putting off decisions, not tasks); reviewer should confirm it counts. Other MDMQ subscales not eligible. Sign is unusual (negative). Inconsistencies: weekly-use criterion vs 13 rare/never users; MDMQ total mean 44.15 over 22 items impossible under 0–2 scoring; malformed DOI.

codes.sample: 418 full-time undergraduate students from several universities in Liaoning Province, China, who frequently used GenAI (58.1% female; freshman to senior; arts, science and engineering majors). Online and offline survey; 83.6% valid response rate.
codes.ai_system: Generative AI (GenAI) in general, used by students for study
codes.dependence_measures: The Generative Artificial Intelligence Dependency Scale (GenAIDS), developed by the authors. It has 12 items on a 5-point scale and three subscales: affective, behavioural and cognitive dependency (4 items each). Overall alpha = .91. Only the total score (GenAID) is correlated with other variables in Table 2.

correlations.correlate_instrument: Self-efficacy Scale (Pintrich & De Groot, 1990; Chinese version by Y. Liang, 2000), 22 items
correlations.quote: GenAI dependency was positively correlated with self-efficacy (r = 0.224, p < 0.01)

codes.possible_duplicate: None identified. The GenAIDS was developed in a pilot study with 150 students that is not reported here.
codes.note: The only eligible correlate is academic self-efficacy; teacher caring and academic achievement are not eligible correlates. No subscale correlations are given. Table 2 looks questionable: grade correlates .78–.84 with AA, SE and PTC; gender–grade r = .504; PTC–SE r is negative, which the authors call counterintuitive. Consider a data-quality flag.

codes.sample: No participants. The article uses a descriptive-analytical method based on library studies and published scholarly articles (abstract, p. 2).
codes.ai_system: Artificial intelligence and intelligent tools in general, as used by lower secondary school students
codes.dependence_measures: None. The article discusses students' cognitive dependence on AI only conceptually and uses no quantitative measure.
codes.note: This is a theoretical/library-based article in Persian with an English abstract, about the school principal's role in preventing students' cognitive dependence on AI. The abstract (p. 2) says: "The research method of this article is descriptive-analytical and is based on library studies and credible scholarly articles." It collects no data, uses no dependence scale and reports no correlations.

codes.sample: University students at the State University of Trade and Economics, Ukraine, surveyed with Google Forms. The total N and the number of LLM users could not be read: the extracted text is font-encoded and the digits were lost. People who did not use LLMs for language learning stopped after an early question.
codes.ai_system: Large language models (ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini) used for foreign-language learning
codes.dependence_measures: Single categorical items, no scale: (1) emotional dependence on LLMs for language tasks (constant / depends on task complexity / rarely / none); (2) whether students 'constantly need AI confirmation even for simple language tasks'; (3) 'feelings of AI addiction', one option in a question about the biggest disadvantage of LLMs.
codes.note: Text decoded by hand (letters shifted +29; digits lost). Methods p.5: 'Data were analysed using descriptive statistics frequencies and percentages'. An anxiety-change item exists (p.7), but items are reported only as marginal percentages, with no cross-tab against dependence. If that item isn't an anxiety measure, the reason is no_eligible_correlate. Not eligible either way.

codes.sample: Romanian online convenience samples, March 2026: 38 Gen Z students (97.4% aged 19-22) and 42 working adults (90.5% aged 36-60).
codes.ai_system: AI tools in general (e.g., ChatGPT)
codes.dependence_measures: Students: AI use frequency (daily, few times/week, etc.) only. Adults: one categorical item on reliance on AI (none/low/moderate/high), reported only as percentages (p.8-9: "40.5% ... moderate reliance ... 4.8%, reported a high level of dependence on AI"). The item wording is not given. No dependence scale.
codes.note: Descriptive working paper with frequency counts only. No dependence scale; only an ambiguous single reliance item for adults. Procrastination frequency was measured but never cross-tabulated with reliance. AI use frequency was cross-tabulated only with perceived productivity and laziness. No zero-order statistics. If the reliance item met I1, the reason would be E4.

codes.sample: 286 graduate (master's/doctoral) students in sport sciences faculties at eight universities in Eastern Anatolia, Türkiye; convenience sample, recruited face-to-face and online; 61.5% male, mostly aged 21–28.
codes.ai_system: AI tools in general: research and chat applications such as ChatGPT (86%) and personal assistants such as Siri (14%)
codes.dependence_measures: Dependence to Artificial Intelligence Scale (DAIS; Morales-García et al., 2024; Turkish adaptation by Savaş, 2024). 5 items, 5-point Likert, possible range 5–25, α = 0.83 in this study. M = 11.68, SD = 4.75.
codes.note: Only correlate: Marmara Creative Thinking Dispositions Scale (total + 6 subscales), not an eligible correlate. Borderline: its 'Self-discipline' subscale correlates with DAIS at r = −0.332, p < 0.001, n = 286 (Table 4). It is a creativity component, not a self-control measure, so not counted; reviewer may decide. Correction: 10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1932993.

codes.sample: Not available: the retrieved text is the NU Repository submission guide, not the thesis. Based on the title, the sample is probably university students at one university in Kazakhstan.
codes.ai_system: Generative AI (based on the title only; can't be checked against the text)
codes.dependence_measures: Can't be determined. The title mentions 'Generative AI Overuse', which may be an overuse or dependence measure, but the retrieved text has no methods section.
codes.possible_duplicate: Possibly a master's thesis in the NU repository. Check whether there is a journal article from the same sample.
codes.note: Wrong file retrieved: the 4,142-character text is the DSpace 'Submission Guide' for the NU Repository (login steps, metadata fields, CC license), not the report. Get the actual thesis PDF from nur.nu.edu.kz. The title suggests GenAI overuse and mental well-being (a possible eligible correlate), so it may be eligible.

codes.sample: 238 college students aged 18–25 in Chennai, India (140 male, 98 female). Recruited by purposive and snowball sampling through an online Google Form.
codes.ai_system: AI tools for academic work in general; most students relied on ChatGPT (85%), followed by Gemini and Meta AI
codes.dependence_measures: Academic AI Dependency SAID Questionnaire (Castro et al., 2025): 13 items on a 5-point scale, used as a total score. Its dimensions are Trust in AI, Informational exclusivity with AI and AI Literacy.
codes.note: The only correlates measured were prospective and retrospective memory failures (PRMQ), which are not eligible correlates. The study reports r = -.112 for prospective memory and r = -.077 for retrospective memory (Table 3, p. 9). The limitations section says stress, anxiety and sleep were not measured. Gender t-tests are also reported.

codes.sample: 421 full-time employees in South Korea, aged 20 and over, from many organisations, recruited through an online research panel. Three-wave time-lagged design: T1 n=963, T2 n=659, T3 n=421 complete. 52% men.
codes.ai_system: AI systems or tools used at work in general (generative AI and algorithmic systems; no specific chatbot named)
codes.dependence_measures: AI dependence: 3 items adapted from Tang et al. (2023), e.g. "I depended on AI to handle or help with work-related activities", "...to make major work-related decisions", "...to check and monitor my work". 5-point Likert scale, measured at T1. α = .811, CR = .821, AVE = .610.

correlations.correlate_instrument: General Self-Efficacy Scale (Chen, Gully & Eden, 2001), 5 items

codes.possible_duplicate: Kim and Lee have published many papers using three-wave samples of Korean employees from the same online panel (IRB Yonsei 202208-HR-2975-01). This sample may overlap with other reports by the same authors on AI dependence or adoption. Worth checking.
codes.note: Only eligible correlate is general self-efficacy; r=-0.16 from Table 2. The Tang et al. items measure workplace reliance ('I depended on AI to...'), not problematic use. The AI is workplace AI in general and may include non-conversational systems. SEM betas (e.g., -0.310) are not zero-order.

codes.sample: No human participants. The data are a synthetic Kaggle dataset ("AI Assistant Usage in Student Life (Synthetic)", Ayesha Saleem, 2023) of 10,000 simulated student–AI assistant sessions.
codes.ai_system: AI assistants such as ChatGPT, used for studying (simulated sessions)
codes.dependence_measures: There is no real dependence measure. The target is AI_AssistanceLevel, a 1–5 ordinal rating described as "the extent to which students feel assisted by AI in completing tasks". It was split into Low, Medium and High bands and relabelled as "level of student dependence on AI". The other variables are session length, total prompts, task type, satisfaction rating and whether the AI was used again.
codes.note: ML comparison (Random Forest vs SVM) on synthetic data. The 'dependence' variable is really perceived AI assistance level, relabelled. Pages 6–7: "the main focus is on predicting the level of assistance students feel from AI". No eligible psychological correlate and no correlation reported. E3 could also apply, because ML is used to detect dependence.

codes.sample: No participant sample is described. The paper describes an Android app (MindGuard) and reports only technical results (latency, battery drain, detection accuracy) and vague 'internal test cycles'.
codes.ai_system: No interactive AI system is used by participants. AI/ML is part of the researchers' app, which detects smartphone addiction and intervenes against it.
codes.dependence_measures: None. The addiction studied is to smartphones, not AI. It is inferred from usage logs (screen time, unlocks, nighttime use). There is no self- or informant-report scale.
codes.note: Out of scope: an engineering paper using AI to detect and reduce smartphone addiction. No AI-dependence measure and no psychological correlates. E1 (no AI-dependence measure) also applies, and arguably E5 (no survey data). Under the strict exclusion order E1 comes before E3, so the reviewer may prefer E1.

codes.sample: 22 undergraduate students (11 female, 11 male; 1 freshman, 20 sophomores, 1 senior) in a Design History course at SUSTech, Shenzhen, China, who took part in three rounds of classroom debates over four weeks.
codes.ai_system: ChatGPT 3.5, used by each debate team on one shared laptop during the classroom debates
codes.dependence_measures: None quantitative. 'Cognitive dependency' came up only as a theme in the thematic analysis of semi-structured interviews (Section 5.4). The only survey items (Appendix A) asked about how often students use LLMs, in which scenarios, and how experienced they are (1–5 scale).
codes.possible_duplicate: arXiv preprint arXiv:2501.09165 (v2), which is the same CHI '25 paper.
codes.note: Qualitative study: observations, interviews and thematic analysis. 'Social anxiety' and 'dependency' are themes from interview quotes, not measured constructs. No dependence scale, no correlate instruments, no statistical associations. The only quantitative data are LLM-use frequency and experience (1–5 rating, M = 3.50, SD = 0.72) and message word counts.

codes.sample: 110 undergraduate students from four universities in South Sulawesi, Indonesia (65.5% female, mostly aged 19, 71.8% STEM). Purposive sampling, cross-sectional online questionnaire.
codes.ai_system: AI tools in general for academic work (e.g., ChatGPT)
codes.dependence_measures: "Dependence on AI" (DOA): 5 ad hoc items (items 1-5), 5-point Likert; Cronbach's alpha = 0.901, CR = 0.926, AVE = 0.716 (Table 3). The paper gives no source reference for this scale.
codes.note: The only other constructs measured were ethical awareness, algorithmic bias awareness and critical thinking. None of these is an eligible correlate. Also, the only DOA associations reported are HTMT ratios (Table 4: DOA–CT 0.476, DOA–EA 0.328, DOA–AOAB 0.392) and PLS-SEM path coefficients (DOA→CT 0.233). Neither counts as a zero-order association, so E4 would apply too.

codes.sample: 305 undergraduate students in Türkiye in programming-related departments (176 male, 129 female; mostly aged 18–23+), recruited through an online Google Forms survey.
codes.ai_system: Generative AI coding tools: ChatGPT (98%), Gemini, GitHub Copilot, Claude, DeepSeek and others.
codes.dependence_measures: A 4-item "Bağımlılık Endişesi" (Dependence Worry) scale in an extended TAM, adapted from Morales-García et al. (2024), Pan et al. (2024) and others; α = 0.627. The items measure worry about dependence (e.g., "I worry my programming skills will atrophy"; "I don't want to depend on AI tools"). They do not measure dependence itself.
codes.possible_duplicate: None identified.
codes.note: Borderline. The AI measure is a TAM worry or attitude about over-dependence, which fits E1. Item BE4 ("not sure I can code effectively without AI tools") comes closest to dependence. Self-efficacy is specific to programming and AI tools. The only association is an SEM path (SE→DW β = 0.506, Table 9). There is no correlation matrix, so the paper would also fail on E4.

codes.sample: 600 Turkish adults (249 employees and 351 university students) after 41 of 641 were excluded; 70.5% female; mean age 27.62 (SD 9.57, range 18–62). Online convenience survey.
codes.ai_system: AI chatbots in general (ChatGPT, Gemini, Claude, Copilot, DeepSeek, etc.); ChatGPT specifically for the PCUS
codes.dependence_measures: Turkish AI Chatbot Dependence Scale (AICD-8-T; 8 items, single factor, α = .86). Problematic ChatGPT Use Scale (PCUS, Turkish version; 11 items, α = .88). Both are eligible dependence and problematic-use measures. No subscales.
codes.possible_duplicate: None identified. The PCUS Turkish version comes from Hoşgör & Güngördü (2025), a different study. Check for other Özsoy/Griffiths papers that may reuse this sample of 249 employees and 351 students.
codes.note: Two dependence measures are both correlated with eligible correlates in Table 2. AICD-8-T and PCUS correlate at r = .68. The Table 2 footnote leaves out the * level (p < .05). Daily chatbot and ChatGPT use hours are also correlated, but they are not eligible correlates.

codes.sample: 1142 Chinese undergraduates (544 male, 598 female; freshman to senior) from 7 universities in 4 provinces; surveyed online and on paper, Jan–Mar 2026; cross-sectional.
codes.ai_system: AI tools in general (e.g., DeepSeek, ChatGPT, Claude) used for academic tasks
codes.dependence_measures: AI Dependence Scale: 12 items, 5-point Likert, with functional and emotional dimensions. Revised from Y. Chen et al. (2025), the Conversational AI Dependence Scale, and W. Li et al. (2026). α = 0.880. Only the total score is correlated in Table 2; no subscale correlations are reported.

correlations.correlate_instrument: Adapted General Academic Self-Efficacy Scale (van Zyl et al., 2022), 5 items
correlations.quote: academic self-efficacy was ... negatively correlated with AI dependence (r = −0.442, p < 0.01)

correlations.correlate_instrument: Self-Control Scale (Tangney et al., 2004; Besalti, 2025 revision), 13 items, total score (impulsivity + self-discipline)
correlations.quote: self-control also showed a significant negative correlation with AI dependence (r = −0.468, p < 0.01)

codes.possible_duplicate: None identified. W. Li and J. Lu also co-authored a 2026 Behavioral Sciences paper on engineering postgraduates, but it appears to use a different sample.
codes.note: Supportive university climate (teacher/peer support, autonomy) correlates r = −0.402 with AI dependence. Not coded: it measures institutional climate, not standard perceived social support; reviewer may check. Table 3 PROCESS betas are multivariable, so not used. Self-control is reported only as a total score, so impulsivity has no separate correlation.

codes.sample: N = 402 Chinese Gen Z active users of the Xingye AI companion (used it in the past month), recruited through an online survey; 53.5% female; mean age 21.51 (SD 2.11); 43.5% undergraduates, 36.3% employed.
codes.ai_system: Xingye AI (星野·AI皆你所见), a generative LLM-based emotional AI companion
codes.dependence_measures: Problematic use (BSMAS-6): a 6-item Bergen Social Media Addiction Scale "adapted from social/smartphone contexts", scored as a mean; α = 0.904; M = 3.44, SD = 1.17. The Contributions section frames it as "problematic use of AIs".

correlations.quote: Table 3 Zero-order correlations among predictors and outcomes: BSMAS-6 row, PHQ-9 column = 0.36

codes.possible_duplicate: None identified. The data are openly available on Zenodo (doi:10.5281/zenodo.18279792).
codes.note: Table 3 gives predictor-by-outcome correlations only, so the BPS-9 (bedtime procrastination) by BSMAS-6 correlation is missing; it might be derivable from the Zenodo data. Sleep disturbance is a higher-is-worse proxy for sleep quality. Quality concerns: the BSMAS was not clearly adapted to AI, and the PHQ-9 and GAD-7 mean ranges (1–3) are odd.

codes.sample: None. This is a conceptual paper based on an integrative literature review, with no primary data collection.
codes.ai_system: AI in education in general (generative AI such as ChatGPT and Gemini, intelligent tutoring, AI dialogue systems), discussed conceptually
codes.dependence_measures: None. AI overreliance is discussed only as a concept, and no quantitative dependence scale was given.
codes.note: Methodology p.79: "This study adopts an integrative literature review approach... The study is conceptual in nature." Limitations p.89: "the study is conceptual in nature and does not involve primary empirical data collection." It proposes the Maqasid Shariah-Based Hybrid Intelligence Framework (MS-HIF). Its reference list may be useful for hand-searching (e.g., Zhai et al., 2024; Gerlich, 2025).

codes.sample: No primary sample. This is a narrative review that summarises published studies, e.g. one of 300 and one of 676 university students cited on p. 323.
codes.ai_system: Generative AI, conversational agents and AI tools in general (narrative discussion only)
codes.dependence_measures: None administered. The paper describes AI dependency only conceptually (cognitive, academic, decision-making, emotional, productivity and information dependency; p. 324–325).
codes.possible_duplicate: Not a duplicate. The cited primary studies may be screened on their own, e.g. 'Do you have AI dependency?' (IJETHE 2024, doi:10.1186/s41239-024-00467-0); the CAEAI 2025 study (doi:10.1016/j.caeai.2025.100381); and Jia, Pan & Neary 2025 (Behav Sci 15(10):1348).
codes.note: The title reads 'A Review', and the text is a narrative literature review and conceptual framework with no original data, no correlations and no methods section. The cited primary studies on AI dependency, academic stress and self-efficacy are worth checking for eligibility.

codes.sample: 424 students at the Ordu University Faculty of Education, Türkiye, spring 2024-2025 (82.5% female, n=350); convenience sample surveyed via Google Form.
codes.ai_system: Artificial intelligence in general (AI tools; no specific system named)
codes.dependence_measures: Artificial Intelligence Addiction Scale (Morales-García et al., 2024; Turkish adaptation by Savaş, 2024): 5 items, one-dimensional, 5-point Likert, total score 5-25. Adaptation alpha .82. Sample mean 12.90, SD 3.35 (Table 1, p. 4).
codes.possible_duplicate: The paper was given as an oral presentation at the 2nd International Congress of Integrated Social Research and Interdisciplinary Studies (ISRIS), so a congress abstract or proceedings record may exist. The same article also appears in Turkish (pp. 361-368).
codes.note: The only other variables were gender, self-rated knowledge of AI risks, frequency of AI use, and department, analysed with t-tests and ANOVA (Tables 2-5). No psychological correlates were measured. The only data collection tools were the AI Addiction Scale and a personal information form (p. 3).

codes.sample: 301 adult active ChatGPT users aged 18-60 living in Türkiye (204 women, 97 men), recruited online through social media and university networks; 310 responded and 9 were excluded.
codes.ai_system: ChatGPT (problematic use); also AI in general (Artificial Intelligence Dependence Scale)
codes.dependence_measures: Turkish adaptation of the Problematic ChatGPT Use Scale (Yu et al., 2024; 11 items, single factor, α = .91). Criterion measure: Artificial Intelligence Dependence Scale (Morales-García et al., 2024; Turkish adaptation by Savaş, 2024; 5 items).
codes.note: Scale adaptation study. The only association is between two AI-dependence measures (PCUS–AIDS r = .517, Table 6; latent .442, Table 8). Neither is an eligible correlate. The introduction says links with 'relevant psychological variables' are explored, but none were measured. ChatGPT usage hours were collected but are not an eligible correlate.

codes.sample: 562 valid questionnaires from college students at one Chinese university (591 distributed, 579 returned), online survey covering different grades and majors (p.3).
codes.ai_system: Generative AI tools in general (ChatGPT, Wenxin Yiyan/Ernie Bot, Tongyi Qianwen)
codes.dependence_measures: Generative AI Dependence scale: adapted from a 'mature scale', 5-point Likert, α=0.873. It covers 'frequency of use, degree of dependence, and tendency to substitute learning' (Table 1). The items and the source scale are not reported. M=3.46, SD=0.72.

correlations.correlate: Mental health (composite of emotional state, psychological stress, psychological adaptation; higher = better)

codes.possible_duplicate: None identified.
codes.note: No correlation table or Fornell–Larcker matrix. Only SEM paths (β=-0.312, 0.541, -0.387) and bootstrap effects. The -0.521 is the total effect from an SEM with gender and grade controls, so not strictly zero-order; listed for reference only. 'Mental health' is a composite (emotion/stress/adaptation) that only loosely matches well-being or distress. Thin reporting (4 alphas for 3 variables).

codes.sample: No individual participants. This is a desk analysis of secondary and institutional data: provider status-page incident logs, the OMB Federal AI Use Case Inventory, industry surveys (e.g., Careerminds n=600 HR leaders, Zapier/Centiment n=542 executives) and a generational adoption index built from published surveys.
codes.ai_system: Frontier LLM providers and products (Claude, GPT models, Cursor, Windsurf, Copilot) at the systemic level
codes.dependence_measures: None at the individual level. "AI dependency" here means systemic or institutional reliance, measured by uptime and incidents, attribution of downstream incidents, sector adoption counts, reversibility (rehire rates, vendor lock-in) and an equal-weight generational adoption index. There is no self- or informant-report scale of dependence, addiction or problematic use.
codes.possible_duplicate: Version 0.3 replaces v0.2 (Zenodo 21192104) and v0.1 (20763481) under concept DOI 10.5281/zenodo.20763480, so the same work exists in several versions.
codes.note: "Dependency" here means infrastructural and institutional reliance on AI providers, not psychological dependence in individuals. So E3 ("dependence in another sense") also applies, and arguably E5 (desk synthesis or commentary on secondary sources). I chose E1 because it comes first in the order. No psychological correlates were measured.

codes.sample: N = 203 users of affective/social AI (chatbots, voice assistants, virtual lovers). 201 were classified into attachment types (fearful 76, anxious 48, avoidant 37, secure 40). The paper gives no details on country or recruitment.
codes.ai_system: Affective/social AI in general (chatbots, AI voice assistants, virtual lovers / AI companions)
codes.dependence_measures: "Emotional addiction", measured with PUCAI: the 6-item Bergen Social Media Addiction Scale (BSMAS) with "social media" replaced by "AI interaction" (α = 0.875).

correlations.correlate_instrument: ECR-S (12 items), anxiety/avoidance dimensions; median-split typology

codes.possible_duplicate: None identified.
codes.note: No correlation table. Only value: single-predictor regression, Table 3 model 1 (Anxious → addiction). β 0.6759 looks unstandardised. "R2" 0.3496 is probably R (0.3496² ≈ 0.1222, the "Adj.R2"), so |r| ≈ 0.35. "Anxious" may be the ECR-S anxiety score or an anxious-type dummy (then r is point-biserial). PANAS was never related to addiction. Please verify.

codes.sample: 240 university teachers (faculty) from public and private universities in Islamabad and Rawalpindi, Pakistan, aged 25–60. Cross-sectional survey with purposive sampling.
codes.ai_system: AI tools in general (dependence on AI)
codes.dependence_measures: Dependence on AI scale (attributed to 'Wilter.C et al., 2024'; probably Morales-García et al., 2024, which is in the reference list). It has 5 items rated 1–5, scores range 5–25, and alpha = .87 (DAI).
codes.note: DAI was correlated only with cognitive load (NASA-TLX) and rational/intuitive decision styles (Table 3, p.7, n=240: CL r=.51, rational r=-.59, intuitive r=.48). None of these is an eligible correlate. The reviewer may check whether workload, which includes a frustration dimension, should not count as stress; if it did, the value is r=.51.

codes.sample: No original sample. This is a narrative synthesis of published studies: HEPI surveys of UK undergraduates, the MIT EEG study (n=54), Bastani et al. in Turkey (~1,000), Kestin & Miller at Harvard (n=194), Zhang et al. in China (n=580) and Vereau Amaya et al. in Peru (n=200).
codes.ai_system: Generative AI in general (ChatGPT, GPT-4o, GPT-4 Base/Tutor, the PS2 Pal AI tutor), as described in the studies it reviews
codes.dependence_measures: None administered by the authors. The paper only describes in words the AI dependence measures used in the studies it reviews (Zhang et al. 2025; Vereau Amaya et al. 2025), without giving any statistics.
codes.possible_duplicate: Not a duplicate. The primary studies it cites could be checked separately: Zhang et al. 2025, Acta Psychologica 260:105725 (AI dependence, fatigue, critical thinking; n=580), and Vereau Amaya et al. 2025, IJLTER 24(12) (n=200, Peru).
codes.note: This is a narrative review or position paper ("we present our synthesis of recent experimental and survey data") with no original data collection. It reports no correlation coefficients. The only correlates discussed (critical thinking, cognitive fatigue) are not on the list of eligible correlates.

codes.sample: 350 full-time knowledge workers in Pakistan (IT/software, banking/finance, telecom, consulting, marketing, media, higher education) who used GenAI for work at least weekly. Three waves, four weeks apart. 54.6% male; 50.0% aged 25–34; mean work experience 8.94 years (SD 6.09).
codes.ai_system: Generative AI tools used for work in general (e.g., ChatGPT, Copilot, Gemini, Claude)
codes.dependence_measures: GenAI Reliance Scale (GAR): 7 items adapted from Morales-García et al.'s (2024) Dependence on AI scale, 5-point Likert, measured at T1, α = .887. Items include "I find it difficult to complete my work tasks without generative AI", "I depend on generative AI to generate ideas for my work" and "I feel uncomfortable when I cannot access generative AI at work".

correlations.correlate_instrument: Rigotti et al. (2008) short occupational self-efficacy scale, 6 items (T2)
correlations.quote: Table 3 row PSE: "−.253 .184 .821 .558"; Note: "below diagonal = correlations; above diagonal = HTMT ratios"

codes.possible_duplicate: None identified.
codes.note: Check: the only correlate is occupational self-efficacy, which is not general or academic self-efficacy, so whether it counts is your call. Meaningful work (r = −.244) is not on the list. Values are composite correlations from a Fornell–Larcker table; the betas come from multivariable models. Odd: the marker-adjusted r (−.371) is larger than the raw r (−.253).

codes.sample: 1,792 Chinese university students (813 male, 979 female; 792 junior college and 1,000 undergraduate students), recruited by convenience sampling via Wenjuanxing; cross-sectional online survey. 2,258 questionnaires were returned and 1,792 kept (79.36% valid).
codes.ai_system: AI tools / generative AI in general (AI use in learning, information processing, task completion and career preparation)
codes.dependence_measures: AI Dependence Scale (AIDep-22; Wu et al., 2026): 22 items rated 1–5, with subscales for emotional, functional and cognitive dependence and loss of control. Only the total score was used in the analyses (α = 0.975). No correlations are reported for the subscales.

correlations.correlate_instrument: Future Employment Anxiety Scale (FEAS; Wang et al., 2025), 17 items
correlations.quote: it was significantly and negatively correlated with future employment anxiety, r = − 0.204, p < 0.01

correlations.correlate_instrument: Career Search Efficacy Scale (CSES; Solberg et al., 1994), 35 items adapted to a 5-point scale
correlations.quote: AI-use dependency tendency was significantly and positively correlated with career search self-efficacy, r = 0.551, p < 0.01

codes.possible_duplicate: None identified. The study uses the AIDep-22 developed by Wu et al. (2026, Front Psychol), but that paper appears to have its own separate sample.
codes.note: The dependence measure and zero-order correlations are valid. The question is whether any correlate is eligible. Employment anxiety is anxiety about future employment, not general anxiety. Career search self-efficacy is neither general nor academic. GenAI acceptance is not eligible. Eligible if the reviewer counts employment anxiety as 'anxiety'; otherwise no_eligible_correlate. Preprint.

codes.sample: 608 non-English-major undergraduate EFL students from five universities in central and western China (382 female, 62.8%; 226 male, 37.2%; most aged 19–22).
codes.ai_system: AI tools for EFL learning in general (e.g., Kimi, Doubao, machine translation, Grammarly, Quillbot, speech recognition, AI dictionaries)
codes.dependence_measures: AI Learning Dependence (AD): 6 items adapted from Yuan et al.'s media dependence scale, rated on a 5-point Likert scale, α = 0.915 (e.g., "If I do not use AI in EFL learning, I would find the learning process dull and uninteresting").
codes.note: Table 5 correlates AD only with UTAUT constructs, AI ethical awareness (r = −0.225) and interpersonal incompetence (r = 0.393, n = 608). None is an eligible correlate. One interpersonal incompetence item mentions feeling lonely, but the scale is not a loneliness measure; the reviewer may want to confirm.

codes.sample: 131 university students surveyed, 122 of them ChatGPT users, mostly from Universidad Estatal de Milagro, Ecuador (84.7%), via convenience sampling, late January 2026. Also semi-structured interviews with 7 university teachers.
codes.ai_system: ChatGPT
codes.dependence_measures: An ad hoc 23-question Google Forms survey with Likert items. It includes what appears to be one frequency item on depending on ChatGPT (Figure 3: "rara vez dependen de esta herramienta (40,1 %)... solo el 8,1 % respondió que depende frecuentemente/siempre"). The exact item wording is not given. Only descriptive frequencies are reported.
codes.note: Descriptive mixed-methods study with no inferential analyses. No eligible correlate was measured (no depression, anxiety, stress, loneliness, self-esteem, procrastination, self-efficacy, etc.); only use frequency/types, perceptions, prompting skill and ethics knowledge. If the single item is not accepted as a dependence measure, the reason would be E1 instead.

codes.sample: None. This is a theoretical/critical essay (book chapter) with no empirical sample.
codes.ai_system: Generative AI (ChatGPT), adaptive platforms, automated assessment and tutoring systems in education (discussed conceptually)
codes.dependence_measures: None. Dependence on AI is discussed only conceptually; no quantitative measure was administered.
codes.note: A Portuguese-language critical/theoretical chapter (Seven Editora eBook) about the risks of students depending on AI. It reports no data collection, methods, or statistics. The few empirical claims (e.g., '68% dos usuários frequentes', attributed to Cotton et al., 2023) are cited from other work, not original data. The full text was retrieved (pp. 1-17).

codes.sample: 478 Turkish undergraduate students at state universities, aged 18–28; 57.1% female (n = 273), 42.9% male (n = 205); convenience sample, cross-sectional survey, spring 2025.
codes.ai_system: AI-based tools in general (AI dependency among university students)
codes.dependence_measures: Five-item Dependence on AI Scale (DAI-5; Morales-García et al., 2024; Turkish adaptation by Savaş, 2024), five-point Likert; Cronbach's α = 0.795, AVE = 0.525, CR = 0.846 (Table 2).
codes.note: The only other variables were AI attitude (AIAS-4), online privacy concern (OPC-14) and demographics. None is an eligible correlate: the text sometimes calls privacy concern "anxiety", but it is privacy concern, not general anxiety or fear of AI. Also, no correlation matrix or Fornell–Larcker table is reported, only PROCESS Model 59 path coefficients (Tables 3–4), so E4 would apply as well.

codes.sample: 147 ninth-grade students at SMPN 198 Jakarta, Indonesia (2024/2025 academic year), chosen by proportional random sampling (p. 3).
codes.ai_system: ChatGPT
codes.dependence_measures: An ad hoc questionnaire on 'Ketergantungan ChatGPT' (dependence on ChatGPT), built from the variable's indicators and answered on a 4-point Likert scale. Observed range 13–52, M = 30.01, SD = 8.07 (Tabel 1, p. 4). The text does not report the items or a reliability coefficient; it says only that validity and reliability were tested.
codes.note: The only correlate is academic independence / self-regulated learning ('Kemandirian Belajar'), which is not on the eligible list (it is not self-efficacy or self-control). Its Spearman correlation with ChatGPT dependence is rho = -.276, p = .001, n = 147 (Tabel 4, p. 5). If reviewers map 'kemandirian' onto self-control or self-efficacy, the study becomes eligible on this rho.

codes.sample: N = 92 adolescent psychiatric outpatients in Tunisia who used generative AI chatbots for mental-health concerns (mean age 13.2, SD 1.1; 60.9% female). Recruited consecutively, July–December 2025, Gabès University Hospital.
codes.ai_system: Generative AI chatbots used for mental-health concerns (general)
codes.dependence_measures: AIAT-20: Young's Internet Addiction Test adapted for AI chatbots (20 items, 6-point scale; α = .888). CIAT-10: 10-item short form taken from the AIAT-20 (α = .794). Also a binary clinician classification based on ICD-11 impairment criteria. Only the CIAT-10 total was correlated with the psychosocial correlates.

correlations.exposure: CIAT-10 total (problematic AI chatbot use severity)
correlations.correlate_instrument: UCLA Loneliness Scale Version 3 (20 items, Arabic)
correlations.quote: UCLA Loneliness Scale total score −0.037 (− 0.240 to 0.168) 0.726

correlations.exposure: CIAT-10 total (problematic AI chatbot use severity)

codes.possible_duplicate: The authors' contributions say the study was the first author's university diploma thesis (Hajji Hazem, Gabès). That thesis may describe the same sample.
codes.note: Eligible primary correlate is loneliness (zero-order ρ = −0.037 with CIAT-10). Brief COPE coping is borderline: coping style, not motives. Table 4 also gives problem-focused −0.332, emotion-focused −0.326 and subscales; partial ρ not eligible. Family satisfaction and trust are not eligible correlates. No zero-order statistics for the AIAT-20.

codes.sample: None. This is a theoretical/mathematical modelling paper with no participants or empirical data.
codes.ai_system: Generative AI in general (conceptual; no specific system studied)
codes.dependence_measures: None. 'AI dependence' is defined formally (utility model, Augmentation Lock-in Premium Λ), not measured with any self-report instrument.
codes.possible_duplicate: The revision record says this English edition is based on Version 1.0.1 of a Japanese manuscript by the same author (kurato). That is the same theoretical work, but neither version has data.
codes.note: Theoretical paper: 'This paper presents a theoretical model that represents human capability using a single scalar H' (p. 12, Limitations). Sections 14–15 only propose predictions and an experimental design for the future; no data were collected and no psychological correlates were measured.

codes.sample: 466 full-time undergraduates (339 male, 127 female) from five ordinary universities in China who had used at least one AI learning tool. Recruited by convenience sampling through an online Wenjuanxing survey, Sept–Oct 2025. Cross-sectional design.
codes.ai_system: AI learning tools / generative AI in general (e.g., ChatGPT, Gemini, Doubao)
codes.dependence_measures: Conversational AI Dependence Scale (Chen Y. et al., 2025): 20 items in 4 dimensions (Uncontrollability, Withdrawal symptoms, Mood modification, Negative impact), 5-point scale, total α = 0.735. Only the total score is correlated with other variables; no subscale correlations are reported.
codes.possible_duplicate: None identified.
codes.note: Correlates are only technology acceptance, AI self-efficacy (confidence in using AI tools) and learning burnout; none is eligible. Borderline: AI self-efficacy is domain-specific, not general/academic self-efficacy. If counted, Table 1 (N=466) gives r = −0.334** with AI dependence. Learning burnout r = 0.241**; this is not academic stress.

codes.sample: 200 undergraduate and postgraduate students (100 UG/100 PG; 100 male/100 female) from four public universities in a province of Pakistan, all regular generative AI users; stratified random sampling.
codes.ai_system: Generative AI tools in general (ChatGPT 47%, Google Gemini 24%, Claude 16%, Microsoft Copilot 9%, other 4%)
codes.dependence_measures: Generative AI Dependence Scale (GAIDS): researcher-developed, 16 items, 5-point Likert, α = .91. Four subscales: passive reliance, substitutive use, reduced independent effort, loss of confidence without AI (4 items each).
codes.possible_duplicate: None identified.
codes.note: The only correlates are critical thinking (CTSS) and academic self-regulation (ASRS). Neither is on the eligible list. Even if ASRS counted as self-control, no GAIDS–ASRS association is reported. The only statistics are descriptives and critical-thinking means by group, with no SDs. Table 3 also has inconsistencies, e.g. identical CT means in two rows.

codes.sample: 276 valid undergraduate students (154 male, 122 female) from several comprehensive universities in Chengdu, China; convenience sample, online survey on Questionnaire Star (311 distributed).

correlations.quote: 2. Academic self-efficacy −0.424 0.739 ... off-diagonal values represent Pearson correlation coefficients.

Some self-efficacy items mention AI ("Even without using AI tools..."), so content may overlap with the dependency scale. Learning burnout (r = 0.45) is not an eligible correlate. Reviewer to decide if teacher support counts as perceived social support.

codes.sample: 404 regular users of companion chatbots (at least weekly use for at least one month), aged 18+, recruited via CloudResearch Connect. Ages 18–73; 93.6% US residents; 59.7% men.
codes.ai_system: Companion chatbots (Snapchat MyAI 31.6%, Character.ai 30.4%, Replika 22.6%, others)
codes.dependence_measures: Adapted Generalized Problematic Internet Use Scale (GPIUS2), adapted to measure problematic chatbot use and shortened based on factor loadings. Only the total score is reported; alpha .91 is given for the original scale.

correlations.location: Page 22, Appendix D (Significant correlations with Loneliness)
correlations.quote: Significant correlations with Loneliness (ULS-8): • Problematic Use of Chatbot (GPIUS-2): r = 0.3649, p < 0.001

codes.possible_duplicate: This is arXiv 2410.21596 v3. Earlier arXiv versions, or a later conference or journal version by Liu, Pataranutaporn & Maes, would describe the same sample of 404.
codes.note: Spearman with BH correction, though written as "r". GPIUS2 correlations with neuroticism, other Big Five traits, self-esteem and MSPSS appear only in the colour-coded matrix (Fig. 1/6), with no numbers; consider asking the authors. Regression betas are multivariable, so they do not count.

codes.sample: None. This is a proposed 4-arm RCT with a planned N = 450 students (112–113 per group). No data were collected.
codes.ai_system: AI assistants for learning (AI that gives hints or direct answers)
codes.dependence_measures: Planned only: "AI Dependency — CAID Scale (14 items)" (Conversational AI Dependence Scale). The plan also lists GASE self-efficacy (5 items). Neither was administered.
codes.note: This is a research proposal or protocol with no results. Page 5 says: "I have NOT collected any data... I have NOT conducted the study... This is a research proposal". It plans to measure CAID dependence and GASE self-efficacy, but reports no associations. Tambwe et al. (2025) and Liu et al. (2026, CAID validation) are cited and might be worth checking as separate records.

codes.sample: 360 undergraduate students from five programmes (IT, Construction, Mathematics Education, Electrical/Electronic Engineering, Civil Engineering) at a Ghanaian university (USTED, Kumasi). Online survey with proportionate stratified quotas, collected March–April.
codes.ai_system: Generative AI tools used for mathematics learning in general, mostly conversational AI such as ChatGPT
codes.dependence_measures: AI Dependence (AID): 8 items adapted from Bond et al. 2024, Holmes & Tuomi 2022 and Wang 2024. After EFA, 4 items were kept (AID4–AID7, e.g., "I frequently depend on AI recommendations when making academic decisions"). 5-point Likert scale; CA = 0.826, CR = 0.828, AVE = 0.549.
codes.possible_duplicate: The authors' earlier study, Kusi et al. (2026, Eur. J. Math. Sci. Educ. 7(1), 55–69), used the same PAQ→MLO framework with learner trust and self-regulated learning in Ghanaian students. The text does not say whether the sample overlaps with this one.
codes.note: Only three constructs were measured: AI feedback quality, AI Dependence and self-reported math learning outcomes. None is an eligible correlate. Self-efficacy appears only in theory and in a remark about dropped AID items; it was never measured. The only statistics are HTMT ratios (Table 4) and SEM paths (Table 5). There is no correlation matrix.

codes.sample: 551 Chinese college students at T1 (57.5% female, M age 19.02), from two universities. 533 completed T2 and 521 completed T3. 503 had complete data across all three waves. Each wave was about 30 days apart (Oct–Dec 2024).
codes.ai_system: AI chatbots in general: Doubao 68.2%, DeepSeek 21.9%, others 9.9% (Yuanbao, Qianwen, ChatGPT, Gemini)
codes.dependence_measures: Problematic AI chatbot use (PUAIC) at T3. This is an adapted 11-item Problematic ChatGPT Use Scale (S. C. Yu et al., 2024), with "ChatGPT" replaced by "AI chatbot". It uses a 5-point scale (α = .89, ω = .90).

correlations.correlate_instrument: Chinese short-form UCLA Loneliness Scale (8 items, Hays & DiMatteo)
Chinese short form Boredom Proneness Scale (12 items)
Dual-System of Self-Control Scale, impulsive-system subscale (12 items; Xie et al., 2014)
Dual-System of Self-Control Scale, control-system subscale (9 items; Xie et al., 2014)
correlations.quote: the control system correlated negatively with PUAIC at the bivariate level (r = −.15)

codes.possible_duplicate: None identified. The authors are not named in the retrieved text, so check for other papers from the same 551-student, three-wave Chinese sample.
codes.note: The n for Table 1 is not stated. Because missing data were multiply imputed (20 datasets), the correlations may use N = 551 or the 503 complete cases (cc). The variables were measured at different waves (T1/T2 vs T3), so these are cross-lagged zero-order correlations. The betas in Table 2 are multivariable and were not used. There are no page markers, so locations are given as table labels.

codes.sample: 800 Nigerian education stakeholders: 320 students, 250 educators, 100 administrators, 80 policymakers and 50 EdTech professionals (Table 1, p. 11).
codes.ai_system: AI in education in general (adaptive learning platforms, chatbots such as ChatGPT, grading and plagiarism tools)
codes.dependence_measures: None. The study has no individual measure of AI dependence. 'Over-reliance, loss of critical thinking' appears only as one perceived-risk category that respondents could endorse, reported as counts and percentages per stakeholder group (Table 4, p. 16: 'Over-reliance, loss of critical thinking 70 (21.9%) ... 26.3%'). This measures a perceived risk, not the respondent's own dependence.
codes.note: A mixed-methods position paper whose results are only descriptive frequency tables (awareness, perceived benefits, risks, policy priorities). No psychological correlates were measured and no correlations are reported, even though the tables are called 'a well-structured correlation'. Exclusion as E5 is also arguable, since it reads largely as a narrative review.

codes.sample: 450 academics working at public and foundation universities in Türkiye; mean age 42.42±10.37; online survey March–April 2026; participants who had never used AI tools were excluded.
codes.ai_system: AI tools in general (most used: ChatGPT 84.0%, Gemini 56.0%, NotebookLM 30.4%, Copilot 16.2%)
codes.dependence_measures: Digital Addiction to Artificial Intelligence Scale (DAI; Morales-García et al., 2024; Turkish adaptation by Savaş, 2024), called the AIAS in the paper: unidimensional, 5 items, 5-point Likert, total score 5–25, α=0.81. M=11.12±4.17.
codes.note: Only correlates: technostress (Technostress Creators Scale, i.e. ICT stressors) and work-life balance; neither is on the eligible list. Table 3 (p.9), n=450: AIAS–TCS r=.421, AIAS–WLBS r=.347. Reviewer may check whether technostress creators count as 'stress'. I judged no: it measures ICT stressors, not perceived or psychological stress.

codes.sample: 300 university students in Seoul, South Korea, all ChatGPT users (150 male, 150 female; 85% aged 19–29; 90% undergraduate). Online survey via Embrain, August 2023.
codes.ai_system: ChatGPT (generative AI)
codes.dependence_measures: AI dependency: 6 items adapted from Andreassen et al. (2012), i.e. the Bergen Facebook Addiction Scale adapted to ChatGPT (e.g., "I tried to reduce the use of ChatGPT without success"), 5-point Likert, α = 0.852. Only a total score is reported (M = 2.806, SD = 0.788).

correlations.correlate_instrument: General Academic Self-Efficacy scale (Nielsen et al., 2018), 7 items, α = 0.885
correlations.quote: Academic self-efficacy was negatively correlated with AI dependency (r = -0.116, p < 0.05); Table 2 AID row, ASF column: -0.116*
Academic stress (r = 0.242, p < 0.05) and performance expectations (r = 0.575, p < 0.05) were positively correlated with AI dependency; Table 2 AS row, AID column: 0.242**

codes.possible_duplicate: None found in the text.
codes.note: Zero-order r values come from Table 2. Performance expectations (r = 0.575) is not an eligible correlate, so it is left out. PROCESS Model 6 path coefficients are also left out. The total effect of self-efficacy on AI dependency in Table 4 (-0.106) is in different units from Table 2's r, so r = -0.116 is used. The table note gives * p<0.05 and ** p<0.001.

codes.sample: 312 undergraduate students (semesters IV–VIII) in Education and Social Sciences programmes at state universities in Central Java, Indonesia. All were active generative AI users (at least 2–3 times per week). Purposive sampling; 62.5% women.
codes.ai_system: Generative AI (ChatGPT or similar platforms) used for academic activities
codes.dependence_measures: An ad hoc 18-item, 5-point Likert scale of 'Cognitive Dependence on AI' (α = 0.89). It has three dimensions: answer validation dependency, problem-solving dependency and decision-making dependency (p. 7–8, Tables 2–3).
codes.note: Correlates (p. 8): learning autonomy (r = −0.53), metacognitive regulation (r = −0.56), critical thinking (r = −0.49). None is eligible; self-regulated learning is not self-control or self-efficacy. Quality flags: received date (20 Dec 2026) is after acceptance; sample described as semester IV only vs IV–VIII.

codes.sample: 405 undergraduates at a comprehensive public university in China (352 female, 86.9%; 53 male), surveyed online via Wenjuanxing/WeChat, Oct–Dec 2025.
codes.ai_system: Generative AI / "AI tools" and AI learning tools in general, used for study
codes.dependence_measures: AI dependency scale: 5 items adapted from Andreassen et al.'s (2012) Facebook Addiction Scale, drawing on Zhang et al. (2024) and Morales-García et al. (2024) (e.g., "I feel less confident when completing academic tasks without the help of AI"; α = 0.89). Page 7.
codes.note: The AI-dependence measure is valid. The other measures are only AI attitude, AI use motivations (intrinsic, identified, external), gender and year of study, and none is an eligible correlate. Table 1 (p. 9) gives zero-order r values (e.g., dependency with AI attitude r = .22, with external motivation r = .44), but none involves an eligible construct.

codes.sample: 205 undergraduate and postgraduate nursing students from selected nursing colleges in Mumbai, India; non-probability purposive sampling; data collected 1 Sept–31 Oct 2025 via Google Forms.

None of these is an eligible psychological correlate, and no correlations are reported. Results only give the distributions of dependency and ethical awareness levels.

codes.sample: Mathematics teachers (primary and secondary) in Qinghai Province, China; online survey in May 2024; N = 469 analysed (the abstract says 489, and 19 low-quality cases were removed); 68% female; mean age 23.87 (SD 1.34).
codes.ai_system: AI tools in general, including generative AI (ChatGPT, Wolfram Alpha, Julius, Maple calculator, Microsoft Math Solver), used for mathematics teaching
codes.dependence_measures: An AI dependency questionnaire built from DSM-5 descriptions of compulsive behaviour or dependency (refs 13, 14). It has three criteria: Feeling of Vulnerability, Concern about Relevance and Performance, and Seeking External Validation ("emotional dependence on AI tools for decision-making"). 5-point Likert scale, Cronbach's alpha = 0.95.
codes.note: Table 1 (bivariate correlations) is missing from the retrieved text. The text says AI dependency is linked to lower self-confidence and other skills. Neither cognitive load nor fatigue is an eligible correlate, and neither is correlated with the AI measure. Even if the DAI categories were treated as a dependence measure, the study would still be excluded (no eligible correlate). Note the internal inconsistencies: AI-use n = 72/68, not 100.

codes.sample: 40 undergraduate Chemistry Education students, Universitas Negeri Makassar, Indonesia; one online questionnaire (mixed-methods embedded survey design)
codes.ai_system: Generative AI in general (ChatGPT, Gemini, other AI-based systems) used in classroom learning
codes.dependence_measures: AI Dependence: a multi-item scale on a 5-point Likert scale for the classroom-learning context, scored as the mean of its items (Table 2: M = 3.07, SD = 0.70). The items and alpha are not reported.
codes.note: The other measured constructs are positive learning impact, negative learning impact, AI literacy and ethical practice, integrity risk, and AI use intensity. None is an eligible correlate. Pearson correlations are said to have been run but no correlation table is reported; only multiple regression B values appear (Table 3). So even if a correlate had qualified, the report would fail E4.

codes.sample: 561 IT students (high school, degree college, master's programmes) in India, surveyed online with closed-ended questions.
codes.ai_system: AI tools in general, used during IT practical lab sessions
codes.dependence_measures: Called "dependence", but it is a single item on how often students use AI tools: "clustering respondents based on their detailed recurrence of AI device utilization, extending from 'Never' to 'Continuously'" (p.5). This is a frequency-of-use item. It does not ask about dependence, addiction or inability to stop.
codes.note: The 'dependence' measure is only AI use frequency (Always to Never). Other items: confidence in solving IT problems without AI (ad hoc, near self-efficacy), whether AI hinders development, and AI's effect on understanding. Results are only frequencies and K-means/DBSCAN clustering; no correlations. Even with a valid exposure, it would fail on correlate and zero-order grounds.

codes.sample: Survey of 157 university participants (students, Uzbekistan: University of World Economy and Diplomacy authors). Other numbers (n=40 experiment, n=54 EEG, 16 ESP instructors) come from studies by others cited in the paper.
codes.ai_system: AI tools in general (e.g., ChatGPT/LLMs) for homework and academic tasks
codes.dependence_measures: Only descriptive percentages from apparent single survey items: "only 14.3% of students admit to being over-reliant themselves" and "42.9% of participants feel they could not complete their academic tasks confidently without AI assistance" (p. 3). No scale and no item wording given.
codes.possible_duplicate: The survey data are cited as Alisherov & Raximov (2026), "Overreliance on Artificial Intelligence in Academic Learning: An Analysis of Student Usage Patterns and Cognitive Perceptions. Presentation 1 [Internal Academic Source]". This is the same authors and sample (N=157).
codes.note: This is a short conference paper and mostly a narrative synthesis of literature (E5_design also plausible). The only primary data are descriptive percentages from the N=157 survey. No eligible psychological correlate (depression, anxiety, stress, etc.) was measured, and no associations are reported. The only outcome is perceived critical thinking.

codes.sample: 400 undergraduate students from one university in western China (convenience sample, online via Wenjuanxing); mean age 20.36 (SD 1.73); 70% male. 421 questionnaires collected, 21 invalid ones removed.
codes.ai_system: Conversational AI (CAI) in general, e.g., chatbots and smart assistants
codes.dependence_measures: PUCAI Scale: 6 items from Hu et al. (2023), adapted from the Bergen Social Media Addiction Scale with 'social media' replaced by 'CAI'. Rated 1–5, total score 6–30, α = 0.82.

correlations.quote: loneliness was positively correlated with social anxiety (r = 0.328, p < 0.01) and PUCAI (r = 0.411, p < 0.01)

correlations.quote: Social anxiety was positively related to PUCAI (r = 0.276, p < 0.01)

correlations.quote: A negative correlation was also observed between self-control and PUCAI (r = −0.346, p < 0.01)

codes.possible_duplicate: No overlapping sample found. The PUCAI items come from Hu et al. (2023, Computers in Human Behavior), but that was a different sample.
codes.note: Table 3 gives zero-order Pearson correlations, n = 400. Table 1 contains betas adjusted for covariates; these are not eligible. Descriptives: PUCAI M=18.198, SD=4.091; loneliness M=19.995, SD=3.966; social anxiety M=38.475, SD=8.071; self-control M=56.423, SD=11.742.

codes.sample: SSM 1: 300 undergraduate students (medical, nursing, emergency medicine) of the Faculty of Medicine, Universiti Kebangsaan Malaysia; cross-sectional online survey; 4 non-Malaysian.
codes.ai_system: AI chatbots / AI tools in general (generative AI)
codes.dependence_measures: AI chatbot dependency score from "questionnaires adapted and screened from the Bergen Facebook Addiction Scale (BFAS) and other relevant literature" (ad hoc adapted BFAS).
codes.possible_duplicate: Conference abstract (SSM 1, Med & Health 2026;21(2) Suppl). A full article by Tan JWD, Oh HX, Krishnan V, Neo AWM, Jaya Kumar et al. on AI chatbot dependency among UKM students may report the same sample.
codes.note: Only SSM 1 (p.2) is relevant. Academic stress is reported only as a multivariable coefficient: "academic stress (p = 0.001, β = 0.188)" in the "final multiple regression model". A bivariable correlation was run but no r is printed; a full paper or the authors may give it. Other abstracts (SSM 4, 14, 19) are out of scope.

codes.sample: 215 first- and second-year BS Office Administration students (86.4% female, mostly aged 18-20) at Camarines Sur Polytechnic Colleges, Philippines; purposive sampling; AY 2024-2025.
codes.ai_system: ChatGPT / AI tools in general
codes.dependence_measures: Ad hoc checklist checked only by the adviser. Reports only weighted means for AI use (Duration 2.32, Purpose 2.44) and agreement with positive/negative 'effects contributing to AI tools dependency' (accessibility, efficiency, educational pressure, work ethics). No dependence or over-reliance score is reported.
codes.note: Purely descriptive (percentages, weighted means, ranks); no correlations. The AI measures cover use and perceived drivers of dependency, not dependence itself. Even if counted, it fails anyway: no eligible correlate was measured ('educational pressure' is a perceived driver, not academic stress) and no zero-order associations are given.

codes.sample: 381 undergraduate students from 5 Jordanian public/private universities (stratified cluster sampling), online survey, 2nd semester 2024/2025; pilot n=60 for reliability.
codes.ai_system: AI psychological/mental-health chatbots (e.g., Woebot, Wysa, Replika); self-reported actual use
codes.dependence_measures: Ad hoc 10-item "Students' dependence (reliance) on the intelligent psychological chatbot" scale, 4-point Likert, alpha=0.895 (pilot). Most items are acceptance/TAM-like (ease of use A1, availability A3, intention to keep using A7, recommend to friends A8, perceived benefit A4–A6); only A9/A10 ("I think I will rely on the chatbot when I need ... support") explicitly concern reliance.

correlations.correlate_instrument: Rosenberg Self-Esteem Scale, Arabic version (Al-Ansari 2009), adapted 9 items, 4-point
correlations.quote: عدم وجود ارتباط دال إحصائيًا بين الاعتماد على الروبوت النفسي الذكي وتقدير الذات (r = -0.026, p = 0.618)

correlations.correlate_instrument: Rosenberg Self-Esteem Scale, Arabic adapted 9 items

codes.note: Arabic article. If the reviewer accepts the scale as a dependence measure, the report is eligible: self-esteem r=-0.026 (n=381), confirmed by the single-predictor beta in Table 7 (labelled 'multiple' but the text says simple regression). The scale content is largely TAM/acceptance and intention (E1 concern). The other outcome, digital identity esteem (r=0.364), is not an eligible correlate.

codes.sample: Swiss apprentices at vocational schools (target ages 15–19, reported range 15–39). 221 raw cases, N = 170 after cleaning (50% female). Risk Score available for n = 170. Only 84 had complete data on all three psychosocial scales; the logistic regression n is reported inconsistently as 84 and as 170.
codes.ai_system: AI chatbots in general (ChatGPT 93.6%, Copilot, Gemini)
codes.dependence_measures: Ad hoc 14-item exploratory 'Risk Score' of problematic/risky AI chatbot use, rated 1–5 and averaged; upper quartile (≥2.43) defines the Risk Group. Items cover emotional reliance, substitution of human help, and reliance on AI for decisions (items 1, 11–14), but most items are about privacy, disclosure and verification behaviour.

correlations.exposure: Risk Score (problematic AI chatbot use, 14 items)
correlations.quote: Correlations between loneliness, social anxiety and privacy concerns with the Risk Score were all close to zero (all ∣r∣< .10) and non-significant

correlations.exposure: Risk Score (problematic AI chatbot use, 14 items)

correlations.quote: No psychological variable was meaningfully associated with the Risk Score (all r < .10, ns).

codes.possible_duplicate: None identified
codes.note: Exact r values are only in the Figure 4 matrix image, which is missing from the text; group means are only in the Figure 3 image. Check the PDF figures. The exposure is a borderline dependence measure because most items are about privacy and risky behaviour. The n for the correlations is unclear (84 or 170).

codes.sample: 100 higher education students from five universities in Faisalabad, Pakistan (50% male, 50% female; aged 19–32; 48% undergraduate, 32% master's, 20% PhD); online survey.
codes.ai_system: Generative AI tools in general (e.g., ChatGPT, DALL-E) used for academic work
codes.dependence_measures: Ad hoc 3-item latent factor 'Dependency on AI (PD)' tested in a CFA: 'AI reduces critical thinking' (Q9KN, loading 0.65), 'AI diminishes the need for research' (Q8KN, 0.73) and 'Dependence on AI for problem-solving' (Q7KN, 0.70). Table 6 also has a single 'AI Dependency' variable (Table 4 item: 'I use AI for problem-solving in academic tasks').
codes.note: AI dependency is correlated only with age, gender, education and 'perceives AI as barrier' (Table 6), plus Knowledge & Usage (0.30) and Attitudes Toward AI (0.40) (Table 11). None is an eligible correlate. 'Self-efficacy toward AI' (Q1AT) is part of Attitudes, not general or academic self-efficacy. The dependence measure is also weak (perceived cognitive effects and use frequency).

codes.sample: 492 Chinese undergraduate design students from public universities in 16 provinces (47.76% female) who had used AIGD tools in the past six months; online survey via Wenjuanxing, September 2025; cross-sectional.
codes.ai_system: AI-generated design (AIGD) tools, e.g. Midjourney, DALL-E, Stable Diffusion, Canva; 80% also used text generation
codes.dependence_measures: AIGD dependency scale: 4 items adapted from Morales-García et al. (2024) Dependence on AI scale, with "artificial intelligence" replaced by "AIGD", 7-point Likert, α = 0.842. Example item: "I feel uneasy when unable to use AIGD tools".

correlations.exposure: AIGD dependency (4-item, adapted from Morales-García et al. 2024)
correlations.correlate_instrument: 4-item academic stress scale adapted from Jun & Choi (2015), α = 0.864
correlations.location: Results: Descriptive statistics, correlations; also Table 4
correlations.quote: academic stress demonstrated significant positive correlations with ... and AIGD dependency (r = 0.368, p < 0.05)

correlations.exposure: AIGD dependency (4-item, adapted from Morales-García et al. 2024)
correlations.correlate_instrument: 4-item scale adapted from Solomon & Rothblum (1984) PASS, α = 0.859
correlations.location: Results: Descriptive statistics, correlations; also Table 4
correlations.quote: Both academic procrastination (r = 0.392, p < 0.05) and academic help-seeking behavior (r = 0.481, p < 0.05) were positively correlated with AIGD dependency.

codes.possible_duplicate: None found.
codes.note: The text reports these values as r. The same values appear in Table 4 (Fornell–Larcker), so they may be latent correlations; check. The AI is mainly image-generation design tools: borderline for I2 but covered by "AI tools in general". Help-seeking (r = 0.481) is not an eligible correlate. The Table 5 betas are multivariable and are not used.

codes.sample: 174 German-as-a-foreign-language learners, teachers and lecturers, mostly from Indonesia, Thailand, Algeria and Germany (Table 1). Purposive sampling, online Google Forms survey, cross-national mixed-methods descriptive design.
codes.ai_system: AI tools in general for German writing (e.g., ChatGPT, Gemini, DeepL, grammar checkers)
codes.dependence_measures: One self-rated item: "Respondents rated their perceived dependence on AI tools (1 = very low, 5 = very high) when writing in German" (p. 6, section 3.2). Results are country means and SDs (Table 2), with Kruskal-Wallis and Mann-Whitney tests between countries.
codes.note: The single item asks directly about dependence, so it may satisfy I1. Other quantitative measures: self-rated critical thinking and German writing skill (before vs after AI use) and AI use frequency. None is an eligible correlate. Dependence was only compared across countries; no correlations were reported. The rest is qualitative thematic analysis.

codes.sample: 242 adult Chinese university students (undergraduate and postgraduate; 54.55% male) who had used generative AI for learning. Non-probability online sample recruited via Wenjuanxing, Jan–Apr 2026.
codes.ai_system: Generative AI in general (ChatGPT, DeepSeek, Claude, Wenxin Yiyan, Kimi, Tongyi Qianwen, Doubao and others)
codes.dependence_measures: Problematic reliance on generative AI (GA): 4 items covering overuse, difficulty limiting use, interference with doing tasks independently, and unease when AI is unavailable. Adapted from the 'Generative AI Addiction' construct of Du et al. (2026), 5-point Likert scale, α = 0.866.

correlations.correlate_instrument: Academic stress, 4 items adapted from Kohn & Frazer (1986) academic stress scale

correlations.correlate: AI-based mood regulation (possible coping-motive correlate; reviewer to judge)
correlations.correlate_instrument: AI-based mood regulation, 3 items adapted from Du et al. (2026) / Hutchison & Gunthert (2013)

codes.possible_duplicate: None identified. The study adapts the instrument of Du et al. (2026, J Comput Assist Learn), but that study used a different sample (teachers).
codes.note: Academic stress–GA latent r is in Table 3; HTMT and path coefficients don't count. SE is self-efficacy in using AI, not academic or general self-efficacy, so excluded. Positive affect is affect during AI use, not well-being, so excluded. AI-based mood regulation may only partly match coping motives; reviewer to decide.

codes.sample: 508 first-year programming students from public and private tertiary institutions in Pampanga, Philippines (74.01% male; ages 17–34, mean 18.94 years), surveyed October–November 2024. Purposive sample of students who had used AI tools for programming coursework.
codes.ai_system: AI tools for programming in general (GitHub Copilot and ChatGPT are mentioned as examples)
codes.dependence_measures: An ad hoc 2-item 'AI Dependency' measure on a 5-point Likert scale: 'AI tools are an important part of how I do programming' and 'I often use AI tools to help me with programming tasks'. The authors describe it as capturing 'importance and frequency of use'. They report only that all constructs had Cronbach's alpha > 0.70.
codes.possible_duplicate: None identified. This is a pre-copyedited version of the CSTE 2025 conference paper (doi 10.1109/CSTE64638.2025.11091837). The metadata gives the venue as Elsevier BV, but the paper is an IEEE conference proceeding.
codes.note: Other variables: perceived usefulness, AI trust, weekly hours, age, gender. None is an eligible correlate. Dependency is only analysed in a Kruskal-Wallis test across clusters (χ²(3)=3.297, p=0.348). E1 is also arguable: the 2 'dependency' items only ask about importance and frequency of use. Either way, the paper is not eligible.

codes.sample: 172 tenth-grade students (EGB Superior) at Unidad Educativa Fiscal Mejía, Quito, Ecuador, chosen by cluster sampling, plus 16 teachers chosen purposively. Data collected in 2024–2025.
codes.ai_system: Generative AI in general (chatbots: ChatGPT, Meta AI in WhatsApp, Gemini)
codes.dependence_measures: Own questionnaire with a 'dependencia y limitaciones en el aprendizaje' dimension. Only option percentages are reported, and the options are reasons for using AI ('Ahorro de tiempo', 'No entienden la tarea', 'No lo necesitan', ...). There is no scored dependence scale and no item asking explicitly about dependence.
codes.note: Mixed-methods, descriptive only: percentages calculated in Excel, plus a thematic analysis of teacher interviews. No dependence score was calculated. The only other outcome is critical thinking, measured indirectly through perception items, and it is not an eligible correlate. No correlations or group comparisons are reported. The paper could also be excluded as no_eligible_correlate.

codes.sample: 10,683 Chinese adults recruited via WeChat. Analytic N is 10,484, with 10,454 complete cases. The number of AI companion users (the subset used for the AI correlation) is not reported.
codes.ai_system: AI companions/chatbots in general (Replika named as an example)
codes.dependence_measures: Custom 22-item AI companion/chatbot Usage Scale (5-point Likert) with 4 dimensions: Frequency of use & emotional dependence; Anthropomorphism & emotional projection; Substitution for real socializing; Usage intensity & loss of control. The authors frame it as 'problematic use'. Items are in Supplementary Table S1, which was not retrieved.

correlations.correlate: Unified distress index (mean of 7 custom technology-outcome scales); possible psychological distress proxy
correlations.correlate_instrument: Custom composite of seven 20-item outcome scales (not validated)
correlations.quote: Raw correlations, computed among each technology's actual users ... AI companion 0.914 [0.911, 0.917]

codes.possible_duplicate: None identified.
codes.note: The exposure scale mixes dependence and loss of control with anthropomorphism and use frequency. The only correlate is a custom composite 'distress index' that includes the AI outcome scale; PHQ/GAD/UCLA were not fielded. No subscale correlations are given. Data plausibility is a concern (r≈0.91; F=139,277). The reviewer should decide on I1/I3.

codes.sample: 1258 Chinese university students recruited via the Naodao platform (942 female, 316 male); mean age 22.11 (SD 2.69); undergraduates and postgraduates; cross-sectional. 1344 responses were collected and 86 were excluded for patterned responding or failed attention checks.

codes.dependence_measures: 5-item AI Dependence Scale (Huang et al., 2024), rated on a 4-point Likert scale, e.g. "I feel anxious when I am unable to use artificial intelligence"; alpha = 0.78; M = 10.8, SD = 2.86.

correlations.quote: Pearson's correlation coefficients are shown in Figure 1. AI dependence was significantly positively correlated with neuroticism, depression, social anxiety, AI use motivations, and ACE.

correlations.quote: AI dependence was significantly positively correlated with neuroticism, depression, social anxiety, AI use motivations, and ACE.
AI dependence was significantly positively correlated with neuroticism, depression, social anxiety
AI dependence was negatively correlated with extraversion, age, and grade.
Pearson's correlation coefficients are shown in Figure 1.
self-efficacy was not significantly correlated with AI dependence in the correlation or as a significant predictor in the linear regression analysis.

correlations.quote: AI dependence was significantly positively correlated with neuroticism, depression, social anxiety, AI use motivations, and ACE.

codes.possible_duplicate: No clear duplicate. The study uses the AI dependence and AI use motivation scales from Huang et al. (2024), but its sample (N = 1258, Naodao 2025) appears to be separate.
codes.note: Likely eligible. The zero-order Pearson correlations are shown only in Figure 1, probably a heatmap, and the numbers are not in the text we received. A reviewer should read the values from the figure in the PDF. Table 3 gives multivariable betas and the network analysis gives EBICglasso partial correlations; neither counts as a zero-order association.
